To address data aggregation challenges, this paper proposes the Data-Driven Aggregation (D2A) protocol. D2A is designed for large-scale, multi-hop Wireless Sensor Networks (WSNs) to efficiently gather data at a sink node while minimizing energy consumption. It achieves this by dynamically adjusting transmission rates based on the distance of sensor nodes from the sink and by aggregating data at multi-hop intervals. Through the implementation of a media access control (MAC) protocol and the D2A protocol on TelosB WSN nodes, our simulations indicate that the protocol effectively reduces energy usage and transmission hops compared to existing aggregation protocols. The implemented protocols and test programs can be found at: http://www.dia.uva.es/~javier/works/JAVIER_COL_PROTOCOLS.

This article explores various protocols and mechanisms for energy-efficient data collection in Wireless Sensor Networks (WSNs), offering insights into energy consumption, transmission rates, and aggregation strategies. The proposed Adaptive Transmission Rate (ATRA) protocol dynamically adjusts data transmission rates based on the transmission distance from each sensor node to the sink. To validate the implemented protocols and mechanisms, tests were conducted using a TelosB-based WSN testbed. To my knowledge, this represents the initial attempt at data transmission with adaptive rates over multi-hop, energy-efficient distances. The implemented protocols and test programs are available at: http://www.dia.uva.es/~javier/works/JAVIER_COL_PROTOCOLS.

Deep detectors leverage scene context in distinct ways. This study categorizes object detectors into three groups based on their context utilization: those with no context (RCNN via input cropping), those with partial context (two-stage detectors via featuremap cropping), and those with full context (single-stage detectors without cropping). We systematically assess the impact of context across these detector categories by constructing a fully controlled dataset with varying contextual conditions and analyzing context usage in deep detectors. Furthermore, we evaluate the effects of progressively removing background and foreground elements on the MS COCO dataset. Our findings indicate that the context-free RCNN approach achieves the best context efficiency, confirming that richer context does not necessarily improve performance. Additionally, we identify that high-frequency details in the background significantly hinder object detection. Finally, we discuss several effective context enhancement techniques that could boost context efficiency in future single-stage detectors. We release the explicitly context-controlled dataset to facilitate further research into context optimization in detectors. The code for our experiments is available at https://github.com/hjy0225/Context-Evaluation.

This work introduces a simple yet powerful framework for learning knowledge-based recommendations, termed RSK (Relationships-based Semantic Knowledge recommendations). RSK enhances standard matrix factorization by incorporating edge information from a knowledge graph, improving entity and attribute recommendations. It is important to note that RSK operates by directly modifying the knowledge graph rather than extracting relationships to build a separate input representation for factorization. RSK outperforms several state-of-the-art semantic-based ranking methods on two real-world knowledge graphs and an A/B test involving live user traffic. Additionally, the framework is versatile, supporting entity and attribute recommendations and accommodating various types of relationships within knowledge graphs.

We investigate the application of deep learning to improve entity resolution within a Wikipedia management system. Our approach involves training a classifier on extracted relationships between entities to perform inference on a partially joined knowledge graph. This method helps correct errors and fill missing information, thereby enhancing the accuracy and completeness of the data. We evaluated our approach against a set of baseline methods using a live system A/B test. Results indicate that our deep learning-based entity resolution significantly outperforms the baselines, achieving a 0.83 click-through-rate lift on related items and a 1.21 lift on "did you mean" recommendations.

Incompatible transplants require pre-conditioning with donor-specific B and T cell tolerance, necessitating mechanisms to prevent the subsequent attack on the patient's existing tissues. We examine strategies to reduce inflammation, such as preventing complement activation on the graft, utilizing anti-inflammatory agents, and developing polymers with anti-inflammatory properties, with a specific emphasis on polymer-based approaches. Unlike standard control problems, tabular or linear quadratic settings, and general Markov decision processes, multi-pass systems represent a novel and significant Fokker-Planck-type evolution. To address this, the paper introduces an optimal control framework for such systems and develops the Parallel-Reinforcement Learning (PARL) algorithm to solve it. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that under specific regularity conditions, PARL achieves an root-mean-square error (RMSE) rate of $O(n^{-1/2} + d_n^2 n^{-1})$, where $n$ is the number of time steps and $d_n$ denotes the effective dimension of the system. This result indicates that, aside from a variance component tied to the effective dimension, PARL maintains the optimal statistical efficiency characteristic of single-pass Markov chain-based estimators. Numerical simulations confirm the method's accuracy and efficiency. The accuracy of PARL is also compared against other approaches, including those by Song (2017), Guo and Zhang (2016), and Dai and Song (2019). The study concludes that reinforcing historical data within the decision variable space yields the most beneficial impact. Additionally, an open challenge is proposed: extending the method to simultaneously improve both state and transition probability estimates while relying solely on a limited number of Markov chain passes.

The paper further clarifies that the optimal statistical efficiency of single-pass estimators is expressed as $n^{-1/2}$, whereas the term $d_n^2 n^{-1}$ reflects the variance contribution from multiple passes. It is emphasized that the system's accuracy ultimately converges to the optimal single-pass statistical rate.

To ensure the validity of the main theorem, the proof relies on a bootstrap argument utilizing a high-dimensional time series method. While prior literature offers only rough oracle inequalities, the work provides robust pathwise bounds necessary for the argument. These bounds may also have applications beyond the specific system discussed.

Although the work shares similarities with Song (2017), it differs fundamentally in that PARL does not rely on score function estimation, a component that can be computationally expensive. Instead, the method employs a score function-free approach to simultaneously and accurately update both the drift and diffusion components of the system.

The algebra of quantum groups offers one of the richest frameworks within deformation quantization, underpinning deformation theory, knot invariants, and topological quantum field theories. This work aims to construct a concrete realization of the quantum group $U_q(gl_n)$ within the Hall basis space of lower triangular matrices, analogous to how the universal enveloping algebra $U(gl_n)$ is represented. We achieve this by explicitly defining the matrix entries of the $R$-matrix and the $\Delta$ coproduct, which fully determine the Hall representation of $U_q(gl_n)$.

The Hall basis provides an efficient method for normal ordering monomials in free Lie algebras, a process vital in mathematical physics, particularly topological field theory and knot invariants. Since any finite-dimensional Lie algebra is isomorphic to the algebra of matrices under the standard representation, and every Lie algebra possesses a corresponding "Hall" representation derived from its lower triangular matrix form, we can construct computational libraries for specific algebras like $A_n$, $B_n$, $D_n$, and exceptional algebras. This approach has already enabled the development of libcommute (Mendez, 2020b), now extended to libquantum_group for handling quantum group computations.

To illustrate the utility of libquantum_group, we derive the 3R invariants of knots, a result linked to the Hall formulation of the quantum group $U_\zq(2) \cong SU_\zq

In multiband superconductors, the coupling between electronic bands allows electron orbital occupancy to influence superconductivity; however, in strongly correlated systems like iron-based superconductors, electron-electron interactions generate emergent degrees of freedom, such as hole and electron occupancies in electron- and hole-like bands, which also impact superconductivity. This study employs a multi-orbital Hubbard model to investigate the interplay between band and electron occupancies within a five-band superconductivity framework. By employing a superconducting electron-boson coupling scheme, we analyzed the density of states (DOS) and $T_c$ values across different electron occupancies. Our results indicate that the DOS at the Fermi level ($E_F$) is heavily influenced by electron occupancy due to superconducting electron-doping coupling with electron- and hole-like bands, leading to either an increase or decrease in $T_c$. Furthermore, $T_c$ exhibits significant variation in the hole-doped regime across different superconducting electron-phonon coupling strengths within multi-orbital systems. Crucially, we demonstrate that the flattening of the DOS near $E_F$ is directly responsible for the $T_c$ behavior observed in hole-doped Ba-122. Finally, our findings in both hole- and electron-doped regimes align with $T_c$ data from experimental $H_c3$ measurements in Ba-122, suggesting that the superconductivity in iron-based superconductors arises from the combined effects of electron- (or phonon-) banding and electron-doping within multi-orbital systems. These results provide a theoretical foundation for exploring the impact of emergent degrees of freedom on $T_c$ in multi-orbital superconductivity. Investigating the role of these degrees of freedom offers a novel theoretical perspective on the superconductivity in iron-based superconductors. We examine dialogue systems that produce multiple responses by leveraging a vast repository of existing conversations to identify similar instances and retrieve comparable outputs. We introduce a model that balances diversity and coherence by learning to combine predictions from this repository based on predicted distributions across multiple layers of dialogue. This approach, named Diversa, significantly enhances dialogue diversity compared to baselines that prioritize coherence, while also yielding slightly better results on metrics measuring multihop conversation management. Diversa surpasses baselines in an automatic preference study involving hundreds of samples by a margin of over 2-to-1. To ensure a fair assessment, we also constrain Diversa to use only a subset of the repository, comparable to the memory used by baseline models.

We propose a system for generating multiple diverse yet coherent responses in dialogue. The model employs a reinforcement learning framework to optimize for both diversity and coherence, utilizing two complementary diversity assessments: one based on n-gram level differences and another based on the overall distribution of multiple predictions. To encourage variety, we implement a penalty mechanism that penalizes overlapping vocabulary among generated sentences and apply entropy penalty to the prediction distribution across all outputs. To evaluate the system's success, we created a multi-objective evaluation suite for multi-choice dialogue that measures diversity, uniqueness, and a composite score combining both attributes. Diva significantly improves diversity across all test sets while maintaining competitive coherence, with results uniquely showing that such diverse outputs remain at least as coherent as single-choice outputs from baselines.

We demonstrate the efficient simulation of these strongly correlated systems using the density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) method by constructing an effective "density-only" Hamiltonian. Within the thermodynamic limit, this Hamiltonian retains all essential strong-correlation physics while discarding degrees of freedom that merely adapt to local density. We validate this approach by calculating spatial correlation functions and entanglement entropy in the $\times$-Hubbard model at half-filling across various $U/t$ ratios. In the Mott-insulating regime, our study reveals that both spatial correlation functions and entanglement entropy scale with Hubbard $U$ in the same manner as the number of particles. Additionally, we show that for low fillings in the XXZ spin chain, the entanglement entropy scales linearly with $u_{12}$, where $u_{12}$ represents the weight of the two-particle operator within the effective density-only Hamiltonian. Overall, our findings indicate that the entanglement entropy in both the XXZ spin chain and the Mott-insulator regime is fundamentally governed by the available space for particles. The methodology presented here is applicable to a wide range of interacting quantum systems, offering valuable insights into the significance of spatial interactions in quantum many-body systems.

**Overview:** We investigate the strong-correlation regimes of interacting quantum gases within two exactly-solvable models: the XXZ spin chain and the Hubbard model. Our results for these systems imply the existence of a "density-only" phase of interacting quantum gas.

In the low-density XXZ spin-chain regime, we find that low-energy physics is governed by two-particle clusters of spins. Similarly, at the unitary limit in the Hubbard model at half-filling, the system is composed of two-particle clusters. Consequently, we propose an effective Hamiltonian made up of few-body clusters whose numbers and densities depend on the original interaction strength. As interaction strength varies, the typical cluster size increases. Since few-body clusters can be efficiently simulated via DMRG, we can accurately simulate the original Hamiltonians even as they become strongly interacting. Our analysis of the effective Hamiltonians indicates that the Kondo interaction in the XXZ spin chain and the interaction energy in the Hubbard model scale similarly with density. Furthermore, we show that in both models, the leading contribution to entanglement entropy arises from these few-body clusters.

To ensure high availability, replicas must stay synchronized, a process guaranteed by conflict-free replication, which allows conflicts to surface only when data changes, enabling user resolution. in the interpretation of genomic variants, selecting the most accurate prediction among many is challenging due to the prevalence of noisy data. Conversely, statistics derived from DNA sequencing—such as those reflecting functional constraints—offer only a coarse resolution that does not align well with individual genetic variants. Although cross-species conservation is typically calculated at a nucleotide level, it often fails to distinguish between synonymous and near-synonymous mutations. To address these limitations, we propose a Bayesian framework that estimates the functional annotation for every nucleotide within genic and regulatory regions directly from deep mammalian sequence data. Our method infers the impact of variants by integrating sequences from over 150 human individuals with those from more than 50 other mammalian species. By modeling the underlying processes that generate mammalian genomes, we derive the probability distribution of allelic frequencies for each possible two-letter functional mutation. This approach infers the full spectrum of mammalian missense variants, including those with population-specific effects, and effectively discriminates between the thousands of potential local effects of distal regulatory elements. Furthermore, the estimated frequency distributions of substitution rates for mutations of different types serve as a valuable check on traditional phylogenetic inference. Ultimately, our inferred functional impacts for variants are expected to prove valuable in interpreting the pathogenicity of variants identified in clinical whole-genome sequencing. Galactic Nuclei (AGN) has been a significant field for over six decades, with vortex-like structures in polarization often interpreted as evidence of helical magnetic fields. Although these findings have been leveraged to constrain the jet-to-accretion disk alignment and the resulting spin of supermassive black holes, this interpretation relies on specific plasma conditions, particularly a high-degree anisotropy in the scattering medium. This paper argues that vortex-like features in circular polarization are an intrinsic property of helical magnetic fields. This conclusion is reached by simulating the propagation of linearly polarized, self-coherent synchrotron radiation from a helical plasma cylinder containing an AGN. Unlike previous simulations in isotropic plasmas, this work accounts for a anisotropic plasma by incorporating the propagation effect of the refractive index. The resulting synthetic circular polarization maps clearly reveal vortex-like structures regardless of the helical plasma's degree of anisotropy. These vortices are shown to form at various observation angles and along the entire jet axis. Furthermore, analyzing the time series of these features across different degrees of anisotropy, observation angles, and along the full jet axis allows us to define a regime where vortex-like structures in circular polarization can be used to break the degeneracy between an AGN's spin and the orientation of its jet-to-accretion disk. This circular polarization vortex is inherently generated by a helical magnetic field, meaning its presence in observations would allow for the direct determination of a supermassive black hole's spin, provided the AGN is surrounded by a helical plasma. Finally, these predicted vortex-like structures can aid in interpreting the polarimetric observations of nearby AGNs using the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) and its successors. This work also addresses the long-standing question of whether circular polarization variations in the supermassive black hole Sgr A* are caused by flaring activities or vortex-like structures from a central accretion disk. We significantly extend the work of Guu et al. (2020) on Self Critique for Conversational Text Generation by enhancing both model performance and dialogue diversity. We constructed a series of rotating stellar models to evaluate how rotation affects the evolution of very low-mass stars and the distribution of angular momentum within them. Unlike our previous models, the current approach incorporates a more intricate description of turbulence. We examined the distribution of angular momentum by analyzing the specific contributions of advection, centrifugal forces, turbulence, and the Coriolis force to the rotation profile. Our results indicate that the simplified turbulence modeling used in earlier studies overestimated the extent of convective zones in rotating stars, which in turn exaggerated how rotation influences mixing and evolutionary outcomes. Consequently, the influence of rotation on the evolutionary trajectory of stars near the hydrogen burning limit is minimal. Regarding angular momentum, centrifugal forces tend to push it outward, whereas advection pulls it inward; these forces are largely offset by turbulent momentum transport. However, the Coriolis force generates Rossby waves that drive an inward transfer of angular momentum, resulting in a broader distribution of momentum. Therefore, the evolution of very low-mass stars is only slightly influenced by rotation. Keywords: Stars: low-mass, ultralow-mass, and brown dwarfs; Stars: evolution; Stars: rotation; Stars: magnetic fields.

These structures are frequently depicted in a two-tiered layout, where each entity set is shown as a collection of vertices aligned on one of two parallel horizontal lines, and their relationships are illustrated by edges linking corresponding vertices across the lines. A primary goal in creating such visualizations is to reduce edge crossings, thereby enhancing readability. This paper examines a recent method for minimizing crossings in bipartite book embeddings by adapting it for visualization purposes. We introduce a layout that aligns with the book ordering used in theoretical analysis, which ensures the algorithm produces an average of $O(n/m)$ crossed edges per edge (where $n$ is the total vertex count and $m$ is the number of edges, with $n/m \geq 1$). Furthermore, we demonstrate that, unlike the original approach, our adaptation can efficiently render visualization previews with an average of $O(\sqrt{m})$ crossed edges per edge. Our implemented tool, named \textit{BiBook}, allows users to interactively adjust visual parameters, significantly improving the usability of representations that feature numerous crossed edges. In empirical tests, \textit{BiBook} was applied to various datasets, effectively rendering even dense graphs highly readable. The source code for \textit{BiBook} is accessible at \url{https://github.com/NoaFriedman/BiBook}.

Crossing minimization in planar drawings of general graphs is a longstanding challenge in visualizing network structures, where the visualization quality is assessed by the total number of edge crossings. While several algorithms and tools exist for generating low-crossing drawings, they often struggle with large or complex networks, and there is a notable absence of solutions for weighted edges, which are common in real-world applications. Although planarization adds a dimension to visualization by allowing users to follow individual edges, it is crucial that the added layout information does not compromise the graph's inherent structure. We present an algorithm and interactive tool, \textit{CurvedBook}, designed to leverage the unique properties of weighted, directed, and labeled edges to create visually appealing representations without altering the fundamental nature of the data. \textit{CurvedBook} employs a curved, multi-line book embedding that prioritizes edge weights and labels to maximize local consistency, while using less significant factors only as tie-breakers. This algorithm is available at \url{https://github.com/NoaFriedman/CurvedBook}.

While the impact on specific channels is well-documented, the consequences on program performance, correctness, and memory layout remain insufficiently understood, particularly regarding how noise injection alters program behavior. This study analyzes various programs written in C and Rust to assess the impact of noise on performance, correctness, and memory. The findings indicate that performance and memory address allocations are highly sensitive to noise injection, often more so than execution times; even minor changes in address allocation can facilitate address-dependent side-channel attacks under minimal noise. Furthermore, the efficacy of these techniques under noisy conditions is notably lower when dealing with vectorized or parallelized code. Consequently, developers must either avoid parallelization or ensure memory independence to maintain robustness against performance side-channel attacks. These insights into performance side channels may also assist in mitigating vulnerabilities related to branch prediction and microarchitectural issues. Additionally, the effect of noise on cache behavior and side channels is not only significant but often counterintuitive. Although performance side-channel attacks become less effective under mild noise, cache side-channel attacks can actually become *more* effective due to perturbed performance side channels. Therefore, when applying performance degradation, one must either accept the risk of enhanced cache side-channel leakage or intentionally inject spatially localized noise. Finally, the effectiveness of performance side-channel attacks varies significantly depending on whether data is accessed sequentially or via pointer chasing. Accessing data sequentially causes performance side channels to become *less* effective under mild noise, whereas pointer-chasing workloads remain largely immune to counter-noise because their side channels are intrinsically memory access-independent. Additionally, pointer-chasing attacks remain effective under very mild noise if the workload is small, and their robustness improves as workload size increases. Ultimately, performance side channels are most effective on pointer-chasing workloads when the code size approximates one page (approximately 64KB). These insights may aid in designing countermeasures and developing more robust programs. Additionally, certain techniques, such as altering global variables or manipulating the heap directly, can render performance side channels ineffective for medium-to-large workloads by eliminating the dependency between data and stack addresses.

The LHCb experiment currently offers up to 16 independent measurements derived from various decay channels of beauty and charm mesons, though their sensitivity to $\gamma$ varies. Optimal precision is achieved by combining all available results. These proceedings examine several of the individual determinations included in this combination and report the most recent combined value as of Summer 2018. With an accumulated integrated luminosity of 676 pb$^{-1}$, the latest LHCb result yields $\gamma = 66.9 \pm 1.1_{\rm stat} \pm 0.6_{\rm syst}$ degrees. The final combined value is $\gamma = 67.58 \pm 0.70$ degrees. These proceedings do not cover the measurement obtained by exploiting the cross-hemisphere asymmetry in recoiling particles within decays such as $B^0 \to K^+\pi^- \pi^+\pi^-$, nor the systematic uncertainties for both the individual LHCb measurement and the combination. However, a companion paper by the LCWF presents those missing elements. Together, they offer a comprehensive examination of the most recent measurement and update to the world combination of the CKM angle $\gamma$.

An accurate determination of the CKM angle $\gamma$ is essential for the global CKM fit. The most precise values currently stem from decays involving only light mesons, where amplitudes are well understood, although these determine $\gamma$ indirectly and rely on external inputs. The discovery of LHCb has enabled direct measurements of $\gamma$ via tree-level multi-body meson-meson decays, where the invariant mass of the $D^{*+}\to K^+\bar K^+\pi^-$ final state allows the $B^0\to K^+\bar K^+\pi^-\pi^-$ decay to be treated as a $B^0\to B^0_{s0}$ process, rendering the method model-independent. These methods have yielded numerous individual measurements, with ongoing efforts to refine their systematic uncertainties. This talk introduces the various techniques used to extract $\gamma$ at LHCb and summarizes the most recent world combination.

Such an operation is termed "unknotting move of type T" when it enables the conversion of a specific knot diagram into a trivial unknot diagram, and it is classified as "minimal" if it requires the fewest possible operations among all available moves to achieve triviality. Typically, these operations are named based on the specific type of unknotting move they represent, such as the Conway move, the Kauffman move, or the crossing change. The study of these moves often centers on two primary aspects: the unknotting number, which denotes the length of the shortest sequence of moves to trivialize a given diagram, and the global unknotting ability of the move itself, which indicates whether every knot can be trivialized using a finite sequence of such operations. Research in this area frequently examines two related questions: the maximal unknotting number achievable for any knot relative to a specific move, and the set of knots from which one can reach a trivial unknot diagram via a sequence of exactly one application of that move. This article provides a comprehensive overview of fundamental concepts, latest advancements, and open challenges associated with various unknotting moves and their associated invariants.

Knot theory, a cornerstone of low-dimensional topology, explores the properties of knots and links—equivalence classes of embeddings in 3-manifolds, particularly $\mathbb{R}^3$ and $S^3$. While classical invariants like the Jones polynomial, Alexander polynomial, and genus are well-established, the field continues to evolve with the development of new tools from quantum topology, higher-dimensional topology, and 3- and 4-manifold topology. A central theme in this discipline is the investigation of global unknotting abilities, which generalize the classical crossing number by measuring the minimal number of crossing changes required to simplify any knot into a trivial unknot. This concept has extended to higher dimensions and other ambient spaces, sparking intense recent activity. Parallel to this, the theory of local moves, which alter embeddings within small 3-balls, has seen significant advancement. Many of these moves share a direct relationship with global unknotting abilities, often sharing the same theoretical depth. This paper offers an overview of various local moves, with a specific emphasis on those possessing global unknotting capabilities.

We examine the scattering of two ultra-relativistic heavy ions, one or both of which may possess internal structure, within a light-front framework. The ion wave functions are connected to lepton-photon vertex corrections via a simple recursive relation, facilitating the efficient study of deep-inelastic scattering (DIS) and collision processes involving hadrons with fractional charges. We illustrate this with a perturbative calculation of $\gamma$Pb scattering and the hard subprocess $qg\to q$. In federated learning, when participants' data contains certain features that are missing for some samples, the model cannot extract information from those absent features. This paper examines how federated learning models can be trained despite such missing data, analyzing the resulting data heterogeneity and its consequences. Furthermore, we discuss potential strategies for improving these methods, and the discussions and conclusions in this work aim to advance the field of missing data handling in federated learning models.

Federated learning allows the training of machine learning models on distributed datasets located at different sites, offering privacy-preserving and resource-efficient advantages for deep learning applications. A method for imputing missing data in federated learning introduces a data-silencing effect, creating data distribution heterogeneity in addition to the statistical and concept heterogeneity found in standard federated methods. This study compares a proposed method with two baseline approaches across various data silencing patterns, demonstrating that the proposed method outperforms baselines in utility and privacy when data is randomly missing. However, under non-random missing data conditions, baselines may outperform the proposed method in utility, while the baselines incur higher communication costs and utilize more model parameters.

To overcome this, Random Fourier Features (RFF) were introduced to approximate kernel functions using randomized Fourier features, enabling scalability. Despite its popularity, RFF has notable limitations, including high estimation variance at low feature dimensions and performance degradation with increasing dataset size. Recent efforts have attempted to mitigate these issues, but they are often computationally demanding or depend on specific assumptions about the data. This paper presents a study of RFF and its variants to evaluate their performance and data efficiency across classification and regression tasks. Our analysis introduces a closed-form expression for the variance of RFF estimates with respect to dataset size, offering insights into feature count selection without necessitating grid searches that consume excessive time. Furthermore, we introduce Random Kernel Features (KRF), a computationally efficient extension of RFF designed for datasets with limited labels, and compare their performance, though we observe that these methods perform best when feature counts are carefully selected based on data size. In terms of performance, time complexity, and scalability, our experiments show that with adequate features, RFF and KRF achieve results comparable to full kernels and other state-of-the-art methods on large datasets, while also demonstrating superior performance on small datasets. Contextual bandits combine the strengths of classical and reinforcement learning, modeling environments as a sequence of states, actions, and rewards. These systems are inherently scalable, yet they remain black-box models that require extensive data for training and lack interpretability, which hinders user adoption. This study investigates the Shapley values of RFFs and linear models, revealing that RFFs produce uninterpretable Shapley values due to periodic feature patterns that obscure model behavior, a problem that worsens as data volume increases. Additionally, RFF values are computationally expensive. In contrast, Shapley values for linear models are both interpretable and easy to calculate. We develop an extension of RFF called Repeated Random Fourier Features (RFF2), which approximates kernel performance with linear model complexity. RFF2 is the first method to deliver interpretable Shapley values while maintaining high model accuracy on large datasets. Although RFF2 matches the performance of standard RFF and kernel methods, it offers the distinct advantage of providing value-based interpretability through these Shapley values.

Telemanometry offers real-time hemodynamic insights without exposing patients to the cumulative risks of repeated invasive catheterizations or imaging. This study utilized data from 39 single-ventricle patients (n=56 valves) monitored via Telemanometry over 12 months to establish novel, manometry-based criteria for optimal valve intervention. Two machine learning classifiers, Support Vector Machines (SVM) and Random Forest (RF), were trained to identify valves with the highest risk of sudden failure and the lowest risk of imminent intervention. We calculated the cost of deviating from this optimal risk state using a 2D heatmap, with risks of both sudden failure and unnecessary intervention quantified in years along the x and y axes, respectively. Results indicated that RF and SVM classifiers performed comparably, achieving a maximum accuracy of 74% and a maximum sensitivity of 71%. For a risk tolerance of 25%, an accuracy of 64% was attained. The optimal valves were fully filled with blood (minimum TV area: 2.1 cm²/kg, minimum TV diameter: 0.68 cm/kg), whereas intervention-ready valves were nearly closed (maximum TV area: 10.1 cm²/kg, maximum TV diameter: 2.15 cm/kg). Both RF and RF+feature selection methods proved effective for telemanometry guidance, with a 64% accuracy considered acceptable for a new diagnostic modality. However, further refinement is necessary before clinical adoption. Notably, the heatmap revealed that intervention risks increase more rapidly than risks of sudden failure as valve function declines. Adopting this approach could help identify an optimal window for valve replacement in single ventricle patients, thereby enhancing outcomes and potentially delaying procedures in those with robust left ventricles. Furthermore, the methodology presented is applicable to optimizing interventions across various medical scenarios.

This paper examines the network's response to an epidemic-like malicious outbreak characterized by a quarantine mechanism, which is triggered when attack victims notify their neighbors. We analyze attack dynamics across three distinct response scenarios: (R1) victims notify only their directly connected neighbors; (R2) victims notify neighbors up to a distance $k$; and (R3) notified neighbors proactively check their status and notify their own neighbors. The first two response types were previously studied, but we introduce a new protocol, R3, that more realistically mimics real-world quarantine behaviors. Our analytical approach involves defining the network into $k$ layers based on notification distance and calculating the number of attacked nodes in each layer for both synchronous and asynchronous update modes. We demonstrate that the mean-field analysis aligns well with simulation results, particularly in networks with low attack probabilities. Furthermore, we identified optimal values for $k$ and the attack probability that maximize notification efficiency in R3 protocols. These findings offer insights into optimizing response protocols to effectively combat network attacks.

In recent years, malicious node spread on networks has been widely investigated using models where attacked nodes notify their neighbors, mimicking real-world scenarios like virus outbreaks. This study focuses on such networks that possess a finite attack lifetime. We define the length of an attack life, $k$, as the maximum distance a notification can reach. Our results show that for $k=1$, attacks cease after a finite number of synchronous steps, whereas in asynchronous mode, the time to cessation is proportional to the network size. When $k>1$, the total attacks until cessation scale linearly with the network size in both synchronous and asynchronous modes. We also determined the optimal $k$ value that minimizes the number of attacked nodes. Additionally, we introduced a new protocol, R3, where notified nodes actively verify their status and notify their neighbors. We proved that in this protocol, the number of attacked nodes increases linearly with network density. Our findings on notification distances and the new protocol can inform research into active anti-epidemic strategies.

While most theoretical efforts to explain these findings assume that such structures arise from disk-planet interactions, confirmed exoplanet detections in these systems remain scarce. Moreover, certain substructures are unlikely to result from currently known planet-driven mechanisms. Additionally, as the count of submm/mm observations grows, so does the necessity for correlating substructure findings with multi-wavelength data to construct detailed evolutionary models for disk proies. This paper offers a comprehensive overview of observational evidence for substructures in protoplanetary disks and explores various physical mechanisms proposed to account for them. We emphasize that some observed substructures cannot be accounted for by present-day planet-driven theories. Although imperfect, these structure-informed planet interaction models are superior to models derived solely from direct exoplanet detection methods. Finally, we outline strategies to identify distinct substructures and suggest future directions for probing them, particularly through direct detections of planets, planetesimal populations, and molecular gas within or near these regions. Observations targeting disk shadows, self-emission from substructures, and dust or gas depletions behind them could help pinpoint the origins of substructures in planet formation models. To accurately constrain both structures and planetary populations, it is essential to expand the range of resolved observations across all wavelengths and the number of systems probed by direct imaging. Although challenges remain, there is promise in detecting self-emission from substructures to pinpoint the locations where planets, planetesimals, and planet-forming material may be creating or trapping dust. The detection of such substructure-driven gaps and traps in gas and dust across many systems will enable the investigation of planet formation, migration, and the accretion of solid material from planetesimals. Finally, combining substructure data with direct planet detections offers the potential to constrain planet migration models on an individual basis. Although this paper was prepared for the 236th meeting of the Astronomical Society of the Pacific, it is accessible online. Access to this version is unrestricted.

To address this, we propose an effective Dirac Hubbard model on a two-dimensional triangular lattice, derived from a three-band sp²-carbon lattice model via a Schrieffer-Wolff transformation. Despite its simplicity, this Dirac Hubbard model exhibits a rich variety of interaction-driven instabilities, including antiferromagnetic, ferromagnetic, $p$-wave, and $s$-wave (Dirac) superconductivity. We examine various single-field slow-roll inflation models featuring an auxiliary field, focusing on their ability to explain primordial black hole (PBH) formation as a source of dark matter. Specifically, we investigate scenarios where PBHs form via the collapse of density perturbations with a non-trivial spectrum, utilizing the quadratic $Q$-curvature gravity as the underlying effective field theory. We introduce two distinct approaches to generating the necessary spectral features: the resonant mechanism and coupled dynamics. The first approach, termed resonant $Q$-curvature inflation, involves a periodic coupling between the auxiliary field and the Ricci scalar in the action. This method allows the spectrum of primordial perturbations to be tuned through the frequency of this periodicity. The second approach, known as coupled $Q$-curvature inflation, involves a scalar field interacting with the scalar curvature through a term that becomes relevant only when the auxiliary field acquires a non-zero background value. Certain parameter choices in this framework can produce a "bump" in the power spectrum, leading to a significant fraction of dark matter composed of PBHs in the $10^{-10}-10^{-6} M_{\odot}$ mass range. In recent years, Electronic Voting Systems (EVS) have increasingly replaced paper-based voting due to their efficiency and cost-effectiveness. However, vulnerabilities within these systems can be exploited to distort election outcomes. A recent study by Liskov et al. [1] revealed that a widely adopted EVS in Taiwan, utilizing electronic OCR for vote tabulation, was susceptible to malicious magnetic fields. These fields could flip the polarity of ballot sheets, causing the system to misinterpret black marks as white spaces and vice versa. Consequently, if all voters intend to select candidate A but the magnetic field causes iOCR to interpret their ballots as having no marks, the system would tabulate zero votes for A and incorrectly distribute all votes to a "None of the Above" option. This represents a severe flaw, as it prevents voters from choosing a candidate while falsely attributing all votes to "None of the Above." The impact of such an attack scales with the number of participants; for instance, in a election with 100 candidates and 10,000 voters, a successful attack could theoretically grant zero valid votes to every candidate while attributing all 100,000 votes to "None of the Above." To effectively manage vast models, researchers have developed specialized frameworks, with Megatron-LM serving as a prominent example for its methods in training, evaluation, and inference. Inference, however, presents unique challenges due to the extensive memory requirements for storing activations during the processing of long sequences. We introduce Magenta-LM, a extension of Megatron-LM designed for handling ultra-long sequences exceeding tens of thousands of tokens. Our experiments utilizing a 1.6 trillion parameter model demonstrate that Magenta-LM can process and generate sequences up to 409,600 tokens while maintaining competitive exact match scores. Furthermore, our analysis of inference memory consumption reveals that the model can utilize almost its entire 1.6 trillion parameters to store activations, enabling the efficient handling of such extraordinary sequence lengths. The code for Magenta-LM is accessible at https://github.com/Alpxe/Magenta-LM.

We investigate the maximum possible length of sequences feasible with various inference algorithms, memory configurations, and model sizes. Our findings indicate that even with optimized exact match algorithms like our proposed LongAttention, only models smaller than 7 billion parameters can theoretically handle 102,400-token sequences when only CPU memory is available. In contrast, handling 409,600-token sequences is practically impossible for models exceeding 130 billion parameters under these constraints. To facilitate longer sequence processing, models would need to be significantly larger. Additionally, we evaluate the performance of Magenta-LM on four classification benchmarks known for very long inputs: DBQA (~2,000 tokens), ReAL (~2,600 tokens), Convolutional Long Story Understanding (up to ~150,000 tokens), and a generated dataset of artificially lengthened inputs. Results from both training and inference phases confirm Magenta-LM's capability to manage these exceptional lengths, often yielding surprisingly high exact match scores. Our evaluations cover models ranging from 300 million to 1.6 trillion parameters, covering all training, evaluation, and inference stages. The source code for creating these long datasets and for Magenta-LM is available online.

This paper presents a novel deep learning framework for speech enhancement that integrates a comprehensive attention mechanism into a bidirectional sequence-to-sequence approach. For accurate speech recognition, it is essential to predict the current speech frame utilizing both previous and subsequent contexts. While Baselini et al. (Interspeech 2019) initially proposed an attention mechanism for unidirectional feature alignment, its application to speech recognition and synthesis remains limited. This work extends that idea to bidirectional attention, enabling current frame prediction through features from both preceding and following frames. We further enhance the mechanism's effectiveness by adding an intermediate layer that fuses latent information from multiple time steps. Consequently, the proposed method achieves more precise feature alignment and lower error rates compared to existing techniques. Experimental results confirm the superiority of our approach across various decoders and tasks, and the code is available at https://github.com/lshhuang/Speech-Enhancement.

Speech recognition systems typically process only past features via unidirectional networks like LSTMs, often yielding suboptimal accuracy. To address this, we propose an intermediate bidirectional attention mechanism for speech recognition and synthesis. This innovation extends the work of Baselini et al. (Interspeech 2019) by allowing the prediction of the current speech frame through features from both preceding and succeeding frames. Additionally, we improve the mechanism by fusing latent information from several time steps. Our results indicate that this bidirectional approach outperforms existing methods across multiple decoders and tasks, effectively proving the necessity of incorporating future features for accurate speech recognition.

Speech recognition systems usually utilize a unidirectional neural network, such as an LSTM, to map acoustic features to characters or words, predicting the current frame based solely on past observations. This paper investigates whether incorporating future features beyond the current frame can further improve recognition accuracy. Light harvesting in photosynthetic organisms involves capturing photons and directing their energy into special reaction center chlorophylls for use in electron transfer reactions. Although this process is highly efficient, particularly in complex organisms, understanding its mechanism has been difficult. Previous research has explained the process using a random walk model, but this lacks a fundamental physical basis. We utilize a symmetric three-site model to illustrate the fundamental physics of light harvesting. Although symmetric environments cause energy trapping to take a random walk path, we find that slight symmetry breaking can lead to 100% energy trapping probability. This corresponds to the well-known phenomenon of super-radiance, where symmetry breaking alters the decay of dark states. Thus, both random walk and straight path energy transfer can be understood from a fundamental perspective, with the appropriate model dependent on the symmetry of energy levels and site couplings.

In open quantum systems, environmental noise typically causes wavefunction collapse to random pure states, a process known as decoherence. However, when multiple quantum systems interact with a shared environment, their collective entanglement can protect them from noise, a phenomenon called collective decoherence. This study examines the relationship between random walk energy transfer and the motion of an excitation on a graph. Although the probability of finding an excited site on a symmetric graph evolves via random walk, the squared amplitudes of the wavefunction exhibit persistent oscillations. To achieve energy transfer equivalent to a random walk, it is necessary to eliminate the coherent oscillations of all components of the wavefunction.

By systematically varying key parameters such as solar luminosity, land-sea distribution, topography, and surface boundary conditions, we explore diverse climate configurations. These atomic simulations would reproduce the Kim-McCoy statistics, which arise when pairs of bosons are generated from the vacuum at multiple distinct rates. This process is mathematically equivalent to holologic logic gates acting on pairs of fermions. Consequently, our proposal allows for the logarithmic suppression of detection probabilities at coincident events— a hallmark of fermionic pair production— to be observed directly in bosonic systems. This effect represents the fundamental distinction between fermions and bosons when considering pairwise production from the vacuum. Furthermore, our scheme is feasible within current technological capabilities in the manipulation of ultracold atomic ensembles and could find applications in quantum sensing and sampling. A similar approach might also be relevant for certain superconducting systems.

Although any two identical ultracold atoms naturally experience an effective interaction, engineering an effect analogous to fermionization— where two interacting bosons behave as if they are non-interacting— requires a specific formulation. We demonstrate that the effective interaction between two localized bosons, which is a combination of logarithmic and power-law terms with an exponent of $2\nu$, can be engineered by appropriately deforming the radial potential $V(r)$ that confines them. This requires $\nu$ to take on a rational value. The non-interacting behavior of the two bosons can be achieved if the deformed interaction term dominates. We suggest that this counter-intuitive setup could be realized using an optical dipole trap with atomic samples. As a result, the Fermi-Dirac distribution can emerge from the dynamics of two otherwise interacting bosons. This phenomenon may be utilized to encode non-interacting fermionic states within weakly interacting bosons, potentially offering advantages in quantum computing and other areas.

We examine the quantum phase transition (QPT) occurring in a one-dimensional chain of bosons weakly coupled to two external dark atomic modes. This configuration is mathematically equivalent to a system of two non-interacting fermions. By measuring the $n$-th order correlation functions of the bosonic system, which can be done using standard cold-atom techniques, one can effectively observe the Fermi sea of two non-interacting fermions. Specifically, the ground state and certain excited states of the two-fermion system display a power-law scaling of their correlation functions at zero temperature. In contrast, the corresponding QPT for the two-fermion system is characterized by logarithmic correlation functions. We

The next major step involves scaling up the number of qubits and implementing scalable quantum control and readout techniques, which require precise modulation of hyperfine interactions to maneuver qubit states. While previous attempts to achieve this typically involved applying microwave-frequency tones to drive transitions between spin states separated by two flip-flop energies, these efforts have so far failed to generate the expected multi-qubit dynamics. This state is achieved by applying a uniaxial strain along the $X$ axis ($\parallel$ to the $AB$ sublattice bond) within a nanoband structure. In 5G networks, joint power control and user scheduling is essential for maximizing spectral efficiency and overall system throughput. We propose a novel cross-layer framework where power control is formulated as a non-cooperative game and scheduling is determined via cross-layer feedback. Specifically, each base station selects downlink users and target SINR values for the set of cell users achieving maximum throughput, considering current uplink and downlink throughput and available transmit power in both directions. Base stations exchange only the number of schedulable users from the opposite link, requiring no knowledge of transmit power, channel conditions, or standard deviations of interference and throughput. This method is fully distributed, with a low complexity of $O(N)$, where $N$ is the total user count, and remains efficient regardless of network size. Under symmetric TDD settings with balanced traffic, the algorithm remains distributed and requires no power information, though it does rely on a least-squares based cross-layer feedback mechanism for asymmetry. Simulations confirm that the proposed method delivers comparable or superior performance to other methods across both symmetric and asymmetric scenarios, even when exchange information is randomly distributed.

The Hall anomaly refers to deviations from the linear dependence of the Hall resistivity on current density. This letter demonstrates that such behavior arises from a fundamental property of two-dimensional (2D) charged gases when their filling factors are close to half-integer values. This insight serves as a crucial stepping stone for reconstructing the Mott rule for 2D superconductivity. Ultimately, the fundamental nature of charged excitations in a magnetic field within the resolved vortex core of type-II superconductors can be deduced from measurable macroscopic phenomena. The proposed argument relies on standard principles of quantum mechanics and statistical physics.

In type-II superconductors under a magnetic field, the resistance vs. temperature curve typically displays a "knee" where resistance ceases to drop linearly with rising temperature; this point corresponds to the drag of the vortex lattice. While various models have been proposed to explain the associated Hall anomaly (a non-linear resistance component relative to the squared magnetic field), there has long been a lack of fundamental understanding of both its presence and its magnitude. This work offers such a foundational perspective. Specifically, it notes that in the vortex-liquid state, the Hall anomaly emerges from the general properties of 2D charged gases near a half-integer filling factor. This "knee" reflects the intrinsic behavior of the normal metal core inside a vortex lattice. The Kohn-Luttinger effect explains the "knee" in resistance, whereas the Wigner crystal effect accounts for the Hall anomaly. This perspective provides a fundamental basis for the Kohn-Luttinger effect in the context of the Hall anomaly. Consequently, the magnitude of the anomaly is determined by the probability of finding a 2D hole gas with a filling factor near a half-integer value among the vortex lines. This fundamental approach implies a "saw-tooth" dependence of transverse resistivity on the squared magnetic field. Although the resulting roughness of the resistance vs. temperature curve can be smoothed out, the fundamental approach offers a method to estimate its magnitude.

This study examines the temperature dependence of second- to fourth-order (factorial) cumulants of the order parameter by employing the parametric representation of the three-dimensional Ising model, which shares the same universality class as Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD). Results indicate that at the critical temperature, normalized cumulants remain independent of the external magnetic field, establishing a fixed point in their temperature evolution. Monte Carlo simulations of finite-size systems confirm that this fixed point behavior persists for charged matter. Furthermore, this phenomenon is observed at the trajectory of the QCD critical point within a fireball of finite size. The fourth-order cumulant of the order parameter exhibits a maximum at the critical point along the QCD critical trajectory, a feature that could help locate the critical point in experimental data on charge multiplicity distributions. Additionally, the factorial cumulant of the total number of particles shows a minimum along the same trajectory. These (normalized) cumulants of the order parameter and total particle number along the critical trajectory serve as universal signatures of criticality in QCD. It is suggested that the behavior of these thermodynamic quantities along the critical trajectory offers a robust method for determining the critical point of charged matter.

Introduction

The discovery of a phase transition in the early universe linked to the formation of quark matter and its critical point is connected to the matter/antimatter asymmetry. This process is governed by the $B-L$ symmetry, where $B$ and $L$ represent baryon number and lepton number, respectively. In the high-temperature environment of heavy-ion collisions, it is feasible to access the critical point of quark matter. Therefore, identifying the critical point of quark matter through these experiments is of significant importance.

Recent years have seen substantial progress in tracing the phase diagram of QCD and pinpointing its critical point. The sole confirmed phase transition in QCD is the chiral symmetry restoration transition. Employing the parametric method to investigate the phase transition and its critical point within the universality class of QCD is of fundamental significance. This critical point is characterized by specific fluctuations of the total particle number, denoted as $\sigma_N$. Within the critical region, these fluctuations display distinct behavior along the critical trajectory of the second-order phase transition. This phenomenon provides a means to determine the critical point of QCD through measurements of total multiplicity in heavy-ion collisions. The Kauffman bracket $\brf{L}$ of a link $L$ residing in the 3-ball is defined with coefficients in the ring $\Z[q^{\pm 1}]$. It is well-established that the specializations $\brf{L}(q=0)$ and $\brf{L}(q=i)$ correspond to the Kauffman semigroup and the fundamental group of the complement of $L$, respectively. This paper introduces the tord bracket, an invariant for links in the thickened torus (the 2-torus multiplied by the interval) that shares these pivotal properties with the Kauffman bracket. Specifically, the tord bracket evaluated at $q=0$ and $q=i$ yields the torus bracket and the fundamental group of a link's complement, respectively. However, unlike the Kauffman bracket, the tord invariant is not necessarily integral. We illustrate the utility of the tord bracket through several examples.

Proton-nucleus collisions at the LHC have enabled the measurement of various hard-scattering processes involving heavy quarks. This note summarizes the experimental evidence for top quark production, which has been quantified through several metrics. This includes the isolation of top quarks, the rapidity distribution of di-top quark events, and the resulting production cross section.

Top quarks are fundamental components of the Standard Model, and their presence in proton-nucleus collisions offers a unique window into both the mechanism of their generation and the internal structure of the nucleon. Recent advances in experimental data and theoretical models have facilitated the measurement of single-top quark cross sections, as well as the quick and central rapidity distributions for top quark pairs. These measurements yield a lower (higher) quick (central) density profile than previously suggested.

Top quarks, fundamental constituents of the Standard Model, have been produced in proton-nucleus collisions at the LHC. This letter presents a measurement of the rapidity distribution for events with two top quarks, along with the corresponding cross section.

Documentary evidence indicates that approximately 80% of T2SQL parsing errors result from incorrect value filling, highlighting value filling as a critical yet frequently neglected aspect in current research. Although existing zero-shot semantic parsing models can generate syntactically valid SQL, the values they produce are often incorrect, misleading, or unnecessary. Our proposed ValueFill framework introduces two value filling strategies to automate the supplementation of missing database contents within synthesized SQL, thereby enhancing the model's practicality and utility.

We present the second value filling approach, "FillByExample," which leverages the original parsed query and a result sample from the corresponding database to determine where and how to fill in the contents. To automatically locate where documentary evidence can be applied, we identify the `WHERE` clause as the primary target, utilizing the evidence-based parsing technique described in Section 3.3. Furthermore, we implement two filtering strategies to remove redundant information from the filled SQL and ensure compliance with database constraints.

Section 4 provides an in-depth analysis of the value filling results, showing that our framework successfully fills approximately 15% of missing database contents while accurately removing about 12% of unnecessary values. We also provide specific analysis on value formats, filtering strategies, and other related factors.

In Section 5, we discuss the limitations of our framework and outline potential directions for future improvements.

The proposed framework significantly improves execution accuracy and exact set match accuracy for queries where database contents are absent, as it successfully fills approximately 15% of these missing values. However, our value filling capability is limited to `SELECT` and `WHERE` clauses, which means queries involving other types of database columns cannot have their values filled. To address this, future work could incorporate documentary evidence-based parsing to extend value filling support to other SQL clauses.

the complex dynamics of quantum many-body systems that are otherwise computationally intractable. However, these methods are constrained by the "hydrodynamic instability," which causes hydrodynamic shocks and invalidates the hydrodynamic approximation. This limitation has been particularly significant in applications involving quantum information, as it prevented the capture of phenomena such as entanglement fragmentation. This study demonstrates that injecting entanglement into the system through an initial state or boundary conditions stabilizes both long-time entanglement fragmentation and hydrodynamic shocks within the framework of weakly correlated dynamical mean-field theory. We derive a novel master equation for quantum information dynamics that is free of hydrodynamic instabilities. This equation, termed the weakly correlated dynamical Keldysh-Schwinger equation, accurately models the fragmentation of total and bipartite entanglement. Its formulation ensures applicability to a broad spectrum of quantum many-body systems, offering new avenues for investigating quantum phase transitions, scrambling, and other complex phenomena. In the context of isolated quantum many-body systems, we establish that initial state fragmentation divides the total entanglement among disjoint intervals, a discovery that appears counterintuitive compared to typical bulk quantum many-body dynamics. Finally, our work reveals that even minimal amounts of mutual information between the environment and a subsystem are sufficient to stabilize hydrodynamic shocks. This system exhibits a "critical" amount of mutual information, marking a phase transition where the transition time is non-universal and governed by a newly identified universal ratio of two entanglement dynamics coefficients. This confirms the existence of a "fixed point" in the otherwise unstable landscape of hydrodynamics, enabling the reliable study of quantum information dynamics, including fragmentation, in weakly correlated many-body systems. The findings also suggest implications for closed quantum systems weakly coupled to nonthermal baths. The study is based on the extended self-consistent phase-space action approximation.

Introduction

Understanding the time evolution of isolated quantum many-body systems is essential for advancing both fundamental physics and the development of quantum technologies. While exact simulations of quantum dynamics are often limited to small systems, hydrodynamics serves as a powerful tool for analyzing larger quantum many-body systems that lack other solvable methods. Despite its utility, standard hydrodynamic descriptions are susceptible to shocks and other singularities known as hydrodynamic instabilities. Although these instabilities are well-documented in classical hydrodynamics, their implications for quantum information dynamics—such as scrambling, entanglement fragmentation, and the emergence of nonthermal fixed points—have not been adequately explored. Temporal action detection aims to find start and end times for actions using amortized frame-level representations aligned with positive references via attention. This method typically suffers from overfitting to training data, particularly when references are slightly modified, and requires computationally intensive attention operations. We propose a contrastive learning-based approach to replace overfitting attention with invertible generalization for temporal boundary prediction. By learning to generalize to partially seen categories and partially labeled videos, our method improves detection performance in scenarios where recent approaches can only achieve partial generalization.

However, these attention mechanisms often overfit to specific references, limiting generalization to only partially seen categories and partially labeled videos. We introduce SS-TEMP, which learns to generalize to both fully and partially seen categories and labels through contrastive learning. Specifically, we eliminate the need for references for temporal boundary prediction by predicting prototypes through contrastive alignment with self-supervised features. Consequently, our model achieves state-of-the-art performance on several benchmarks while improving generalization to problems where recent methods are restricted to partial generalization.

This study examines these methods from the lens of the Inductive Bias Generalization Hypothesis (IBGH), which posits that a model's training data requirements reflect its inductive biases and that biases stronger than the i.i.d. assumption enhance both performance and data needs simultaneously. We test this across three pretrained models—ResNet-50, EfficientNet-B0, and ViT-Tiny/21—evaluating their generalization gaps (defined as performance loss relative to training data decrease) under various data reduction strategies. Notably, a prolate 0+ excitation was found at a surprisingly high energy of 3461 keV, with a collective 2+ state situated 286 keV above it; this marks the first such observation in Ni isotopes. Approximately half a century ago, Donsker and Varadhan established a link between the probabilistic framework of random walks on $\mathbb{Z}^d$ and the functional analytic properties of an associated family of operators on $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z}^d)$. In this paper, we generalize their results to a specific class of non-homogeneous random walks on $\mathbb{Z}^d$ by utilizing a related but distinct operator family. We demonstrate the existence of a probability measure that acts as an eigenvector with eigenvalue 1 for a subset of this class, termed locally zero-mean random walks. Furthermore, we prove that, under additional conditions, the environment seen by such a random walk forms a stationary process. Leveraging algebraic properties inherent to probability theory and graph structures, we integrate model definition with inference processes. This unified approach enables the efficient, simultaneous execution of both tasks, even across distributed and heterogeneous systems. We have implemented this method using the Probabilistic Computing Language (PCL), a subset of first-order logic designed for defining and performing exact inferences, such as computing marginals or maximum a posteriori configurations, for Markov and factor graphs. Informed by real-world applications, our design specification for PCL outlines a path toward an integrated model of graph-based definition and exact inference. We demonstrate that this methodology is versatile, supporting applications ranging from traditional markov random fields and dynamic Bayesian networks to more complex structures like those found in structured prediction and coding theory. Furthermore, the technique is general enough to handle data inconsistencies and introduce novel, efficient algorithms for solving systems of underdetermined linear systems over arbitrary finite fields. The paper concludes with a survey of potential future directions. We provide implementations of the proposed techniques and the PCL for both sequential execution and distributed environments, including heterogeneous ones. These implementations are accessible via the Model Inference Kernel (MIK), available at https://github.com/MIK-DistributedComputing/MIK. We also present an API, the Probabilistic Computing API (PCAPI), which allows PCL to function as a drop-in replacement for standard graphical model representations such as Hailog and FactorGraphs. We specifically illustrate that MCABC, a sophisticated algorithm for performing Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling, operates seamlessly as a drop-in replacement when executed through our implementation of PCL. Additionally, the PCAPI supports executing MCMC sampling for up to a thousand years without accumulating floating-point errors—a critical requirement for certain chromosomal dating problems that current state-of-the-art implementations cannot handle. The API is available at https://github.com/MIK-DistributedComputing/PCAPI. Our implementations address both single-machine and distributed, heterogeneous scenarios. We demonstrate that the system is practical and scalable, successfully handling data sets too large for main memory in the MCABC implementation and marking random field sampling as a previously unsolved problem. Additionally, the implementations offer significant speed advantages over state-of-the-art methods, reducing execution times from days to minutes for certain chromosomal dating tasks. We note that the PCAPI relies on the underdetermined linear system solver developed by the authors, which lacks the consistency issues present in current state-of-the-art solutions. This abrupt thickening causes particles to aggregate into thick layers that obstruct flow, a critical factor in the processing of thick pastes. In this study, we investigate these abrupt rheological changes using particle-tracking methods with particle diameters of 150 and 300 micrometers within a dense, monodisperse layer. Our findings show that the thick particle clusters observed in macroscopic rheology measurements consist of individual particles moving in coordinated groups. The size of these clusters increases with applied stress, while the friction between particles and the substrate decreases. By linking these microscopic dynamics to the macroscopic shear jaming transition, we show that these clusters emerge from particle motion characterized by a directed random walk. This characterization is particularly evident at lower stress levels, where the walk dimension increases as the system approaches the jamming transition. Finally, we confirm that the microscopic shear jaming transition is monodisperse regardless of particle size, whereas the microscopic unlocking transition is polydisperse. These results provide new insights into the connection between microscopic dynamics and macroscopic rheological behavior in dense, monodisperse particle layers. We further confirm that these clusters are propelled by particles undergoing the directed random walk. These measurements bridge the gap between microscopic dynamics and macroscopic rheology, providing a foundation for understanding polydisperse suspensions.

Search engines play a crucial role in shaping how people gather and synthesize information, yet their personalized nature introduces personal and societal risks through potential information silos and bias. While extensive work exists on the personalization of news and social feeds, similar analysis for generic web search is still nascent. We present a method to quantify personalization by analyzing the differences in results returned by multiple Google instances configured with varying personalization levels. Our findings demonstrate that up to 20% of potentially relevant pages can be missed due to personalization, with over 50% of these missing pages being highly relevant. However, very few participants could identify this issue on their own. Although the average user is unlikely to lose directly relevant information, personalization can create an illusion of completeness, causing users to miss important data that is accessible online. **Design Overview:** This quantitative approach is structured into three main components: (1) an introduction covering the study's background, significance, and research questions; (2) methods detailing the design, e-learning tool, population, and sample; and (3) findings presenting the results.

**Background:** The 2019 coronavirus outbreak (COVID-19) necessitated the shift to e-learning across all Saudi higher education institutions during the 1441/1442 academic year. This change was implemented to ensure student safety and maintain continuity in light of government directives.

**Methodology:** Data were gathered using the General Equivalency Certificate (GEC) exam results from the 1441/1442 academic year and first-semester final exam scores (2020–2021). The GEC serves as a standardized measure to assess students' readiness for university-level studies. The analysis focused on two groups: (1) students who completed the full 14-week semester via e-learning, and (2) those who attended only the first seven weeks before the university closed due to COVID-19.

**Findings:** Statistical analysis revealed a significant difference in first-semester final exam grades between the two groups, with the complete e-learning group outperforming the partial group.

**Conclusion:** The results indicate that students who fully engaged in the e-learning process during the 1441/1442 academic year (2020–2021) achieved higher academic performance in their first-semester final exams compared to those who participated only during the first seven weeks.

**Recommendations:** Future research should incorporate other academic year data to draw more definitive conclusions. Additionally, the university must continue enhancing its e-learning infrastructure to support student academic success.

During recent stock market crashes, market participants at all levels have expressed a marked fear of missing out (FOMO) on potential gains. This FOMO sentiment often drives investors to purchase stocks at exorbitant prices, frequently exceeding the companies' actual intrinsic value. While technical analysis offers techniques to identify overvalued stocks, it relies on the intricate and evolving dynamics of technical indicators. In contrast, traditional machine learning and deep learning models demand substantial labeled data for training, a resource that is difficult to obtain in the stock market due to market shifts and frequent price fluctuations. Additionally, these models often fail to incorporate the influence of technical analysis. To address these limitations, this research employs a deep neural network approach that integrates technical analysis indicators, utilizes self-labeled data, and requires no retraining. The proposed method effectively captures both the valuation and sentiment components hidden within technical analysis, merging them into a single architecture. This approach is particularly advantageous because it can detect overvalued and undervalued stocks by identifying the integrated information regarding valuations and sentiments that technical analysis provides. The proposed method has been validated using a one-day ahead prediction technique on various datasets, with performance measured against fundamental and technical analysis benchmarks. The results indicate that the proposed method significantly outperforms these existing approaches. Finally, the effectiveness of the method was confirmed during the COVID-19 pandemic. Consequently, investors can leverage the derived techniques to time their market entry and exit more effectively.

Recently, deep neural networks have achieved remarkable success across various machine learning tasks, including image recognition, natural language processing, and question answering. However, these networks often contain a vast number of parameters, necessitating careful consideration of both their input and output data. Traditional feedforward networks typically accept high-dimensional inputs but produce a limited number of output classes. In contrast, many contemporary deep learning models, such as those used in sequence labeling, reverse this pattern by accepting low-dimensional input data—often just a single label like a word—in an effort to achieve high-dimensional internal representations before producing a final output label. This paper introduces the Low-Dimensional Input Deep Neural Network (LDDNN), which utilizes low-dimensional input data to yield output labels, offering performance that rivals or surpasses that of deep neural networks. The LDDNN approach has been tested on multiple datasets and problems, consistently outperforming both standard and revised feedforward networks. Furthermore, the method was applied during the COVID-19 pandemic, demonstrating its potential for developing effective prediction models in real-world scenarios.
