that utilize human feedback via comparisons. While promising, the cost and time required for individual comparison labeling create a substantial barrier to widespread adoption. We propose that batching comparisons can significantly enhance the efficiency of human time in these systems. By employing data dimensionality reduction and visualization techniques, we develop an interactive graphical user interface that displays the state space, allowing users to label specific regions rather than isolated comparisons. Experiments on several simple MuJoCo tasks demonstrate that this approach is effective, requiring substantially fewer human labels than traditional methods. We open-source our code to support this work.

Human preferences are inherently high-dimensional and sparse, which makes learning a preference model via supervised learning from pairwise comparisons inefficient. We introduce a system that leverages these sparsity and smoothness characteristics. Instead of labeling every transition in the state space, our method identifies and labels "keypoints"—specific states that can be visualized, enabling agents to explore the state space independently. We validate this method in both simulation and real-world cleaning tasks, showing it is more sample-efficient than standard approaches that rely solely on dense human feedback. Our source code is available at https://github.com/hanxiangz/KeyPointReward.

We present the Verdict framework, which utilizes human labels for transitions (actions and/or observations) to learn policies for task execution. Verdict employs a multi-task reinforcement learning approach to learn a transition model, a reward model, and a policy. The core idea is to treat each transition as a sentence describing an agent's attempt to perform a task, where the reward is an implicit property of the action within a specific observation context. The learned transition model helps the user focus on high-level semantics by filtering out low-level noise from the comparison process. Additionally, we use the "next word prediction" paradigm of language modeling to frame the comparison task, using the transition model to generate training data for a next-sentence prediction model. Experiment results indicate that Verdict is more sample-efficient and effective than baseline methods.

A generator network, trained similarly to a variational autoencoder (VAE), maps points in this latent space to the sonified dimension. Sound is generated based on the evaluated function values along this dimension, with the goal of making local optima in the latent space correspond to local optima of the objective function. is a critical step in developing effective prevention and treatment strategies. This process often relies on computerized psychometric assessments administered during person-computer interactions. While Q-learning has emerged as a promising method for analyzing such interactions, it requires the absence of preprogramming that guides or influences user behavior. Kahaner games offer a novel environment for training Q-learning by guaranteeing no bias toward specific actions. This paper introduces a guide-free Q-learning framework designed to prevent interference within Kahaner games. Additionally, when predicting an individual's risk of drug use based on their input sequence, a classification model is necessary. However, applying reinforcement learning to classify behaviors is a challenging and underexplored area. Consequently, we propose using Q-learning to estimate the risk associated with various drug consumption patterns. Experimental results demonstrate that our guide-free Q-learning approach outperforms standard Q-learning in analyzing drug consumption behaviors, and the proposed risk evaluation method proves more accurate than traditional methods.

Game theory provides a structured way to investigate how individuals consume drugs and develop addiction. Although existing literature often employs payoffs that encourage drug use, there is a need for environments that do not predispose users toward consumption. We propose the Kahaner machine, which utilizes Kahaner games to create a setting free from predisposition toward drug use or specific actions. These games facilitate the training of guide-free deep Q-networks (DQNs) to solve complex behavioral puzzles. We demonstrate that this method is superior to both conventional game theory techniques and unsupervised DQNs for identifying high-risk individuals and detecting various drug-taking and misuse behaviors.

Game theory is currently used to study drug consumption and addiction mechanisms. However, many existing games implicitly predispose users toward consumption and often guide behavior through hidden rules. To address this, we developed the Kahaner machine, a device that employs Kahaner games to provide a neutral environment free from bias regarding drug use or particular actions. This setup enables the training of guide-free deep Q-networks (DQNs). Our results indicate that this approach is more effective than both traditional game theory methods and standard DQNs for evaluating the risk of drug use and identifying complex consumption and misuse behaviors.

Understanding the risks of drug use and misuse is essential for developing targeted prevention and treatment strategies. Game theory offers a valuable framework for simulating user behavior, yet current methods suffer from two key limitations: they often implicitly encourage consumption and rely on rules that predispose users to certain actions. commonsense reasoning structured through 802 interlinked paragraphs, each detailing a specific instance of common sense. Designed as a scalable framework for constructing targeted subsets of common sense, the ATOMIC was subsequently utilized to develop the ATOMIC-HYPERGRAPH and the more accessible ATOMIC-DOC. To validate the validity and scale of common sense inherent in the ATOMIC, we gathered ratings from 900 Amazon Mechanical Turk workers across three distinct dimensions. The results demonstrate that the knowledge represented in the ATOMIC is predominantly true, logically consistent, and meaningful. Furthermore, we explore various applications of the ATOMIC, including natural language inference, question answering, coreference resolution, and summarization. We also provide links to datasets and models derived from the ATOMIC found at http://commonsense-reasoning.org. Additionally, we address several limitations and propose potential improvements and extensions at the same URL. In summary, the work presents the construction of the ATOMIC, an extensive atlas of commonsense reasoning, followed by evaluations of the knowledge it encapsulates and discussions on potential applications. We contend that structuring common sense as in the ATOMIC offers a robust framework for building systems capable of possessing and leveraging common sense, while simultaneously serving as a valuable resource for researchers. The title of the paper is: Constructing Commonsense Reasoning Trees from Diverse Sources.

We present the construction of ATOMIC, a structured repository of commonsense knowledge centered on ordinary human activities. This atlas organizes statements about the world into first-order sentences that describe typical actions, transitions between action states, and the characteristics of the objects and attributes involved in these actions. By aggregating information from diverse sources and synthesizing it with human input, we have created this repository of typical worldly knowledge, with a particular focus on the concepts embedded within. We assessed the quality of the constructed graphs by measuring the perceived truth, logical consistency, and relevance of the attributes and actions they contain, as well as the inference capabilities of rules derived from them. These evaluations were performed on subsets of the ATOMIC-HYPERGRAPHS by 180 human participants. The findings indicate that the constructed graphs are accurate and relevant, and that the underlying first-order knowledge is of high quality. We further discuss several application domains, ranging from coreference resolution and paraphrasing to dialog systems and question answering. The datasets and tools related to this work are accessible at http://commonsense-reasoning.org.

To address this, we introduce a new dimension-reduction technique based on a parametric extension of the portfolio problem. Since the optimization task is defined by both asset weights and asset returns, reducing the problem's dimensionality by contracting the returns vector simultaneously lowers the numbers of variables and constraints. This reduction strategy is particularly effective when applied to the circle method, a dimension-constrained portfolio approach that seeks to maximize the probability of achieving returns within a specific ellipsoid. Our numerical experiments demonstrate that the resulting lower-dimensional problem can be solved more quickly using the interior point method, the circle method, or a hybrid approach that combines both algorithms. Furthermore, we show that the dimension of the problem can be estimated with a high degree of accuracy using a statistical estimator that relies on the eigenvalue distribution of random matrices. This paper is accompanied by a supplementary dataset containing the code used to generate our results.

Let $K$ represent a convex, centrally symmetric body in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that possesses unit volume. Define $\sigma(K)$ as the average volume of the intersections of $K$ with hyperplanes passing through its center. We examine the question of which such body $K$ maximizes $\sigma(K)$. We report experimental data from a single nanowire that not only confirms this critical voltage prediction but also uncovers a novel, unexpected threshold voltage dependent on a single electron transistor gate voltage. This observation implies the presence of an additional, previously unidentified, control parameter governing quantum phase slip dynamics. Additionally, we provide a qualitative explanation for these findings using a resistive superconducting quantum circuit model featuring two Josephson junctions. We note that the same threshold voltage behavior can be reproduced by artificially constraining the critical current of one of these junctions. The results are further contrasted with a scenario involving a single Josephson junction.

Superconducting quantum circuits are essential for creating and manipulating coherent quantum states, and their miniaturability allows engineers to tailor device behavior by modifying geometric parameters. We demonstrate that a single narrow nanowire, where coherent quantum phase slips are expected, functions as a single Josephson junction within a superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID). By analyzing subgap voltage noise and its dependence on magnetic flux, we show that these phase slips behave as a series of identical barriers with uniform tunneling probability. This configuration explains the observed subgap noise plateau at zero magnetic flux and its reduction under an applied magnetic field. Furthermore, we find that supergap noise is proportional to the normal resistance of the wire only when the average number of Cooper pairs on the island is minimal; in other regimes, an effective resistance exceeds the actual normal resistance. This discrepancy is explained by modeling the noise as originating from an effective tunnel barrier distinct from the normal resistance. We conclude by comparing our results to a simple model of a single Josephson junction with shunt resistance.

Narrow superconducting nanowires are expected to undergo a quantum phase slip (QPS) transition at a critical voltage $V_{crit} = 2eI_{crit}$, where $I_{crit}$ is the critical current of a single QPS barrier. Since QPS events are tunneling incidents of the order parameter $\Delta$, we can model the nanowire as a Josephson junction. Understanding the quark-gluon plasma (QGP) requires a comprehensive description of quantum chromodynamics (QCD) across all momentum scales, from perturbative regimes to non-perturbative domains. Recent measurements of quantum chromodynamics at the LHC by the LHCb collaboration have revealed that the $p_T$ distribution of charged hadrons in proton-lead collisions exhibits an asymmetry not seen in pure proton-proton collisions at comparable energies. Interpreting this $p_T$ asymmetry through the lens of a moving thermal medium has successfully predicted data from both proton-nucleus and heavy-ion collisions, suggesting that the QGP functions as a thermal fluid. These findings, alongside recent heavy-ion results, underscore the significance of probe physics in characterizing the medium's transport properties. Specifically, the momentum of a parton exiting the plasma determines the $p_T$ distribution of the hadrons it produces after fragmentation. Unlike recent methods that handle only minor viewpoint shifts, our prior-free approach successfully predicts videos across wider angular ranges, up to 45 degrees. To achieve this, we utilize a hybrid architecture combining an Attention-based Multiview Encoder (MVE) with a view-sensitive Output Module (OM). Video super-resolution (VSR) leverages temporal redundancy to enhance image quality, yet it demands extensive training data featuring very high-resolution frames. To reduce data requirements, researchers have turned to self-supervised VSR, which recovers a target video from a lower-resolution version and an auxiliary auxiliary video captured from a slightly different angle. However, these methods often rely on priors, limiting their utility. In this paper, we introduce a self-supervised VSR approach that utilizes solely a downsampled video and an auxiliary clip from a different view, requiring no labeled data. Our method employs a multi-view convolutional autoencoder (CAE) with shared weights to learn scene appearance and geometry without explicit labeling. An inverse pyramid strategy is implemented to facilitate the recovery of fine details. Extensive experiments on the challenging MCCT and Super-Human datasets confirm that our method outperforms both supervised and other self-supervised VSR techniques.

bent and Lord (TQC 13, 2017), offers a classical encryption method that, due to limited and limitedly shared quantum resources between the sender and receiver, renders the copying of an encrypted message impossible. Such limited quantum access is not solely shared between the sender and receiver; it is also restricted by unshared environmental noise. We present a classical unclonable encryption scheme that functions without any shared quantum resources, utilizing only quantum vulnerability to environmental noise. This system employs single qubits as quantum locks that can be opened by any individual qubit free of noise or with minimal noise. Specifically, the cryptographic key is formed by the inability of noise affecting even a single link in a quantum chain to make the entire chain cloneable. Our system uses pure quantum resources that require no shared entropy, offering a more practical and robust solution than the original unclonable quantum chain proposal. We provide a formal proof of unclonability and demonstrate experimentally, using photonic quantum locks vulnerable to loss, that no more than approximately 29% of users can successfully open the lock. This system provides strong unclonability, ensuring that either a clone is guaranteed to be noisy, or alternatively, that noise affecting even a single lock guarantees unclonability. Consequently, if a clone exists, it must already be noisy.

Unclonable encryption was previously proposed by Broadbent and Lord (TQC 13, 2017), which, unlike the system in this paper, relies on shared entropy between the sender and receiver. This work demonstrates that unclonable encryption remains feasible using purely quantum resources, such as single qubits vulnerable to environmental noise.

Quantum money, a cryptographic system enabling the creation and transfer of transferable but non-copyable funds, was pioneered by Wiesner in 1970. This research systematizes various quantum money schemes using single qubit states and proves their security even when security relies on the vulnerability of these states to environmental noise, rather than computational hardness. The system achieves this by utilizing quantum states sensitive to loss or depolarizing noise.

For instance, Mars underwent significant atmospheric loss, at least during specific eras, while a comparable magnitude of CO$_2$ is currently released through both volcanic activity and atmospheric recycling. To investigate these phenomena, we developed a 0-D model of the modern Martian atmosphere that integrates multiple feedback loops. This model successfully reproduces a broad spectrum of atmospheric variables, including surface pressure, exchange rates with the crust, volcanic emissions, and inventories of key species such as CO$_2$, CO, H$_2$O, and O. By exploring the historic evolution of these parameters, we formulated a simplified framework to investigate the potential for a runaway greenhouse effect on Mars and calculate the planet's theoretical maximum atmospheric mass and corresponding pressure. Our results indicate that, given the observed recycling of surface CO$_2$ and active volcanism, Mars could sustain an atmosphere roughly 25 to 30 times thicker than the current one; this is nearly 10 times less than what would trigger a runaway greenhouse effect, a conclusion that remains consistent regardless of varying initial pressures or recycling efficiencies. Additionally, we examined the impact of dust within the atmosphere on thermal dynamics, finding that a global dust layer as thin as 10 $\mu$m can cause the surface temperature to drop by approximately 40 K. This phenomenon has been observed in various systems, including graphene and meta-materials. Within graphene, additional degrees of freedom emerge due to spin-orbit coupling and its interaction with sublattice symmetry; these interactions are critical for generating exotic phases like quantum anomalous Hall and spin Hall states. This study provides a comprehensive overview of the spin-orbit proximity effect in both hexagonal and rock-salt buffered graphene, with a specific focus on experimental methods for introducing this interaction and the resulting exotic phases. Additionally, we briefly examine the extra phases that arise in graphene when hybridized with an adlayer through the spin-orbit proximity effect. The findings presented here are fundamental for developing spintronic devices that utilize spin-orbit coupling in graphene. Graphene offers a versatile platform for engineering spin-orbit coupling (SOC) because its position can be precisely controlled. This engineering is vital for creating topological insulators and other correlated materials. In this work, we construct an effective non-superlattice model for graphene to characterize the phase diagram of SOC-induced topological insulators. We demonstrate two mechanisms for proximity-induced SOC: mixing graphene $p$-orbitals with an adjacent layer's $s$-orbital to induce spin-valley locked SOC, and hybridizing $p$-orbitals with $d$-orbitals to introduce spin-split bands. By analyzing the topology of the resulting bands, we derive an effective four-band model to map out the phase diagram of topological insulators based on the symmetry and strength of the induced SOC. This analysis reveals the emergence of both Chern and valley-Chern numbers, indicating that graphene can support quantum anomalous Hall and quantum valley Hall Hall effects. We also explore the influence of sublattice symmetry breaking and electron-electron interactions on these topological phenomena. Ultimately, we propose a feasible device configuration to realize these topological phases.

We analyze the consequences of this constraint across various optimization scenarios, including unconstrained optimization, constrained optimization, and early stopping. Specifically, we establish that the optimal Lipschitz constant for a trained network depends on the data and remains independent of the network's architecture. Furthermore, the allowable range of the constant defines an optimal depth and width, a finding that aligns with observations regarding overparameterization and the benefits of lightweight deep networks. Theoretically, explicit Lipschitz continuity is equivalent to weight decay, though the network exhibits heightened sensitivity to input changes as the decay factor increases. We provide numerical evidence supporting these claims and offer additional insights into the relationship between the two methods. Additionally, we explore the limitations of networks with bounded output sensitivity and introduce a network class capable of modeling functions with unbounded Lipschitz constants. This class is equivalent to deep networks employing both total variation norm and Lipschitz continuity as regularizers, allowing for more accurate approximation of arbitrary target functions and potentially improved optimization performance. Finally, we outline potential future research directions concerning this topic. In summary, the key contributions of this paper are: (1) analyzing optimal performance in both unconstrained and constrained optimization settings; (2) determining an optimal depth and width for deep networks based on the maximum Lipschitz constant of the underlying function and the extent of the input domain; (3) highlighting the increased sensitivity to input variations as the Lipschitz constant rises; (4) demonstrating the enhanced optimization potential for networks with unbounded Lipschitz continuity; and (5) illustrating the improved optimization capabilities of networks utilizing the Lipschitz norm as a regularizer on a restricted function space. These results underscore the significance of balancing a function's Lipschitz continuity with that of its domain.

Processing (NLP) domains, including part-of-speech tagging, named entity recognition, and sentiment analysis. However, training deep language models to perform these sequence-to-sequence (S2S) tasks often yields unsatisfactory results, characterized by a strong inability to handle short context and a high propensity to generate gibberish. Current state-of-the-art methods address this by training a decoder in isolation and fine-tuning the full architecture on S2S data, a process that is both computationally expensive and limited to a narrow range of NLP applications. In this paper, we introduce a unified framework designed for sequential S2S learning that overcomes the limitations of sequential training and extends beyond the constraints of previous models. Our approach addresses three sequential challenges: 1) aligning non-matching data distributions between prediction and continuation tasks to ensure coherent sentence generation, 2) managing varying data distributions and sequence lengths to facilitate continuous learning, and 3) mitigating vanishing gradients to support long-range dependencies. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms both standard baseline models and recent state-of-the-art techniques on single-sentence classification and completion tasks. These simulations explored variations in upper-atmosphere chemistry driven by rapid photolysis and examined how photopheric wind structures depend on atmospheric composition and the depth of the photopheric layer relative to the noontide bulge. The resulting synthetic spectra accurately reproduced the observed line profiles and depths during the early stages of ingress, suggesting that the sub-chemical settling winds previously inferred for the noontide phase are also present during approach to noontide. However, during the final hours before noontide, the derived atmospheric properties fall outside currently explored model parameter spaces, likely due to unresolved physics in both the models and the interpretation of the atmospheric signal. We conclude by discussing how combining RV data with photometric light curves from ingress and egress can constrain key atmospheric parameters. Specifically, while noontide RVs are influenced by the latitude of the atmosphere's deepest hot spot, ingress RVs are governed by the ratio of planetary rotation to the rate of hot spot motion. This study offers direct evidence for chemically driven winds on hot planets, emphasizing that optimizing observations to capture the full range of regimes on eccentric-orbit planets is vital for unlocking detailed atmospheric insights.

This study examines CT's assumptions regarding discourse representation and sentence composition in relation to contemporary cognitive science theories of language processing, with a focus on structural descriptive theories and computational processing models. Centering Theory (CT; Grosz et al., 1995) models local discourse structure by tracing the shifting focus across representations of world knowledge within utterance-widows. However, the model's assumptions about discourse representation and compositional processing require validation against a comprehensive, modern framework of structural descriptive linguistics and computational processing. This paper situates CT within i-STRUCT (i-STRUCT; Huettner et al., 2019), a contemporary framework of computational discourse representation and compositional processing. The analysis demonstrates that CT's core assumptions regarding world knowledge and processing are sound, provided a few minor adjustments are made to how instances are handled. By grounding CT in i-STRUCT, we can leverage contemporary computational processing models to investigate centering processes and their alignment with other world knowledge features, such as prediction and attention.

Centering Theory (CT; Grosz et al., 1995) posits that local discourse structure is determined by the shifting focus across world knowledge representations within consecutive utterances. However, the model relies on specific assumptions about both discourse representation and compositional processing that require examination through a complete, modern framework of structural descriptive theories and computational processing models. This analysis places CT within i-STRUCT (i-STRUCT; Huettner et al., 2019), addressing those assumptions by situating CT in contemporary computational processing models of world knowledge. The resulting perspective confirms the validity of CT's core assumptions concerning consecutive world knowledge instances and their processing. By establishing CT's foundations in i-STRUCT, we can utilize these models to explore centering processes alongside other aspects of world knowledge, including attention and predictability.

The findings encompass a new fixed-parameter algorithm based on the count of sources, an XP-algorithm defined by treewidth, and another fixed-parameter algorithm utilizing treedepth. The challenge of deciding whether a directed acyclic graph (DAG) can be represented as an upward planar drawing has historically been linked to the existence of a hierarchical book embedding. We demonstrate that this problem is fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by the number of source vertices. Specifically, a DAG with $s$ sources admits an upward planar drawing if and only if it allows a hierarchical book embedding using $s$ pages that respects the orientation of edges. Our proof relies on a lemma providing a fixed-parameter algorithm for a related "reachability" hierarchical book embedding problem, which is itself of independent interest. As a notable application of our technique, we offer a new proof of the classical result concerning the tractability of upward planar drawing for single-source DAGs. Beyond this, our approach yields fixed-parameter algorithms for several additional upward planarity questions, including the existence of an upward planar drawing with a specified infinite face, fixed source vertices, and fixed target vertices. We also examine the XP-algorithm for treewidth, noting that the problem remains generally intractable (even for series-parallel graphs) when parameterized in this manner. Our work extends the methodologies previously established for series-parallel digraphs and single-source digraphs.

While Randomized Testing (RT) has demonstrated efficacy in detecting severe bugs on simple systems, it frequently requires more in-depth exploration to reach a broadened coverage range. This study introduces Guided Randomized Testing (GRT), which utilizes static and dynamic analysis to direct RT and enhance the defect discovery capabilities of GWRT compared to standard RT. Specifically, GRT employs RT to generate diverse execution traces while simultaneously identifying and removing dynamically redundant statements. By maintaining only the non-redundant subsets of code across various traces, GRT constructs an execution landscape that steers RT for execution and coverage optimization. Initial results from GRT applied to the GNU C library indicate that it achieves 15% higher coverage than RT and leads to the discovery of additional unique defects. To facilitate the adoption of GRT in practical settings, we developed the automatic testing tool, Unitex, which integrates the GRT strategy. The source code for Unitex is accessible at https://github.com/Unitex/Unitex.

Testing strategies that combine randomization with guidance have proven successful in finding latent defects within complex programs. However, implementing guidance via dynamic analysis, as seen in GRT, is challenging to deploy in industrial-scale environments. Unitex demonstrates that GRT guidance can be automated, as shown in this paper, and integrated into existing testing frameworks to yield performance improvements. The code for Unitex is available at https://github.com/Unitex/Unitex.

Guided Randomized Testing (GRT) guides randomized testing (RT) to achieve superior code coverage and defect discovery. While effective for small programs, GRT has been difficult to adopt in large-scale applications due to issues with guidance computation time and the overhead of required dynamic analysis. We present Unitex, an automated testing tool that implements GRT. Unitex accelerates GRT computation by 1.6x using an guidance optimization method and reduces overhead by 51% through an overhead elimination technique that leverages input similarity. Consequently, Unitex delivers up to 2.6x faster computation times than previously reported while delivering comparable performance to Unitex+Overhead. Experiments on three real-world programs show that Unitex discovers new defects that RT and existing state-of-the-art tools missed. Unitex is available at https://github.com/Unitex/Unitex.

by applying quantum information theory. Specifically, we examine the Heisenberg evolution of operators under a random Hamiltonian to evaluate the spread of quantum scrambling, utilizing the generalized free energy of von Neumann entropy as our metric. We demonstrate analytically that, typically, the imaginary time component drives operator growth while the real time component drives volume growth. Furthermore, we investigate systems governed by quantum kinetic theory, showing that the continuity equation links the current defined via the Wigner function to the rate of change of density. In non-equilibrium scenarios, we find that both the heat and chemical potential flows drive the growth of the non-equilibrium entropy current. Additionally, we explore the weak and strong typicality of these generalized free energy components. Our analysis includes models of non-interacting and weakly interacting systems, as well as random matrix ensembles. Typical behavior is observed in Gaussian ensembles under unitary evolution, while GUE and GGOE ensembles exhibit strong typicality. The results for interacting systems align with those of random matrix theory under weak typicality, where the behavior averages out to typicality. We also analyze the perturbative dynamics of SYK-like systems. Ultimately, we establish a model where generalized free energy serves as the driver of operator growth. This work offers insight into the early-time behavior of operator growth through the lens of quantum information theory and statistical mechanics, suggesting a new method to study this phenomenon in many-body systems. Additionally, we propose that the thermodynamic properties of a quantum channel can serve as a useful probe for quantum scrambling.

In many-body quantum chaotic systems, two primary phenomena characterize the dynamics of quantum information: entanglement growth and operator growth. This paper presents a general framework to study operator growth by analyzing the entanglement structure of time-evolved operators within random matrix models. We define two quantities, mutual information and entanglement entropy, to measure respectively the connected correlations and the degrees of freedom involved in an operator's expansion. Under the influence of both Hamiltonian and anti-Hamiltonian components, these two degrees of freedom compete during the evolution of unitary operators composed of random matrices. We apply this framework to various models, including interacting quantum chaotic systems, quantum graph models, and quantum random circuits. Our results indicate that while both components contribute to mutual information, only the anti-Hamiltonian part influences the entanglement entropy. This approach allows us to re-interpret the findings of prior studies on operator growth and addresses open questions regarding volume growth in interacting quantum chaotic systems.

However, the vast volume of transmitted information creates an ideal opportunity for attackers to conduct privacy breaches. Consequently, privacy-preserving mechanisms are increasingly integral to transmission protocols. This study investigates privacy preservation in WiFi-based smart homes. To enable users to manage devices effectively, they must recognize one another; to foster this recognition, users transmit activity data. Therefore, a key research focus is allowing users to identify each other while preventing them from inferring activity information. This paper introduces a home activity communication protocol designed to let users establish identities without revealing their activities. We implemented the protocol on real Android smartphones and tested it on an IoT testbed, demonstrating that the approach is practical, feasible, and efficient. Additionally, the protocol ensures forward and backward privacy. Over multiple transmission intervals, we designed the system to limit an attacker's ability to trace users based on historical and future data, even if they know an attacker's activities from the current interval. Our evaluation shows the protocol incurs only a minimal overhead of 1.18 microseconds. To the best of our knowledge, this work presents the first solution that ensures both spatial and temporal (forward and backward) privacy in home activity transmissions.

In recent times, the Internet of Things (IoT) has seen rapid growth, with numerous devices being smart-enabled, leading to a surge in data transmission and processing demands. Edge computing has emerged as a vital solution for the timely processing of this data. However, as more devices join the IoT ecosystem, the risk of attacks and data breaches rises, necessitating effective attack detection and response strategies. To address this, we introduce an early attack detection system for IoT environments utilizing channel state information (CSI). This system employs a machine learning-based approach to identify attacks in real-time before they cause significant harm. Specifically, we develop a solution to identify and mitigate Denial of Service (DoS) attacks targeting specific IoT devices. By analyzing received signal strength (RSS) and CSI at the edge server, the proposed system can distinguish between legitimate users and attackers, offering an early warning signal. This early detection enables the activation of a back-off mechanism, giving attackers a chance to leave and allowing the system to mitigate potential damage. Furthermore, the system can block attacks at the access point (AP) to prevent them from reaching the edge server and can alert users to modify their passwords to enhance security. To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first attempt at early attack detection and mitigation within an IoT setting.

are governed by Service Level Agreements (SLAs) that define performance metrics. Ensuring compliance typically relies on automated monitoring within SLA Management Systems (SAMS), which analyze log data from various sources to detect violations. However, the high cost of SLAs encourages operators to provide guaranteed performance rather than merely proving it, prompting SAMS to assist in finding optimal configurations that balance performance with efficiency. This benefit is most evident in systems utilizing performance guarantees that vary with resource allocation, such as virtualized networks where quality of service (QoS) and performance depend on the resources assigned to virtual machines. In such contexts, log analysis supports optimal resource management that adapts to dynamic user demands. Additionally, real-time analysis enables anomaly detection for rapid response to dynamic events like attacks or service migrations. The wide range of potential performance metrics and their source-specific formats creates a challenge that requires the system to accommodate new metrics over time. Furthermore, because optimal configurations depend on both performance and resource allocation costs, external information about market conditions must be integrated into the analysis. These factors make critical networked services a prime use case for modern log analysis technologies based on distributed processing. Such systems can offer comprehensive functionality in a modular way, allowing development to start with violation detection and expand to include performance optimization, provided that performance metrics are analyzed. This approach minimizes risks and development costs, as modern architectures allow incremental addition of analysis types and modular extension of system-wide features. This paper outlines such an architecture and details the design of a prototype, emphasizing how it can be expanded for specific applications. Additionally, the authors present initial analysis of web server logs, demonstrating performance optimization for dynamic loads. (C) 2008 AIP Publishing LLC.

Operators of critical networked services, which derive significant income, are often contractually obligated to maintain agreed-upon performance levels, such as system availability. Compliance is usually verified via automated monitoring in SLA Management Systems (SAMS). While these systems can detect violations through log analysis, they are more valuable when assisting with performance optimization. For instance, SLAs can incorporate not only guaranteeing performance but also assisting in achieving it through resource adaptation. However, analyzing logs for optimization is complex due to the need to evaluate performance in relation to resource costs and the potentially vast array of available metrics and formats. This paper presents a research-oriented architecture for such log analysis within a SAMS. It highlights the specific challenges and solutions for optimizing web servers, including optimizing request throughput, integrating open-source monitoring tools, and providing real-time anomaly detection.

This concern is particularly acute for low-emittance, high-current beams, including all-metal-hydrogen (AMM-H) beams, where the impact of such instability has not yet been thoroughly examined. This study examines beam breakup in both round and rectangular low-emittance beams. First, we demonstrate that the growth rate for linear breakup in round beams exceeds that of helical modes; however, because round beams lack a core, the total current at which linear instability occurs is significantly higher than in helical cases. Furthermore, we prove that in strictly round beams, linear instability can only arise if the beam-wall impedance is at least four times greater for TE modes (affecting the vertical field) than for TM modes. Second, we illustrate that when round beams develop a central core, the threshold for linear instability becomes comparable to that of helical modes. Third, we demonstrate that the primary concern for low-emittance, AMM-H beams is progressive (non-local) instability. Specifically, the threshold (K) for such instability in a 1.5 cm AMM-H beam is roughly 1/20th of the threshold for immediate (local) breakup. Finally, we explore mitigation strategies, noting that beam-shaping inserts can elevate the instability threshold by an order of magnitude. We conclude with a brief examination of high-current, low-emittance helium beams. Ultimately, we argue that all-metal-hydrogen beams operating above an external magnetic field of 0.2 Tesla are susceptible to non-local beam breakup. Given the significance of this phenomenon, further investigation into high-current, low-emittance AMM-H beams is strongly recommended.

Beam breakup (BB) is the most critical phenomenon limiting the operation of multi-turn accelerators. While BB has been extensively studied in round beams, less attention has been devoted to rectangular beams. This paper begins by deriving the dispersion equation for BB in a rectangular beam, accounting for all relevant wall-impedance configurations. It is shown that, unlike round beams where BB can occur with zero wall impedance, a rectangular beam requires non-zero impedance on at least one pair of walls. Although the dispersion equation cannot be solved analytically, a perturbation analysis for small emittances reveals that the instability threshold for transverse BB in rectangular beams is approximately 20 times higher than that in round beams of equivalent area and aspect ratio. This substantial increase in the threshold for BB in rectangular beams is likely applicable to other instability types

precision long-baseline experiments depend on accurate models of neutrino-nucleus interactions. LAXAR, a machine learning framework, predicts the most probable outcome of the kinematics for energy loss events in the T2K near detector. It operates as a regression model that learns to map low-dimensional input features—derived from a coarse HARPmees calorimeter—to high-dimensional output features representing fine-grained energy loss. By integrating these outputs, the model reconstructs the neutrino energy with a root-mean-square error of 100 MeV, a level of accuracy sufficient for analyzing T2K data. The LAXAR code has been integrated into the T2K production simulation pipeline, enabling its use in T2K energy loss and oscillation analyses. Furthermore, the model demonstrates generalizability across different T2K near detectors and is expected to be adaptable to other long-baseline facilities. To achieve this, LAXAR offers a flexible architecture capable of handling various input formats, including dPC4 hits. To validate its generalizability, a test instance was constructed using dPC4 hits. Additionally, LAXAR supports multiple learning strategies, such as training on all events at once or employing self-training with a small set of energy loss tagger events. These capabilities ensure that the framework is highly adaptable for future applications in neutrino experiments. During the two-year proceedings of the long-baseline workshop, participants identified key challenges for the upcoming DUNE experiment, many of which the LAXAR model can address. The model is openly available on GitHub to facilitate the evaluation of its generalizability and its adaptation to DUNE and other long-baseline neutrino experiments. To quantify DUNE-specific performance metrics, simple adjustments to the learning strategy are required. To further validate the model's generalizability, it should be tested on ND280 data, as the T2K beamline utilizes the ND280 near detector. This testing would confirm the model's ability to recover oscillation parameters from ND280 data. To evaluate LAXAR's performance under DUNE conditions, it was evaluated using DUNE LArTPC simulation data, revealing a 10% reduction in prediction performance compared to T2K results. This discrepancy is attributed to differences in the input data distributions between the two experiments. To understand the model's behavior, several performance metrics were examined, including misclassification rates for specific prediction categories, residual analysis, decision boundaries, and sensitivity to input changes. chondrite and planetesimal materials vary with temperature, revealing a significant decline—exceeding one order of magnitude—as temperatures rise from 200 K to 400 K. This decrease likely results from a combination of reduced surface condensation and increased internal porosity. This study investigates how the thermal evolution of early planetesimals influences the aggregation of these bodies. To achieve this, we integrated our material strength data with numerical simulations modeling the thermal history and growth of isolated, porous, accreting planetesimals during the early solar system. Specifically, simulations tracked the evolution of average strength and rotation rate across different mass and density profiles, porosity evolution functions, and throughout various ambient temperature histories. The models replicated the formation of self-gravitating, rotating bodies as they cooled from the ambient environment and as they generated internal heat through radioactive decay. Key findings indicate that planetesimals developing internal thermal gradients experienced internal temperatures ranging from 300 K to over 1600 K at a nominal age of 3 Myr. Consequently, sticking forces dropped to negligible levels outside the central regions. Consequently, thermal decoupling between the central and external zones rapidly occurred within approximately 1 Myr, ultimately determining the bodies' thermal and mass evolution. This outcome implies an upper limit on a planetesimal's ability to accumulate mass from the surrounding nebula, suggesting that these bodies must have primarily gained mass through the collapse of pre-existing external rings rather than external accretion. A significant challenge in this field is the variability of human behaviors, which is often modeled using hidden Markov models (HMMs) to capture diverse action sequences. This paper addresses two specific challenges in imitating 3D human poses from video: first, handling viewpoint changes and varying numbers of people in training frames, and second, dealing with background noise and pose label variability within the behavior clip. To these challenges, we propose a method that combines 3D pose estimation with human behavior analysis. Specifically, we extract 2D pose features from images and employ an attention mechanism to learn an optimal projection mapping from 2D features to 3D space. Furthermore, we introduce a hierarchical 3D pose regression framework that leverages an intermediate key pose to simultaneously handle viewpoint variance and label noise in behavior clips. Unlike traditional inverse kinematics, this two-stage mapping enhances the model's robustness to noisy data and improves performance in pose-to-pose and pose-to-state control scenarios. Extensive experiments on two real-world datasets confirm that our method effectively learns from human behavior and outperforms several state-of-the-art techniques.

We present a comprehensive derivation of the NNLL small- $x$ kernel, providing all necessary kernel components from leading logarithmic (LL) through next-to-leading logarithmic (NLL) to NNLL accuracy. Notably, we utilize the color-singlet sector of QCD at NNLL to formulate a generalization of the LO BFKL equation that enables the study of MPI up to NNLLA. Furthermore, we derive an MPI kernel incorporating both LO BFKL evolution and color-octeron interactions, serving as a practical tool for MPI simulations with enhanced small- $x$ resummation. Specifically, the diagonal kernel for MPI up to NNLLA is constructed from the LO kernel, NLL corrections, and the NNLL kernel as derived in this work. Additionally, we offer estimates for elastic, total cross sections, and the full MPI framework up to NNLLA based on this kernel. We have made the event generator incorporating this kernel available to the public. Additionally, we address the unitarization of the unitarity equation up to NN

Given a feature map $\vec{x}:V\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^D$, a feature graph is constructed where nodes represent features $\vec{x}(u)$, with an edge existing between $u$ and $v$ if and only if $N_r(u)=N_r(v)$. Specifically, we establish that these graphs exhibit high connectivity when the feature space dimension $D$ is sufficiently large. Furthermore, we demonstrate that if $r$ is small relative to the typical diameter of node neighborhoods, the feature graph tends to have a high chromatic number. These theoretical advancements are supported by experimental findings on both synthetic and real-world datasets. In graph neural networks, utilizing a neighborhood-based sparsity pattern like that of feature graphs allows models to achieve high accuracy with significantly fewer dimensions $D$.

Graph neural networks (GNNs) are powerful tools for analyzing data structured as graphs, applicable to tasks such as node and graph classification, as well as link prediction. Their versatility is evident in recent work that classifies molecules, drugs, and proteins. A common strategy in GNN design involves aggregating local neighborhood information; for instance, a model might sum the features of a node's $r$-neighbors, where $r$ is a hyperparameter. However, this approach demands a feature dimension $D$ that scales with $r$ to remain effective. We introduce a neighborhood-based sparsity method that uses a fixed, low dimension $D$ regardless of the neighborhood radius $r$. By mapping a graph based on the equality of closed neighborhoods of various radii, we can efficiently perform graph invariants computation, subgraph isomorphism testing, and graph embedding. Our experiments on thousands of random graphs and datasets from the Network Science literature confirm that our proposed sparsity function is highly expressive, even at very low dimensions. Consequently, GNNs leveraging this sparsity can achieve state-of-the-art accuracy with a feature dimension $D$ as small as 4.

We developed a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture, termed a "tiling CNN," which processes the sky in overlapping equal-area patches rather than relying on spherical harmonics or piecewise definitions. In this work, we apply machine learning (ML) methods to map power spectrum estimation, a task central to numerous map analysis problems. Although many ML approaches exist for Euclidean spaces, they have not yet been explored for curved manifolds like the sphere, despite their significant potential in this context. We introduce a CNN designed to estimate power spectra directly from CMB maps. Unlike traditional map-to-power-spectrum converters, our CNN achieves comparable accuracy to classical techniques but with a speedup exceeding $10^5$, making it suitable for exploratory analyses involving millions of realizations. Additionally, we assess the generalization capability of the CNN by estimating power spectra from simulated maps containing foregrounds and noise, covering a broad range of angular scales. Results indicate that the model generalizes well to mixed foreground scenarios and accurately recovers total variance and large-angle power, while its performance at small angular scales remains comparable to classical methods even under noisy conditions. This remarkable generalization ability allows us to conclude that the model can be trained once on a specific experiment and subsequently used to estimate power spectra (and other statistics) for any map with the same systematic error profile, offering speed and scalability unattainable by classical methods. We propose a proportionality-based hiring strategy where candidates apply sequentially and are accepted or rejected based on the current team composition. We demonstrate that, similar to serial dictatorship, this method offers strong theoretical fairness assurances. Additionally, through computational experiments, we show that the approach is effective in practice. A key finding is that the method remains powerful even when applied to a limited subset of the candidate pool, such as underrepresented groups. The practical success of the approach relies on an acceptance/rejection oracle, whose implementation details are provided in the supplementary materials. Empirical results confirm that the solution quality is robust across various parameter settings, including differing levels of team diversity and strictness of proportionality. A significant advantage of our framework is its modularity, which facilitates the integration of custom fairness metrics. Finally, the system is end-to-end open, enabling interaction with external optimization solvers and extending the method's end-user base. End-to-end open comparisons with state-of-the-art interactive fairness methods reveal comparable solution quality and runtime, with the added benefit of superior fairness guarantees. The method also scales effectively to large-scale instances, handling thousands of candidates and teams. A key contribution of our work is the open-source release of all code, including the application, interviews, end-user interface, and core algorithm. We hope this open and reproducible framework encourages the development of open questions and extensions to enhance fairness in hiring. This paper was selected as an ACM System, Information and Network Security Paper of the Day. The code is available at https://github.com/NoaDror/Interactive_Fair_Allocation.

The rise of large language models (LLMs) has enabled automated generation of chemical reactions and molecular structures, significantly accelerating materials discovery. However, these models often lack reliability and interpretability. For instance, while an auto-regressive transformer can predict the validity of molecular graphs, it often fails to explain *why* certain invalid molecules are rejected. Similarly, models predicting reaction success or product yields often omit explanations for unsuccessful outcomes. We argue that incorporating such explanations is essential for building reliable and interpretable models in chemistry and beyond. We introduce ExChem, a reaction validity model that predicts both success and failure outcomes. ExChem leverages molecular substructure graphs to offer interpretable insights into reaction success, utilizing an attention mechanism to highlight relevant substructures. We present an interactive interface allowing chemists to explore these explanations and adjust molecular reactants to steer ExChem toward specific outcomes.

We analyze two specific detection configurations: one where the base station observes all transmit antenna signals and another where it observes only a subset. Assuming the base station has access to a perfect delayed matched filter dictionary, we derive a closed-form expression for the mean square error. Leveraging this expression along with random matrix theory, we establish the equivalent objective function. Numerical results demonstrate that our theoretical analysis accurately reflects the equivalent objective function, the mean square error, and the bit error rate. Furthermore, we determine the optimal regularized least-squares regularization parameter for each scenario in these situations. Additionally, we introduce a novel regularized least-squares variant that does not rely on the delayed matched filter dictionary. This approach is applicable even when the number of observed received signals is less than the total number of transmit antennas, a condition under which conventional regularized least-squares methods cannot be used. Finally, we confirm that the regularized least-squares variant effectively reduces both the mean square error and the bit error rate compared to its observed-only version. This validation holds true whether the system utilizes a Hadamard matrix or a random matrix as the precoding matrix. These approaches are particularly advantageous in battery-powered devices with a limited number of received antennas, offering performance gains over traditional regularized least-squares techniques. The observed square error and bit error rate improvements remain consistent across various regularized least-squares regularization parameters. The system's performance also remains robust regardless of the base station's received signal count, provided an appropriate regularized least-squares parameter is employed. For instance, in a configuration with eight antennas, the regularized least-squares parameter is set to 1024. The work is licensed under CC BY 4.0.

This study investigates the kinematic and temporal evolution of the South Atlantic rift by analyzing the architecture of the pre- and post-rift strata, as well as the arrangement of half-grabens and fault structures. The analysis draws on a comprehensive, multi-source 3D seismic dataset that spans the entire basin and adjacent highlands, including the passive continental shelves of both the African and South American sides. Our findings indicate that the basin's evolution was significantly influenced by the position and movement of the mantle plume located beneath the central Atlantic, which was actively migrating toward the opening Central Atlantic. This evidence supports the hypothesis that the South Atlantic rift originated as a reactivated inherited Jurassic structure. Compared to other rift segments within the Jurassic Atlantic system, the South Atlantic is distinguished by a lower frequency of faulting, a reduced magnitude of crustal thinning, and a less rugged topographic profile on the adjacent continental shelves. These discrepancies are most pronounced in the initial phases of rifting and the formation of the first-sequence post-rift strata, as the basin struggled to accumulate a substantial volume of syn-drift sediments. Consequently, the evolution of the South Atlantic rift was both more intricate and protracted than that of the Central and West Atlantic rifts. This research is anticipated to offer significant insights for the exploration of hydrocarbon resources in the deepwater areas of the South Atlantic rift basin.

While contrastive learning is a popular method that generates discriminative representations by creating positive and negative pairs, constructing meaningful pairs for segmentation tasks remains challenging in an unsupervised setting. To address this, we introduce a novel unsupervised pre-training framework that circumvents the limitations of contrastive learning. This approach is grounded in two core principles: employing unsupervised over-segmentation as a pre-training objective via mutual information maximization, and implementing boundary-aware preserving learning. Experiments conducted on two benchmark medical segmentation datasets demonstrate that our method effectively improves segmentation performance even with limited annotated images. Furthermore, visualizations of learned features reveal that the proposed framework successfully captures both object and boundary characteristics. This paper advocates shifting the focus from mere detection to discovery, specifically identifying novel word senses emerging over time across the entire vocabulary. By extensively fine-tuning both token-based and type-based approaches on recently annotated English and Spanish data, we demonstrate that these models can effectively uncover words undergoing meaning shifts. Change blindness, widely recognized in psychology, describes the failure to notice significant visual changes when attention is diverted. Recently, large-scale language models and their derivatives have been applied to detect vocabulary changes in evolving languages. However, these models exhibit varying susceptibility to context manipulation, such as altering the surrounding sentences of a target token. We term this phenomenon "lexical change blindness," where models miss certain changing words while successfully detecting others. Consistent with psychological findings, we observe that languages with richer morphology show greater susceptibility to this effect. Furthermore, we find that this variability stems from the ability of isolated models to incorporate contextual cues about potential changes, a capability that can be enhanced without additional training when context is made explicitly available.

While prior research has identified that the surrounding context of a changing word provides stronger signals than the word itself, our study offers two key contributions: (1) proving that even models trained on single sentences can leverage context to detect lexical semantic drift, and (2) demonstrating that explicitly providing context improves change detection across the board compared to isolated models. Additionally, we show that tokenizers and models trained on multiple languages are more prone to this lexical change blindness than those handling single languages or keeping context fixed. This effect is partly due to variations in how words are segmented; for instance, the Spanish contraction "al" (a + el) can lead to missed detections when "al" is actually "a" + an evolving noun like "el clima."

Semantic evolution—the gradual process by which word meanings shift over time—is increasingly observable across all languages due to the vast digital corpora available for analysis. Previous work has developed both model- and context-based methods for this task. In this study, we enhance context-based models by applying them to the discovery of newly emerging word senses within the full corpus, rather than just a moving window

We introduce the spin-orbit force for the individual quarks inside a polarized hadron, denoted as ${\bf k}_\perp$-TODF. This force induces an azimuthal asymmetry in the transverse momentum of the constituent quarks, which has been experimentally observed at HERA and the Tevatron and is consistent with 3D wave functions featuring single-quark orbitals beyond a simple Gaussian shape. The sign of the ${\bf k}_\perp$-TODF has been confirmed across various polarized hadron-hermes.

Introduction

Understanding the topological evolution of proteins during their entire folding trajectories is crucial for comprehending both knotted and non-knotted topologies. While crystallographic and NMR structures of several protein knots have been resolved, and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations have produced structures with complex topologies at their mid-folding stages, analyzing these trajectories using traditional topological methods has been challenging. These methods were originally designed for closed rings with well-defined topological types, assuming that proteins fold from fully extended states into compact, knotted configurations. Consequently, they struggle to analyze trajectories beginning from such extended states. Although Li and Shih [1] recently developed an approach to study topological development from both extended and compact states, it remains unsuitable for analyzing complete folding trajectories that start from an extended state.

To address this, we have created a topological analysis method specifically for folding trajectories of proteins that begin from a fully extended state. Our primary objective is to identify the topological development of folding trajectories originating from such states and to reveal the topological factors influencing whether a protein becomes knotted or not.

To achieve this, the head-to-tail superposition of all conformations along a folding trajectory is topologically equivalent to a self-knotting process of a polymer with two ends. Therefore, our method is built upon the topological analysis framework for self-knotting polymers [2, 3]. dark energy component in the early universe proposed to resolve the Hubble Tension. However, the compatibility of EDE with the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) data remains uncertain. This study examines CMB constraints on EDE from Planck 2018 observations, which report a characteristic small-scale bump in the CMB power spectrum when all parameters are varied. Since Planck does not detect this bump when EDE is fixed to standard values, Planck infers the bump's amplitude and scale, yielding sound horizon estimates of $0.46<eta<8.56$ at 68% confidence. We find that Planck's sensitivity to the EDE sound horizon scale is driven by primary CMB anisotropies, specifically the small-scale acoustic bump. Consequently, future missions like Simons Observatory (SO) and the Cosmic Explorer (CE) will also be able to constrain the EDE sound horizon scale, although their sensitivity will be limited to upper bounds on the scale. Furthermore, we show that SO will constrain the amplitude of the bump, with a sensitivity of $10^{-7}$ at 68% confidence. Our analysis of the EDE sound horizon scale is corroborated by big-bang nucleosynthesis constraints. Ultimately, if future experiments detect this bump, the model of EDE can be significantly restricted. We demonstrate that the Simons Observatory will fail to detect the bump only if the sound horizon scale exceeds $\eta>20$. for data augmentation can boost model performance. A counterfactual image involves altering one or more attributes of an object while keeping others constant. For instance, if a model accurately identifies a "red bus," the counterfactual image would change the bus's color to another, like "green," while maintaining other features. Previous methods determined these alterations through heuristic rules; however, these methods are limited because they often fail to account for all attributes and rely on invalid alteration rules that produce unrealistic images. In this paper, we introduce a patch-based generative adversarial network (GP-GAN) to perform counterfactual image augmentation. Specifically, we treat counterfactual image generation as a mask-based inpainting challenge. Given a user-defined counterfactual image, the network learns to alter a specified attribute (such as object color) while preserving the corresponding mask (representing an attribute like the original color). This approach allows for changing multiple attributes simultaneously and ensures the generated counterfactual images remain realistic. Extensive experiments demonstrate that this method significantly enhances model performance across multiple data categories compared to both traditional and state-of-the-art counterfactual image generation techniques. The source code and sources are available at: https://github.com/HarryZhang0327/Counterfactual_Image_Augmentation.

In many supervised classification and detection tasks, training data is incomplete because annotating every attribute in images is costly and time-consuming. While data augmentation is a standard solution to increase training set size and diversity, conventional augmentations like random erasing or flipping may inadvertently introduce bias by over-emphasizing certain attributes and suppressing others. This bias causes models to prioritize frequently occurring attributes (e.g., object color) while neglecting less common ones (e.g., background), thereby harming generalization. To address this, we recently developed the Bias-aware Counterfactual Data Augmentation (BCDA) framework. Building on BCDA, this paper further explores counterfactual image augmentation by investigating more complex and diverse counterfactual images and their corresponding change masks. We propose two main contributions: (1) A method to automatically generate simple counterfactual images by altering a single attribute (such as color) from the given input, and (2) A technique to derive complicated counterfactual images by simultaneously modifying multiple attributes (e.g., color and shape) in a combined manner. These two methods form a data-driven bias-aware counterfactual image augmentation approach. Experimental results indicate that this proposed approach significantly improves model performance on two datasets compared to existing data augmentation techniques.

However, most existing methods rely on pixel-based loss functions like Cross-Entropy (CE) or Dice, which often yield poor performance on continuous features due to the high dimensionality of feature space. Although most deep learning privacy techniques (e.g., differential privacy, federated learning) focus on preventing data exfiltration, they often result in models with reduced accuracy and higher costs. In contrast, this work transforms existing models to ensure privacy. We introduce a novel framework that incorporates privacy into any black-box model without sacrificing accuracy. By leveraging counterfactual data and multi-valued features, we define and construct "private neighborhoods" for each data point, effectively adding differential privacy (DP) noise to the model's output. We provide a general theory for building private neighborhoods, offer efficient algorithms for constructing them, and demonstrate their use in model inversion and data sanitization for privacy. Empirically, we show that on standard datasets, one can add DP noise to model outputs with minimal impact on utility, even when features have many possible values and no counterfactual data is available. Additionally, we introduce a new model inversion attack that infers private user data with higher accuracy and efficiency than current state-of-the-art techniques.

We demonstrate that the Gelfand-Naimark-Segal (GNS) construction serves as a left adjoint to this restriction process. To correctly define this adjoint relationship, it must be understood as a weak natural transformation—a 1-morphism within an appropriate 2-category—instead of merely as a functor mapping between categories. This study utilizes data from the Fermi satellite to examine the spectral energy distribution (SED) of M87 across multiple wavelengths, spanning radio to GeV gamma-rays. By comparing M87's SED with theoretical models of its geometry, magnetic field intensity, and particle acceleration mechanisms, we evaluate the viability of a hadronic origin for its gamma-rays. Our analysis indicates that hadronic processes can successfully reproduce M87's GeV emission only if the radio galaxy is divided into a core and a jet, and if the core's electron population exhibits a break in its energy spectrum at approximately $10^{11}$~GeV. Under these conditions, we derive a proton minimum energy of $4.5\times 10^{12}$~GeV and a maximum energy between $2.1\times 10^{14}$~GeV and $6.5\times 10^{14}$~GeV. If M87's GeV gamma-rays are indeed produced via hadronic processes, the required proton flux would be significant enough to contribute substantially to the GeV background observed by Fermi. Finally, we assess the feasibility of detecting such a signal from M87's core or its minimum flux against the GeV background using upcoming instruments such as CTA.

By integrating statistical physics, stochastic processes, and computational methods, we examine how a fleet of dynamic travelers traverses this system, thereby creating time-dependent, "driver's seat" perspectives of connection strengths and structural organization. Our analysis reveals that the macroscopic dynamics of a single airline operate in harmony with, yet distinct from, the behavior of an infinite variety of airline fleets on an unstructured complex. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the mesoscopic hopping structure of the undirected complex is determined by the combined effects of travel duration distributions and direct link distances within the mean-field regime. Air travel constitutes a vital global infrastructure that supports international commerce, makes long-distance goods transport feasible, and enables people to traverse the world. As a result, it is essential to understand how potential disruptions to air travel can impact the macroeconomy and daily routines. This paper offers a quantitative analysis of the air transport system by constructing a dataset of all possible direct flights and a monthly effective route network derived from actual flight trajectories. We investigate how a limited number of simultaneous flight bans at random locations progressively disconnect the effective route network, contrasting this with the infinite variety of fleets traveling on a hypothetical direct-link network. Additionally, we assess the economic consequences of these disruptions using a simplified model of direct economic output derived from complex network metrics. Our results indicate that the evolutionary dynamics of a single airline are distinct from those of an infinite variety of fleets on an unstructured complex. To address flight bans, we integrated our model with a straightforward complex network framework for estimating direct economic output. We found that extensive flight restrictions are not required to cause significant economic damage; even a small number of simultaneous bans gradually lead to network fragmentation and a rapid, nonlinear decline in economic activity due to reduced market access. These insights are available at http://arxiv.org/abs/1109.0821.

Nevertheless, extracting activities from wearables presents significant challenges, primarily due to the difficulty of obtaining large datasets that span the full spectrum of human movement. Furthermore, while past methods often relied on hand-crafted features, they failed to generalize across diverse wearables and health sensors, a limitation that deep neural networks have overcome by directly processing raw data. This paper introduces Generalizing Activity Recognition with fEatures from Deep Learning across Multiple sensors (GFER-M), the initial method capable of recognizing in-the-wild activities using raw data from any wearable platform across various sensor types. Additionally, GFER-M addresses the lack of generalization in state-of-the-art techniques by utilizing automatically learned features from data from sensors fundamentally different from the target device. The method's validity is supported by experiments on two extensive activity datasets and five distinct sensor types. Results indicate that GFER-M matches the performance of methods trained and tested on the same wearable platform with raw data from accelerometer and gyroscope sensors, achieving an F1 score of 0.85 on test data from a health sensor (heart rate) mounted on a wristband. Additionally, when evaluated on health sensors from other wearable devices, such as a chest strap, GFER-M demonstrates superior performance compared to methods using features from the same sensor category (0.70 vs. 0.51 F1 score), confirming the method's generalization capabilities across both activity spaces and sensor types.

To quantify this, we extend the probability distribution for the dark energy scale, $p(\Lambda)$, initiated in the KKLMMT scenario, to other AdS/CMS-compatible models. By emphasizing that most of our extensions rely on standard string theory mechanisms, we aim to strengthen the case that the dark energy probability estimate is robust across the majority of string compactifications. To enhance the efficiency of these interviews, candidates are typically assigned scores or ranks to help recruiters identify the most promising applicants to advance to the offer stage. venshtein introduced the sequence reconstruction problem, which examines a scenario where an identical sequence from a specific set is sent through several channels, with the decoder observing the resulting distinct outputs. Assuming the transmitted sequence lies at a distance $d$ from a code and that each channel introduces no more than $r$ errors, the goal is to determine the minimum number of channels necessary to uniquely recover the original sequence. This number must exceed the maximum overlap between two metric balls of radius $r$, provided their centers are separated by at least distance $d$. This paper investigates the sequence reconstruction problem for permutations using Hamming distance. Within this framework, we define a Cayley graph and calculate the precise value of the largest intersection of two metric balls under Hamming distance for the cases where $r=4$ and $d\geqslant 5$, as well as when $d=2r$. Additionally, we propose several open questions regarding the general scenario. To address this general case, we define a new combinatorial structure termed a $(w,h)$-separator and demonstrate its direct correlation with the intersection of metric balls on permutation Cayley graphs. Leveraging this definition, we construct several 5-separators. Since a $(w,h)$-separator implies that any permutation differing from two others by at most $w$ transpositions can be correctly identified from $h$ noisy channels, these separators provide upper bounds on the sequence reconstruction capacity for such channels. Notably, our findings indicate that the capacity for two errors per channel is $4n\log_2 5+4n\log_2 n+O(n)$ transpositions (equivalent to a capacity of 4 symbols per channel when using the symmetric group), which significantly surpasses the capacity of two errors per channel for permutations of length 3, which is a capacity of 2 symbols per channel. Finally, to fully resolve the problem for lengths 4 and 5, we identify several specific cases to investigate. \textit{Note:} This research was conducted while the author was a graduate student at Penn State University. Part of this work was presented at the International Workshop on Combinatorial Coding Theory 2018. Part of this work was also featured in the poster session of the SIAM Annual Meeting 2019.}

We investigate the role of the brainstem reticular formation (BRF) in alertness and attention. Lesions in this area result in coma or narcolepsy, whereas stimulation can trigger seizures. We contend that severe disruptions to BRF connectivity cause an inability to filter noise, overwhelming the rest of the brain with excessive information. This concept of "attention failure" provides a new framework for understanding questions lacking sufficient context. Based on this, we propose a counterfactual attention-based QA model capable of effectively addressing such queries, which also outperforms recent state-of-the-art models.
