In this study, we examined the Shannon entropy of linear Majorana fermions to determine how an external linear potential alters this quantity. We then constructed an ensemble of these particles to analyze the model's thermodynamic characteristics. Ultimately, we demonstrated how both Shannon entropy and thermodynamic properties change under the influence of a linear potential. The findings indicate that for both entropy and thermodynamic variables, the growth rate under a linear potential is exactly half of what is observed in standard Fermi or Bose statistics or for Dirac fermions. Furthermore, these differences become even more pronounced when the chemical potential is zero, a condition that makes Shannon entropy vanish for Dirac fermions and Bose-Einstein statistics but results in non-zero values for Majorana fermions and Dirac fermions with a non-zero chemical potential. A key feature of the Shannon entropy and thermodynamic properties of linear Majorana fermers is their ability to be simply derived from the corresponding quantities of Dirac fermions with half the number of particles. Finally, we provided a physical interpretation for these phenomena. This research is significant because it provides an often-overlooked perspective on Majorana fermions, a topic of current interest in the direct generation of single electrons. Keywords: Majorana fermion, Shannon entropy, thermodynamics, particle statistics. \\\\ arXivId: 2206.03001 [quant-ph]

Brain tumors are abnormal growths within the brain that can be either benign or malignant, affecting people of all ages and potentially causing severe health issues. Accurate and early detection and diagnosis are critical for managing and treating these conditions. Researchers utilize MRI imaging for detection because these scans clearly distinguish between healthy and tumor-affected brain tissue. While radiologists and neurosurgeons manually segment tumors from T1, T1CE, and other MRI sequences to aid treatment planning, such as radiotherapy, this study develops an automatic segmentation technique for brain tumors using only T1 and T1CE MRI sequences, leveraging the fact that not all tumors enhance with contrast. The proposed method utilizes level set-based active learning, where the boundary evolution function is defined by boundary, centroid, and connectivity metrics to create a robust classifier for estimating and removing over-segmented healthy brain tissue. Experimental findings confirm that the proposed method performs effectively.

Recently, differentiable rendering has become increasingly accurate, yet modeling observation visibility remains challenging. This paper presents a method for accurately computing render gradient values in shadow regions. Unlike prior approaches that rely on finite differences or additional multi-scale rendering, our method integrates differentiable visibility constraints directly into the backward pass. By applying the chain rule, we derive closed-form expressions for partial derivatives of pixel observations with respect to 3D point coordinates. This allows for the accurate inversion of visibility parameters from input images when using an observer-specific renderer. To validate our method, we constructed a dataset of 200 images featuring six distinct light source types. Our experiments confirm the accuracy of the proposed algorithm and demonstrate its effectiveness in inverting both observation space and object space render gradients.

To stabilize shaky camera footage, users typically select a deinterlacing algorithm, blend it with other editing choices, and then choose a telecine method to extract frames, creating a cumbersome workflow with numerous points of potential error. Videos captured by handheld cameras often consist of fields rather than complete frames, a problem especially acute during playback on lower-bandwidth displays or when played back at the camera's capture rate. Our work introduces simultaneous deinterlacing and frame extraction, addressing both issues with several novel algorithms. These methods outperform existing manual and automatic techniques in terms of visual quality, speed, and memory usage. By automatically removing interlacing and decimating the video, our approach reduces memory usage by up to 50%. Users can choose to display the video at its original frame rate, double it, or any other rate. However, these objectives often conflict, and in many operations, stability is prioritized even at the cost of reduced performance. Adjusting reactor conditions to maintain stability frequently involves lowering the reaction rate, which can cause the system to become trapped in unstable local steady states that operate far below potential capacity. Current control systems typically rely on iterative adjustments, taking significant time to reach a stable equilibrium; during this period, the fluctuations between unstable steady states can trigger dangerous fluctuations and potentially lead to runaways. This study examines reactor dynamics during the search for a stable steady state, highlighting the risks of oscillations and runaway reactions. It further analyzes the conditions required for the existence of multiple steady states and introduces an analytical method to identify when the dynamics remain monotonic. By anticipating these scenarios, control strategies can be optimized to reach a stable steady state monotonically, thereby eliminating the hazards of oscillations and runaway reactions. The findings also reveal that the critical reactor volume can vary depending on whether the objective is monotonicity or the absence of unstable steady states. Ultimately, the insights gained from analyzing steady-state dynamics can be leveraged to significantly improve control performance. The approaches and conclusions presented are broadly applicable to catalytic reactors exhibiting runaway behavior, including CSTRs, tubular reactors, and three-stage adiabatic CSTRs.

Rapid advances in both controlled and unsupervised deep learning are increasingly being harnessed to uncover hidden dynamics within complex dynamical systems. This letter demonstrates that a control strategy rooted in Volterra-Wiener frequency domain decomposition can be integrated with a support vector regression meta-model to efficiently identify stable and unstable manifolds, even in high-dimensional systems. These identification capabilities are essential for ensuring the safe exploration of a system's state space. The examples provided include a continuous stirred-tank reactor, a chemical batch process, and a Lorenz system.

Although Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at natural language understanding and reasoning, they often struggle with spatial awareness and geometry, limiting applications in 3D scene understanding and manipulation. We present the 3D Language Model (3DLM), which integrates 3D scene encoders, object relators, and a LLM within a unified framework to facilitate bidirectional interaction between text and 3D scenes. This model supports tasks such as describing and editing 3D scenes, as well as reverse tasks like completing descriptions or generating modifications from natural language. By leveraging pre-trained text encoders and cross-attention mechanisms, 3DLM efficiently achieves this interaction with just 0.17% of the parameters of the base LLM. On both in-domain and out-of-domain datasets, 3DLM significantly outperforms current approaches in descriptive and editing tasks, as well as reverse tasks. Additionally, it demonstrates strong zero-shot capabilities in spatial reasoning and object relationship understanding. The source code can be found at https://github.com/zhijianshu/3DLM.

This study examines the dispersion of a population of fractional Brownian walkers, which exhibit long-time correlations and possess time-dependent, heterogeneous diffusivity. The goal is to derive the scenarios arising from these individual-level characteristics by analyzing the temporal evolution of the population's spatial distribution. We investigate the feasibility of extracting these microscale properties from macroscale observations using an extension of the central limit theorem for summing independent, non-identically distributed random variables. Our findings indicate that when all walkers share the same self-similar diffusivity, the resulting processes include subdiffusion, superdiffusion, and Gaussian diffusion. Furthermore, if the population possesses a heterogeneous diffusivity distribution, the overall behavior is superdiffusive, even if every individual walker is moving diffusively. To validate these theoretical outcomes, we utilize the Python package `fwalk`, which simulates fractional Brownian walkers and various other walk types while estimating their kinetic parameters. This study demonstrates that walker heterogeneity can mimic the effects of inter-walker correlations, making it difficult to distinguish between these mechanisms based solely on the broadening of the population's spatial distribution. Consequently, understanding whether behavior stems from individual walker properties or population dynamics is crucial, as these processes can be influenced most effectively by targeted interventions. The `fwalk` tool can also serve to identify the underlying mechanisms of observed spreading behaviors. Keywords: Anomalous diffusion; fractional Brownian motion; walk heterogeneity; differential central limit theorem; superdiffusion; subdiffusion; stochasticity.

Introduction

This paper explores the spatial distribution of a population of fractional Brownian walkers to establish a direct link between the potential for anomalous diffusion and two specific factors: long-time correlations and heterogeneity. These elements are examined through the evolution of the population's spatial distribution and the application of a generalized central limit theorem for sums of independent, non-identically distributed random variables. The findings are expected to be relevant to systems where components possess complex, potentially heterogeneous properties. Key questions arise regarding whether observed deviations from Gaussian diffusion stem from correlations among individuals, their intrinsic nature, or a combination of both. Resolving this is vital because, for instance, in biological contexts, the anti-cancer efficacy of a drug targeting walker correlations might be completely undermined by walker heterogeneity. Additionally, the *fwalk* package is essential for investigating these systems to validate findings derived from other methods, offering an alternative to `fwd`.

Field quantization is widely recognized as a pivotal step toward understanding the quantum nature of matter, yet it typically requires an infinite number of modes, a concept that remains controversial within classical physics. To address this, we examine the conditions under which field quantization can occur without relying on quantum frameworks, using only classical physics and its transformation rules across inertial frames. By utilizing the general solution to source-free Maxwell's equations, we derive a specific relation for the charge density that allows quantization while maintaining the continuity equation and the full equations of motion for charged particles. This quantization must satisfy a non-radiation condition that applies to all inertial frames, a state we term "quantum equilibrium." The spatial distribution of charge and current densities in this equilibrium is not arbitrary; it imposes a differential equation on the spatial part of the charge density that is mathematically equivalent to the Schrödinger equation for the hydrogen atom. Consequently, the energy spectrum of hydrogen emerges as eigenvalues of this equation, and their corresponding eigenfunctions resemble standing waves.

Field quantization is often viewed as a consequence of the general solution to source-free Maxwell's equations, a state we define as "quantum equilibrium." This quantization is governed by a specific charge distribution that fulfills a differential equation identical to that for the hydrogen atom, thereby explaining its unique energy spectrum. Furthermore, a non-radiation condition in any inertial frame is shown to be equivalent to the charge and current satisfying the same differential equation. Classical electromagnetic field energy, subject to this constraint, yields the discrete energy levels of hydrogen. Additionally, we demonstrate that an uniformly accelerating observer perceives charges in quantum equilibrium as radiating, which we interpret as a classical foundation for the Unruh effect.

Furthermore, we observe that even with low-performance baseline detectors, our approach significantly improves in-domain detection performance. In summary, our contributions are: (1) a theoretically grounded method for enhancing the confidence calibration of object detection models, (2) evidence that this method can simultaneously boost detection performance, and (3) an extension of the approach for class-agnostic object detection. Our code is available at https://github.com/AmirHJ/C2OD.

This paper introduces a discovery algorithm that generates Dynamic Condition Response (DCR) graphs representing declarative processes from event streams. The algorithm identifies both static and dynamic characteristics of these processes to construct a model that is minimized, thereby preventing over- or under-approximation, and is compact, meaning it contains no redundant information. Over the last few years, researchers have introduced multiple process discovery algorithms. The DCR graph approach represents a declarative process model that effectively balances expressiveness with simplicity. This work presents two primary contributions. Firstly, it details a declarative process model suitable for representation in that format. Secondly, it outlines algorithms for achieving this, a task that remains unresolved in existing literature. To accomplish this, the method leverages the three core properties of the declarative process model: enabledness, exclusivity, and responsiveness. Additionally, the proposed approach benefits from utilizing process mining metrics, specifically selected mining measures that assist in capturing the nuances of a mining algorithm. The experimental results confirm the method's efficacy.

Process discovery algorithms reconstruct process models from event logs, yet no single optimal format exists as different models highlight distinct process attributes. We examine two process models—the BPMN and BPEL notations and the Ac-Triples model—and develop algorithms to translate event logs into each. Our proposed approach represents a declarative process model that successfully captures all core properties of ongoing activities. We present the ac-tuples and an algorithm for deriving declarative process models. This model explicitly incorporates the attributes that set it apart from other formats. Our findings are effective, demonstrated by the URL http://www.cs.unibo.it/~ghedami/teaching/MI2/DeclarativeProcessMining.pdf.

Key innovations of Liger include the cross-dispersed low-resolution spectrometer for AO testing and acquisition, an expandable low-resolution IFS for IFS acquisition, a high-acquisition-speed high-resolution imager with an adjustable FOV for AO-imaging. Previous attempts to overcome this resolution barrier have either compromised the one-to-one mapping between source and detector intensities or incurred excessive computational costs. In this paper, we propose a method to surpass Rayleigh's curse in aperture-limited scenarios that are both linear and quadratic. Specifically, we present an algorithm to invert a convolution with a Gaussian kernel—imposed by the transmitting antenna—in the presence of a convolution with an unknown, but strictly positive, Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) kernel. To ensure uniqueness, the GMM kernel must exhibit bimodality. Our approach relies exclusively on the positive GMM component of the convolution. We demonstrate that, aside from handling the Gaussian convolution, a bimodal GMM with two equal-weighted components yields a resolution of $\sigma_{\rm eff}^2 = \sigma_1^2 + 0.2444\dots d^2$, where $d$ represents the separation between the two peaks and $\sigma_1$ is the standard deviation of the individual components. This technique has significant implications for Tomographic Angular Spectroscopy (TAS), potentially enabling the resolution of closely spaced tumors. We have open-sourced the code for this inversion on GitHub at \url{https://github.com/AmirHJ/TAS-Inversion-Paper}.

We examine a continuous-time linear system where the state vector is periodic with period $T$. It has been demonstrated that if the system is controllable, there exists a time-varying, periodic state vector that can reach any arbitrary value at specific time instants within the interval $[0,T]$. This implies that for periodic systems, rayleigh's curse is eliminated. Building on this finding, we introduce a technique to image an arbitrary, time-independent source distribution using sensors with finite apertures, thereby achieving super-resolution. Our methodology involves determining the sources by observing the distribution of a single delta function. To facilitate this, we provide a MATLAB repository containing code for imaging arbitrary distributions and for constructing a non-trivial periodic solution from a time-independent source.

mechanisms driving regime shifts is a critical yet challenging goal in population biology, especially for non-linear systems. A key factor underlying these shifts is the loss of stability in the equilibrium states that characterize the fluctuating species' abundance. In this study, we monitor the asymptotic stability of the coexistence equilibrium within the discrete Hassell map, a habitat modification model, by analyzing its complex eigenvalues across the parameter space. Our primary objective is to trace the boundary of a stability region adjacent to a Neimark-Sacker (complex eigenvalue) bifurcation, where the species reaches its maximum vulnerability to collapse. This boundary is defined by two superimposed curves in parameter space: the inner curve marks the onset of the bifurcation, while the outer curve, termed the safety curve, indicates the limit of stability before the species enters a high-risk state. Tipping points and the associated bifurcation scenarios lie beyond this safety curve. The area enclosed between the two bifurcation and safety curves in parameter-space dynamics offers a premature warning sign for an impending species collapse. We validate these theoretical findings using the population data of the red fox (*Vulpes vulpes*) in the Netherlands. Although the Hassel map was originally developed to capture the destabilizing effects of rapid habitat changes on population dynamics, this complex bifurcation scenario suggests that adverse outcomes can also stem from gradual, monotonic habitat deterioration. Consequently, the safety curve provides a warning signal and a framework for the early detection and prevention of collapse events.

This work extends the methodology of Delayed Bifurcation by T. H. H.uan and S. Ruan to investigate the safety curve phenomenon in a habitat modification model. Specifically, we confirm that the non-linear Leslie map with density-dependent recruitment and habitat modification also exhibits a safety curve and a bifurcation set. These delayed bifurcations explain why population crashes often occur after the species appears to have stabilized at a lower, seemingly new equilibrium following habitat degradation. Both the safety curve and the complex bifurcation scenario provide a framework for the early warning and prevention of population collapses.

Species extinctions frequently result from the deteriorating habitat quality, yet the delayed nature of these events often creates a misleading impression of resilience even as environments degrade. This phenomenon, where a system appears to have reached a new stable state before suddenly collapsing, can be mathematically explained by the delayed bifurcation along a safety curve. The proposed system utilizes a trilingual BERT-based model trained on English, Slovene, and Croatian. The study evaluates various configurations using two-language datasets and introduces a straightforward multi-task model for sentiment classification. Documents containing multiple languages are increasingly common, especially in news and social media, yet few models exist for analyzing sentiments within this context. This paper assesses the generalization capabilities of BERT-based models across different languages. We collect parallel datasets in English, German, and Dutch to train a cross-lingual model and then test it on various text classification tasks using Dutch and German documents. Our generalization tests reveal that models perform poorly on languages with limited data, notably lacking support for sentiment classification in Dutch. Additionally, we examine and mitigate the impact of mixed-language documents and provide an analysis of the factors influencing our findings.

Although BERT-based models have been adapted for document-level sentiment classification in German and Dutch, their performance across multiple languages remains under-investigated. The generalization of pre-trained models to texts in other languages often yields disappointing results. This study investigates the effectiveness of BERT-based models for sentiment classification in German and Dutch by: 1) building upon existing German and Dutch models to create a combined two-language architecture, 2) testing its performance on multi-label sentiments in German and as a binary classifier on single-label sentiments in both languages, and 3) investigating the causes of performance disparities in low-resource scenarios to propose potential mitigations. Nevertheless, these mechanisms can trigger excessive self-invalidations or -downgrades when processes receive numerous random writes to distinct values. This phenomenon, known as the "storm effect," can severely impair multi-process applications. We introduce a low-overhead solution based on switching between self-invalidation and shared caches to mitigate this issue. Furthermore, we present multi-granularity locking, a novel approach enabling fine-grained locking with minimal overhead by combining self-invalidation and shared caches to resolve storms at any level of the invalidation hierarchy. Our evaluation of these techniques on both real hardware and modern coherence protocols demonstrates significant multi-core performance improvements. The proposed multi-granularity locking technique has also been implemented in hardware to validate its effectiveness.

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a graph where every edge $uv\in E$ is assigned a unique label $l(uv)\in \{1,2,\ldots,|E|\}$. A graph is \textit{H-distinguishable} if there exists an edge labeling $\varphi: E\rightarrow \{1,2,\ldots, |E|\}$ such that the sets of labels incident to any two distinct vertices $u,v\in V$ do not both contain an edge of a given induced subgraph $H$. The \textit{H-distinguishable number}, denoted $\chi_H(G)$, is the minimum value of $|E|$ across all such labelings. This note defines the \textit{Thomas-Halton number} of a graph as the smallest number of edges required to make the graph H-distinguishable. We determine this number for paths $P_n$ and determine which graphs can be distinguished by a single labeling. As a byproduct, we generalize a finding by Thomas-Halton regarding paths. \bigskip \noindent \textit{Keywords:} Distinguishing edges; H-distinguishable number; Thomas-Halton number; Paths. \bigskip

By employing a Jackiw-Kerman style Hartree-type two-body trial wavefunction, we derive an effective semiclassical Hamiltonian. Numerical findings demonstrate that quantum effects can indeed generate chaos within the non-chaotic regions of the classical H\'enon-Heiles system. Furthermore, as the $\hbar$ parameter approaches zero, the quantum chaotic states converge upon the classical chaotic states, with the Lyapunov exponent of the quantum system matching that of its classical counterpart. Consequently, within the non-chaotic domains of the classical H\'enon-Heiles system, the stability of classical orbits can be interpreted through the instability of their corresponding quantum ground states. Additionally, the classical turning points of the orbits are shown to arise from the node formation in the quantum wavefunctions. The consistency of this study is further validated by the agreement between the classical energy and the sum of the quantum kinetic and potential energies at the fourth order of $\hbar$. This work offers additional evidence for the significance of the correspondence principle in systems exhibiting both classical and quantum chaos. Consequently, the Chaotic Bootstrap can arguably be reformulated based on the principle of non-chaotic quantum stability. Finally, the Chaotic Bootstrap is suggested to have significant implications for the search for a classical theory of quantum gravity and related frameworks.

According to the Big Bang theory, all matter, energy, space, and time originated from a single point. By tracing the backward evolution of the universe, one can observe a gradual contraction from its maximum size toward zero, culminating in a singularity. The gravitational dynamics governing this process are governed by the Friedmann equation: $\left(\frac{\dot{a}}{a}\right)^{2}=\frac{8\pi{G}}{3}\rho$, where $a$ represents the scale factor, $\dot{a}$ its time derivative, $\rho$ the total energy density, $G$ the gravitational constant, and $t$ the time variable. Classical physics dictates that if $\rho$ remains positive, the left side of the equation cannot be negative, implying that the scale factor $a$ must reach zero, thereby creating a singularity. Consequently, the expanding universe will eventually cease growth and contract back to a singular point in the absence of a negative energy density component. If patients with specific X-ray characteristics are precisely those at highest risk, these individuals could potentially receive targeted medical attention. Nevertheless, explicitly defining and validating such predictive features remains challenging due to the complex modeling required and the limited availability of confirmed clinical data points. Consequently, the primary objective of this study is to validate the hypothesis that a specific pattern of lung opacities, located in the lower lungs and arranged laterally in a bilaterally symmetric fashion, indicates a significantly elevated risk of respiratory failure. To test this, we compiled a dataset of 1,800 imaged patients, for whom 914 X-rays were labeled with outcomes regarding respiratory failure. We developed an ensemble model specifically designed to predict this particular opacity pattern rather than the general diagnosis of COVID-19. The model's key feature, a features-from-features map, effectively highlights where these opacities appear. While the model demonstrates an impressive ability to distinguish between patients with and without respiratory failure (area under the curve = 0.80), these features do not match those typically seen in standard models. Furthermore, analysis of the features-from-features map reveals that the model focuses on COVID-19 patients with a distinct "batwing" pattern (where wings extend to the outer edges of the lung fields), scoring significantly higher on a risk scale for those with respiratory failure. This pattern contrasts with the central "butterfly" pattern often associated with the disease. Crucially, the model exhibits very low false negatives among patients with respiratory failure, suggesting that failing to identify the "batwing" pattern in an X-ray could have severe, potentially fatal, consequences. Additionally, we compared feature importance across models trained to predict either the batwing pattern or the broader disease, finding that the models for these two tasks rely on largely dissimilar features. Finally, the spatial distribution of these features indicates that radiologists might potentially miss these predictive signs. In summary, this study confirms that a specific "batwing" pattern significantly increases the risk of respiratory failure, a finding that aligns with the intuition that deeply learned features from imaging can sometimes surpass radiologist predictions. The identified pattern is clearly visible in the provided figures and films. The research questions addressed in this study are: Can we identify patients at risk of respiratory failure using only their X-ray images? We analyze existing models and construct a unifying theoretical framework, demonstrating that KGC models often assign high probabilities to nonexistent edges simply because they are unaware of their existence. To illustrate this, we develop a novel causal diagram that clarifies the factual mismatch between the models' limited knowledge and the complete set of knowledge inherent in all KGs. Furthermore, we derive a new perspective on how the bias toward popularity in KGC models stems from the selection bias inherent in KG construction. Based on this foundational analysis, we investigate four key issues: the inconsistency of entity and relation embeddings, the impact of neighbor sampling depth, the false positive problem in self-attention mechanisms, and the necessity of normalization in rotation-based models. To address these inconsistencies, we explicitly define the search space for entities and relations within KGC models and propose two frameworks to standardize embeddings within this space. This comprehensive analysis offers essential insights for enhancing the intrinsic explainability of KGC models and fills significant gaps in current research. As a practical contribution, we introduce the header `Search Space Standardization` to improve the overall performance and reliability of existing KGC models. The source code for our entity and relation normalization methods, `ESSN` and `RSSN`, is available at https://github.com/Elham2004/ESSN. These innovations have been successfully integrated into various KGC models, notably enhancing the performance of TransH. Our experimental results indicate that False Positive Rates are 16.1% lower in TransH+ESSN compared to the original model, and 14.7% lower in TransH+ESSN+RSSN relative to TransH. Additionally, we demonstrate that the RGCN model also suffers from the false positive issue. In conclusion, our work provides fundamental insights into enhancing both the performance and intrinsic reliability of KGC models and their extensions.

Introduction {#sec:intro} ---------- ----------

Quasinormal modes (QNMs) are fundamental characteristics of black holes, representing damped oscillations that occur after a perturbation and before the final stationary state is reached. These modes are defined by complex frequencies $\omega(q,k)$, where the real part indicates the oscillation frequency and the imaginary part determines the damping rate or lifetime. The concept of QNM was first introduced by Regge and Wong for Schwarzschild black holes without a cosmological constant and was subsequently termed quasinormal mode in that context. The dispersion relations of these modes help identify the spacetime geometry near a black hole. For instance, the specific form of these relations near an AdS boundary can be linked to the critical exponents of a dual conformal field theory (CFT).

In many prior studies, dispersion relations were derived by linearizing perturbations. However, this method has clear limitations, as the resulting relations depend linearly on the wave number $k$. Consequently, such calculations cannot determine higher derivative couplings in the dual CFT Lagrangian. To overcome this, it is essential to compute non-linear (non-perturbative) dispersion relations.

Anomaly detection in data streams is critical for identifying and flagging irregularities in real-time, a capability that underpins many modern technologies. Traditional statistical methods often underperform on high-dimensional data, while existing deep learning-based stream anomaly detection algorithms typically require cyclic access to data, limiting their ability to identify anomalies in continuously flowing data.

The RNN-based anomaly detection model described herein was evaluated on both synthetic and real-world data streams and proved effective in flagging anomalous instances. On synthetic streams, the RNN model significantly outperformed both statistical and deep learning-based approaches. Testing on real-world streams—including Enron (high-dimensional time series), Twitter hashtags, and flowing data streams—further confirmed the RNN's superiority over statistical and deep learning methods.

Fluent anomaly detection refers to the process of identifying anomalies in entire sequences or flows of data rather than individual isolated points. Traditional statistical methods and most deep learning-based techniques often fail to effectively capture these fluent patterns.

The RNN-based approach outlined in this paper successfully learns from data streams in a single pass, offering an efficient solution for both point and fluent anomaly detection. Beyond performance, the RNN provides the distinct advantage of being interpretable, as it can be inspected to reveal how and why specific anomalies were identified.

The burden of proving competency does not always lie with the state, and the "clear and convincing" evidence standard is not universally required. We introduce a novel class of dynamical R-matrices, termed 'factored,' which is demonstrated to be equivalent to other established classes. This finding offers an alternative proof of the conjecture regarding weakly set-theoretic R-matrices and yields a non-trivial, non-degenerate dr-bialgebra that is not a quantum group. The findings in ~\cite{CS2} and ~\cite{C2} rely on a non-degenerate dynamical R-matrix constructed via the 'factored' method, thereby confirming that not all non-degenerate dynamical R-matrices are quantum groups. These results extend the findings of ~\cite{C1}, ~\cite{C2}, and ~\cite{C3}. The research was supported by grants from CONACyT (No. 227650) and CONAHCyt (No. 237440).

In this paper, we extend GCMs to multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays (GCA) and introduce new construction methods for GCA pairs and quads. These constructions are enabled by a set of identities defined over a commutative ring. We demonstrate that a quaternary GCA pair is feasible when the product of array sizes across all dimensions equals a quaternary Golay number, subject to an additional constraint on the factorization of that product. Regarding binary GCM quads, we conjecture that feasible sizes can be arbitrary and verify this for dimensions up to 78×78 and other sparsely distributed sizes. For quaternary GCM quads, we show that all positive integers up to 1000 can serve as the size for a single dimension. We also provide constructions for binary and quaternary GCA pairs in dimensions as small as 3×3 and 1×1×1×1, respectively. Finally, we confirm that binary and quaternary GCA pairs with a total product of size equal to 12 can achieve an aperture of 2×2. Constructions for other cases are either straightforward or follow methods similar to those for GCMs. Unlike existing GCM constructions that rely on Hadamard matrices and thus require sizes to be powers of two, our approaches are applicable to any dimension. The proposed methods are also expected to facilitate future work on multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays of other moduli. In recent years, research into Golay Complementary Codes (GCC) has expanded from its original one-dimensional definition to include time-frequency, multi-dimensional, and multi-dimensional time contexts. This body of work is now being extended to multi-user scenarios, specifically Generalized GCCs (G-GCCs), which are critical for next-generation wireless networks. This study focuses on multi-dimensional G-GCCs utilizing a binary quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM) scheme. By employing a Gergonne decomposition, we establish an upper bound on the product of array sizes for quaternary G-GCC quads in two dimensions and propose a construction that meets this limit. While many theoretical models explore tunneling, they are constrained by the lack of experimental realization. This study employs a fully classical simulation of light-wave dynamics within spatial dimensions to demonstrate tunneling across statistical ensembles. By applying the canonical ensemble canonical ensemble ensemble canonical ensemble to the near-field evolution of light-wave phases, the simulation captures tunneling through both rectangular and resonant potential barriers. Furthermore, it reveals coherent turn-around oscillations that mirror the mirror-image evanescent oscillations occurring before and after the potential step in standard tunneling events. These findings provide a fully classical framework for understanding wavefunction behavior near potential barriers, offering an alternative to the conventional Schrödinger equation approach that requires unexplained, non-classical mappings between light-wave phases and quantum probabilities. The proposed model suggests new methods for directly visualizing wavefunction dynamics and suggests that the conceptual understanding of quantum phenomena, including tunneling, can be grounded in classical physics. Additionally, it opens avenues for directly observing the wavefunction in future experiments.

While significant research has been conducted on the superconducting quantum critical point, which marks the transition from a normal to a superconducting state as carrier density or temperature varies, far less attention has been given to the underdoped regime. In this area, the metal exhibits non-Fermi liquid characteristics, and the energy gap shows an $|n_x,n_y|$-dependent "pocket" structure that resembles quantum tunneling. This paper demonstrates that the dynamics of an electron gas at a surface can naturally generate such a pocket structure in the energy gap and explain the non-Fermi liquid behavior of underdoped metals. Although the current work relies on a simple classical model, it provides a compelling classical analogy for the complex quantum behavior observed in underdoped cuprates.

Although a single-mode drive can only overcome a potential barrier equal to half its height—limiting control over quantum wavefunction dynamics—engaging multiple modes within a cavity enables the full exploration of quantum tunneling. This report utilizes the Discrete Variable Representation (DVR) method to simulate multi-mode quantum dynamics. It illustrates how multi-mode drive protocols can be leveraged both to characterize the complete behavior of a quantum particle across potential barriers and to establish a potential pathway for manipulating ultra-cold atoms within optical lattices.

Although graph neural networks (GNNs) offer a promising avenue for encoding and analyzing these systems, their potential for discovering laws of physics and understanding system behavior remains limited. In this context, we present a framework for formulating and analyzing complex systems as dynamical networks. Specifically, we develop GNNs to encode interacting particle systems, thereby enabling the analysis of temporal dynamics and the extraction of interaction graphs from time-series data. We demonstrate that these models can learn systems' dynamics, visualize their interaction graphs, and classify diverse interaction types based on derived features. Furthermore, we show that the graphs learned from specific systems (such as cellular automata or flocking models) can accurately represent other dynamics occurring within the same system class. Consequently, our framework successfully learns and generalizes dynamical laws and their associated interaction graphs, offering a pathway to analyze and understand complex systems through learned graph structures. This approach facilitates a data-driven discovery of dynamical laws, enhancing our ability to generalize and make predictions about such systems. While we focus on interacting particle systems, the framework is applicable to any system that can be modeled as a dynamic network, and we provide an open-source implementation.

Although GNNs can effectively encode and analyze complex systems, it is not inherently straightforward to define the graphs they should represent. We introduce a method for learning interaction graphs that incorporates prior knowledge about system dynamics. By integrating this with GNNs, we can more accurately encode and evaluate the dynamics of complex systems. Our approach learns graphs by optimizing an objective function grounded in typicality theory, which assesses how characteristic a state is within a specific system class. We illustrate this technique using various information-theoretic measures of typicality and apply it to both static and evolving graphs. Through numerical examples, we confirm that this method can discover interaction laws, accurately analyze system dynamics, and distinguish between different dynamical laws and graphs.

While GNNs can successfully encode and analyze complex systems, there remains a challenge in learning the interaction graphs they are designed to represent. We propose a solution that leverages prior knowledge about complex system dynamics. Our method learns these graphs by optimizing an objective function rooted in typicality, which quantifies the typical nature of a state within a given system class. We demonstrate this framework on both static and dynamic graphs, showing its ability to learn interaction graphs, analyze system dynamics, and differentiate between various typical graphs and states.

We establish a lower bound for the homological stability range of mapping class groups of oriented surfaces with boundary, formulated as a function of the valence (the count of boundary components). This extends prior stability results to four additional cases and determines the optimal stability interval. The proof relies on interpreting the classifying space of the mapping class group as a configuration space on a surface with a "punctured" homology ring of integers as the coefficient ring.

represents a new minimally invasive approach for ablating intracranial structures to manage mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (MTLE). Accurate planning and real-time monitoring during stereotactic needle placement and laser fiber insertion are critical for maximizing seizure freedom while minimizing memory, endocrine, neurological, and neurodevelopmental side effects, which are influenced by the extent of tissue removal. Although advanced imaging is employed, visually interpreting the progression of contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (ceMRI) and T1-weighted post-contrast MRI into tissue necrosis zones remains challenging for neurosurgeons. While image processing techniques have been explored to overlay predicted ablation zones onto ceMRI, no current method allows clinicians to monitor ablation dynamics in real-time using imaging. This study introduces a method to track ablation zones within LITT-constrained diffusion processes, specifically the Thomson-Shixian model, to generate ablation zone maps in image space. The proposed approach, which incorporates an inversion step to reverse light field effects from stereotactic procedures, was validated using an open-source LITT dataset. Results indicate that the ablation zone map proves valuable for visualizing ablation progression. Furthermore, when combined with a mean first passage time model for predicting ablation, the map enables determination of the time required for ablated ions to reach the hippocampus—the brain region most pivotal for seizure generation in MTLE patients. Consequently, this technique offers a straightforward and efficient strategy for real-time ablation zone monitoring and strategic fiber positioning to mitigate adverse effects in patients with MTLE.

Recent years have seen significant strides in imaging and computation for brain surgery, yet their application to LITT remains limited. To develop the algorithm described herein, we required an open-source LITT dataset, prompting the release of the Mount Sinai LITT Dataset (MSLIND). This release includes ground-truth ablation zone maps derived from ceMRI across 12 cases. We developed algorithms to predict these zones and validated them against the remaining MSLIND dataset. The proposed method and the newly created MSLIND dataset will facilitate the advancement of lobe-specific LITT planning and real-time ablation zone monitoring through open access.

For individuals with severe, drug-resistant epilepsy, surgical intervention remains the only viable option to halt seizures. Since the 1950s, resecting the hippocampus has been the primary treatment for MTLE, typically achieved through craniotomy-assisted procedures. This paper assesses the safety and performance of automated fiber assignment (AFA) systems, which are responsible for optical fiber-target safety checks and the selection of the most suitable AFA configuration for each target list. To validate the safety of an operational system, we developed unit tests and simulation-based tests for all safety check algorithms within the Korean-African Large Scale Structure (KALSS) survey's AFA system. These KALSS AFA unit tests serve as a reference for KALSS and other telescopes utilizing similar systems. To verify the performance of the check algorithms, a simulation environment was created, and the check algorithms' safety were confirmed to be correct, with a performance gain of over 2.5 times achieved through algorithm optimization. Additionally, to ensure the KALSS AFA system's reliability, we evaluated its KALSS fiber safety check algorithm, which prevents fibers from touching bright stars and double or multiple galaxies. For the check algorithm preventing fibers from touching bright stars, a simulation environment was established to test its performance; the algorithm was found to perform 1.5 times better than expected, and a safety check algorithm for fibers touching double or multiple galaxies was also developed and tested. In summary, this environment can be applied to ensure the safety and performance of AFA systems for various large-scale spectroscopic surveys. To facilitate the verification of safety and performance, the code for the KALSS AFA system, including its check algorithms and simulation environment, has been open-sourced to assist in the development of other systems. As these surveys progress, it is essential to establish standard methods for evaluating the safety and performance of AFA systems.

Contexts are crucial for the accurate interpretation of data within various domains, including science, as they enable the aggregation of similar entities to maximize data utility. To efficiently assign optical fibers to targets in large-scale spectroscopic surveys, safety check algorithms are employed to prevent collisions. However, to fully leverage the potential of optical fiber astronomy, a similar approach to context usage should be implemented in the OFA. In this study, we explored context-based optimization for safety check algorithms using a one-dimensional dimensionality reduction technique to reduce computational costs. To validate this method, we applied it to the assembly of galaxy clusters using photometric data from the KALSS survey. We developed an external override algorithm that selects optical fibers based on their three-dimensional context to prevent fiber-target collisions. To mitigate this, GP 2 introduces rooted rules that, provided mild conditions are met, allow for constant-time matching. Recently, we enhanced Bak's GP 2-to-C compiler with several modifications to accelerate graph programs. A pivotal advancement is the introduction of BigArray, a novel dynamic array structure composed of pointers to arrays that double in size successively. To illustrate the performance gains from this updated implementation, we showcase a binary DAG recognition program; while it was previously among the slowest in its class, it now achieves competitive performance against state-of-the-art static-checkers. Specifically, our updated compiler handles inputs with 10^6 nodes in under 0.5 seconds, a marked improvement over the former limit of approximately 10^5 nodes. Additionally, we demonstrate that our general-purpose graph compiler can handle various program verification tasks more swiftly than dedicated graph programs written in related transformation languages. We further provide an overview of graph programs illustrating how to construct efficient solutions for specific verification problems. To facilitate future research, we have released the revised compiler and all associated benchmarks at https://andrewfoster2.github.io/GraphPrograms/.

Since its inception, BP 2 has been shown to support the construction of highly efficient programs for specific tasks. For instance, we recently built a binary DAG checker in BP 2 capable of processing graphs with up to 10^7 nodes within a second. In this paper, we present a more practical version of that checker and utilize it to evaluate the capabilities of our newly developed BP 2.2 compiler. Although the new implementation successfully processes the same input sizes, it does so roughly ten times faster. This significant performance boost stems from several key updates in the BK 2.2 compiler, including a revised strategy for allocating memory to graphs, a substantially faster BigArray structure, and other optimizations. To ensure the reliability of these results, we also discuss the methods we employed to measure performance and validate the performance of the new compiler. To support ongoing research in GP 2, we have made the entire codebase, along with all benchmarks used to assess its performance, accessible at https://andrewfoster2.github.io/BP2/.

dimensionality challenges inherent in high-dimensional datasets. Given the recent surge in interest toward contrastive learning as a prominent self-supervised technique, this study introduces a unified framework grounded in a novel perspective of contrastive learning (CL). The framework encompasses various CL algorithms, including contrastive predictive coding (CPC), supervised contrastive learning (SCL), and negative selection learning (NSL), alongside their corresponding hyper-planes and margins. Furthermore, the approach extends to deep contrastive learning (DCL) through a corresponding DCL framework. Consequently, the proposed method represents a general and efficient technique for assessing feature quality within both supervised and unsupervised contexts. Performance evaluation relies on a derived decision tree that offers a standardized evaluation metric for DC methods. Performance analysis within image and video datasets confirms the approach's efficacy and robustness. Additionally performance was tested on text and brain datasets, where it identified features suitable for classification tasks. Finally, the method demonstrated success in a semi-supervised learning scenario. Since performance was measured across diverse data types, the decision tree and extracted features remain applicable to various downstream tasks. Feature extraction is crucial for reducing dimensionality while preserving essential information; therefore, this study provides performance data across different domains to guide feature selection based on specific application needs. The decision tree ensures that performance evaluation remains consistent and robust regardless of whether the learning paradigm is supervised, unsupervised, or semi-supervised. In summary, the introduced feature extraction method and the consistent evaluation protocol provide valuable guidance for future research directions. Performance outcomes indicate that the extracted features yield higher quality than results from other established methods.

Feature extraction is a technique employed to lower dimensionality while retaining the most relevant information. Determining optimal features for a specific task is critical, as it facilitates more accurate learning. This paper outlines various extraction techniques and offers performance data to assist in selecting the appropriate method for different applications.

In many scenarios, it is necessary to eliminate redundant information from high-dimensional data to enhance processing speed and reduce memory usage. Feature selection achieves this by identifying a subset of attributes that best characterize the data. For instance, in the context of contrastive learning, performance data can guide the selection of features that minimize misclassifications of semantically similar instances. The contrastive prediction score calculated in this work offers a robust mechanism for evaluating extraction quality across both supervised and unsupervised learning environments.

Performance results validate the effectiveness of the extraction method across diverse data types, ensuring that the selected features are well-suited for subsequent tasks.

This research advances the classification initiative launched by Giudici, Li, and Praeger by demonstrating that the star normal quotient twisted wreath category encompasses infinitely many such graphs. Furthermore, the interpretability of sparse solutions is vital for many applications, especially when users need to identify the minimal set of parameter combinations that yield performance close to the optimum. This paper introduces a sparse, mixed-integer, differentiable algorithm (SMIA) designed for a broad range of selection problems with continuous, convex, and convex-like (convex + smooth) penalties. Depending on the penalty type, the SMIA either exactly matches or closely approximates (within $\epsilon$) the sparse solutions found by efficient but non-sparse mixed-integer algorithms. Key advantages of our method include its sparse complexity, which matches that of the non-sparse exact algorithm, full compatibility with continuous constraints, and the ability to handle both convex and smooth penalties. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness and accuracy (for small $\epsilon$) across various sparse modeling tasks, including main effects and interactions in ANOVA, differential analysis, dictionaries, and graphs. The paper also defines the often-overlooked finite suboptimality inherent in sparse algorithms and discusses algorithms and parameters required to achieve it. Finally, the proposed SMIA significantly enhances the accessibility of exact sparse solutions for applied researchers. The code is available on GitHub.

We address the $\ell_0$-constrained optimization problem where the objective function is represented as a sum of two functions, $f_1$ and $f_2$, with $f_1$ being convex and $f_2$ being smooth. Existing algorithms typically rely on linear (first-order) smooth approximations of $f_2$, which may result in inexact sparse solutions when applied to purely smooth objectives. To resolve this, we develop two algorithms incorporating an exact smooth approximation of $f_2$. The first algorithm minimizes a lower bound of $f_1(x_t)+\lambda \|x_t\|_0$ at each iteration, while the second employs a bundle of subgradients of $f_1$. Both methods converge to an exact sparse solution within a polynomial number of iterations.

Consider the challenge of identifying a sparse solution to a general nonconvex function composed of a convex component and a smooth component under an $\ell_0$-norm constraint. While it is well-established that the intersection of a convex set, a smooth set, and the coordinate subspaces allows for an exact sparse solution via first-order methods, this property generally fails when the smooth component is present.

This study examines LLMs' internal and external representations of events by comparing their knowledge against the WikiEvents KG and assessing their ability to resolve WikiEvents' entity links. Our results show that pre-trained LLMs contain knowledge about a vast number of event types that the WikiEvents KG lacks, confirming that these models have ingested diverse information from their training data. However, despite their impressive natural language understanding, LLMs performed poorly at link prediction compared to both the baseline (direct lookup in WikiEvents) and simpler models trained specifically on WikiEvents. Furthermore, we identified 1 million types of noise in the WikiEvents KG that LLMs successfully filtered out, indicating that LLMs possess knowledge of proper entity syntax and semantics not captured by the graph's definition of "knowledge." Finally, we introduced an algorithm that leverages LLMs to enrich existing knowledge graphs, potentially adding up to 2.3 billion additional event types. Our code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/rohan-varma/LLM-Event-Knowledge.

LLMs have recently surpassed previous system records on textual reasoning benchmarks, yet their actual utility in logical entity and event link prediction remains unverified. In this work, we evaluate state-of-the-art language models, including T5, BART, and various transformers, on logical link prediction for both entities and events. We construct new, large-scale datasets by integrating information from existing knowledge graphs with those of Dbpedia and Wikidata. Our experiments demonstrate that LLMs exceed existing baselines in precision, recall, and $F_1$ scores. Additionally, we show that models fine-tuned on logical link prediction can capture billions of pieces of knowledge not present in their original pre-training corpora. These findings suggest that combining LLMs with existing knowledge graphs could yield even greater improvements, and we discuss how such models could be applied to information extraction and natural language inference. We hope this research inspires future work in knowledge graph completion and related fields.

We present a unified framework for learning logical link prediction using any language model, whether trained solely on text or augmented with an existing knowledge graph. Our framework learns to perform inductive logical link prediction—linking entities and events not explicitly listed in a knowledge graph—by directly optimizing an objective function that assesses the plausibility of potential head-tail

Our analysis explores their consistency with analogous inhomogeneous boundary value problems in classical partial differential equation (PDE) frameworks as the nonlocal kernel becomes localized in the limit $\delta \to 0$. Simultaneously, for rescaled kernels that remain localized at a specific point $x_0$ on the boundary in the limit $\delta \to 0$, we investigate the emergence of nonlocal boundary conditions at $x_0$. Comprehensive numerical experiments are presented to illustrate the kinetic behavior of the kernel at a boundary point, demonstrating its ability to model inactivation and migration phenomena. All findings are derived using only standard tools from nonlocal analysis and PDE theory. Leveraging this prior knowledge allows us to assume the camera y-axes are aligned, reducing their relative orientation to a single degree of freedom (1-DOF). Building on this assumption, we introduce novel minimal solutions for stitching panoramic images captured by cameras sharing the same optical center, meaning they undergo pure rotation. We evaluate four practical camera setups, accounting for unknown fixed or varying focal lengths with or without radial distortion. Our solvers were tested on synthetic data and over 500,000 real image pairs from the Sun360 dataset, outperforming both general and specialized panораmic solvers by more than 1.0 absolute mean error (MSE). Additionally, our method is 7 times faster on average compared to the best existing solution, making it ideal for mobile and real-time applications. In many 3D reconstruction tasks involving rotating cameras, such as camera pose estimation, structure-from-motion, or photogrammetry, image pairs often share the same camera center, resulting in 2D-to-2D homographies. When the rotation axis is known, this knowledge can be integrated into pose estimation to create more efficient algorithms and to derive closed-form solutions for other photogrammetric problems. This paper addresses finding the essential matrix element $e_{xz}$ and the full rotation matrix when the rotation axis is vertical, scenarios common in mobile and indoor 3D reconstruction. We present four general methods to compute $e_{xz}$ from image pairs with a shared camera center, covering cases where focal length is unknown, known, undistorted, or distorted. Our approach requires no iterative optimization, uses less data than the full essential matrix, and needs no assumptions about scene geometry. Extensive tests on synthetic data and the Sun360 dataset confirm our methods outperform state-of-the-art techniques in both accuracy and speed.

Panoramic images are frequently oriented so that one of the camera's principal axes aligns with the vertical direction. This creates a specific constraint on the essential matrix used for camera pose estimation between two such images rotating around a vertical axis. This work explores various scenarios of known or unknown focal lengths and provides efficient algorithms to estimate the full rotation matrix from an image pair under these conditions. This work extends their methodology and findings to Eisenstein series formed by inducing two Speh representations, $\Delta(\tau,m)|\cdot|^{s_1}\otimes\Delta(\tau,n)|\cdot|^{s_2}$, for the group $GL(m+n,\mathbb{A}_\mathbb{Q})$, where $\tau$ is a self-dual cuspidal automorphic representation. The extension is achieved by identifying and analyzing the specific cancellation patterns that result in pseudo-Eisenstein series. At the outset of his proof of the Generalized Riemann Conjecture, Goldfeld observes: "The Riemann conjecture represents the most profound unsolved problem in mathematics, while automorphic forms constitute one of the most vibrant fields in the discipline today." This statement underscores the central role of the Riemann Hypothesis within automorphic forms. Specifically, the theory of special values of zeta functions is intrinsically linked to the distribution of zeros of zeta functions, as illustrated by the classical case of Riemann's zeta function. It is through the study of special values that the framework of automorphic forms is deepened. Within this context, Hashimoto has made substantial contributions to the theory of special values for zeta functions, particularly concerning self-dual cuspidal automorphic representations of $GL_n$. His work often relies on the cancellation of poles in Eisenstein series. This paper focuses on investigating the cancellation of poles in Eisenstein series constructed by inducing two Speh representations, $\Delta(\tau,m)|\cdot|^{s_1}\otimes\Delta(\tau,n)|\cdot|^{s_2}$, where $\tau$ is a self-dual cuspidal automorphic representation

the retinal outer plexiform layer (OPL) that explicitly incorporates biologically grounded parameters and mechanisms. By integrating bionic electrophysiological recordings from OPL-intrinsic horizontal cells (HCs) and M-type cone photoreceptors (Phs) from mouse and human specimens, we constructed precise electrical parameters for each cell type and defined their synaptic connections within the OPL. These components were integrated into computational HCs and Phs models, which served as the foundation for building a biophysical OPL model. The system exhibits key feedback dynamics, notably that light stimulation of long-wavelength-sensitive cone Phs triggers a spectral shift in the electrophysiological output of HCs from short- to long-wavelength sensitivity. Furthermore, we investigated how specific pathophysiological conditions—such as the loss of Phs and reduced expression of the amino-potassium channel (BK) in HCs—progressively impair the computation of spectral opponent signals within the OPL. These findings offer fresh biophysical insights into the retinal mechanism generating signals for the brain's color vision. Additionally, the successfully developed biophysical OPL model provides essential groundwork for subsequent neuromorphic investigations into retinal color vision. Because the OpenGL API has limitations, a standard approach involves splicing multiple triangles at different scales to approximate finer details. However, this method suffers from significant rendering artifacts, particularly when cameras move, changes pitch, or alters zoom levels. To address this, we propose a novel technique that anti-aliases joins by adapting the number and radius of spawned triangles based on viewing distance. Furthermore, instead of using flat triangles, our method employs curved meshes that closely mimic road geometry, all generated in the vertex shader to ensure compatibility with existing rendering pipelines. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach anti-aliases all scalar values across various viewing distances, outperforming the baseline method in rendering accuracy while requiring roughly 50% less GPU time on average. Road networks are inherently sparse, and while Dijkstra's algorithm functions correctly regardless of network density, its runtime increases with the number of nodes and edges. To mitigate this, we propose sparsifying a road network by removing redundant nodes and merging collinear road segments, which reduces the total node and edge count. To maintain query efficiency, we introduce two novel data structures designed to accommodate this reduced network format. Additionally, to address potential memory constraints, our solution supports memory-mapped files, allowing road networks to reside partially on the host CPU's heap and partially on the system's virtual memory. To facilitate this, we developed a custom memory manager that offers anti-aliasing for memory allocations and provides 2.5x more usable memory on average compared to standard APIs like `new`/`delete` or `malloc`/`free`. To ensure rapid pathfinding, all algorithms in our solution are parallelized using OpenMP, and the implementation has been tested against industry leaders including Google's GraphPath and Mapbox's Vector Tiles library. As demonstrated in our evaluations, our solution typically queries faster than competing methods for small networks, paths of varying lengths, and memory-constrained environments, while offering greater flexibility for road network modifications and supporting diverse memory management strategies. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/MaximilianKraus/SparsifiedRoadNetwork.

Current approaches typically rely on sensor arrays or in-vehicle cameras to forecast weather, yet these methods incur incremental costs and offer limited scope. To guarantee the uninterrupted operation of all transportation services regardless of conditions, a robust detection system capable of classifying weather in the wild is essential. This study evaluates the feasibility of using deep learning to classify weather on the "Infrared Earth" satellite dataset. Building upon an existing convolutional neural network (CNN) model, we introduce two modifications: replacing fully connected layers with global average pooling and integrating a multi-task learning framework. The resulting infrared satellite image classifier, when applied worldwide, could ensure transportation stability in all conditions, thereby enhancing overall safety. Beyond its primary application in both multi-spectral and infrared datasets, the proposed method is particularly valuable for resource-constrained environments. On these datasets, the approach achieved a macro F1 score of 0.7926, surpassing the baseline by 0.1006, while also delivering competitive results on real-world data. Furthermore, the integration of multi-task learning demonstrated a 0.1499 improvement in classification accuracy for global infrared images compared to the baseline. By leveraging openly accessible satellite imagery, this technique could be globally optimized, considering both cost and energy efficiency. Additionally, the method's 0.5007 lower average error rate relative to the baseline confirms its superiority in terms of confidence interval width.

Logistic transportation faces significant challenges due to unpredictable weather and uncooperative road conditions. While transportation managers can leverage weather forecasts, their granularity and scope are often restricted. Although vehicles are equipped with sensors, their capability to independently and accurately assess on-road weather and road states is not always optimal. This study examines how in-vehicle sensors can classify weather and road conditions. A classification scheme for on-road weather and road states is first established, followed by an evaluation of sensor data quality and a discussion on feature selection. Although sensor-derived features are not perfectly accurate, their integration into a machine learning model can yield a more reliable weather classification than any single data source alone.

the depiction of convection within weather and climate simulations. This approach is appealing because it relies on fundamental physics, thereby circumventing the invalidation of single-fluid buoyancy expressions at flow scales comparable to or smaller than the thermal length. Multi-fluid models achieve this by resolving advection-dominated flows using a time step suitable for the thermal scales, thereby circumventing computational costs associated with forcing the thermal time scale to match that of convection.

In this study, we develop a multi-fluid framework where the single-fluid time step is ratioed to the thermal time step. We apply this model to a single column containing one large and multiple progressively smaller thermal scales. Results indicate that the multi-fluid solution aligns well with direct numerical simulation (DNS) data, even when the single-fluid time step is 200 times smaller than the largest thermal diffusion time. Furthermore, employing a time step based on the thermal time scale, rather than the convective time scale, yields more stable and physically accurate predictions of total kinetic energy. Additionally, the multi-fluid model exhibits superior stability and accuracy in simulating both the kinetic energy and overturning circulation, even when accounting for thermal scales as small as 0.5% of the domain depth. Consequently, this method offers a robust approach for explicitly resolving heating and cooling processes across a extensive spectrum of length and time scales.

We analyze the conditions required for these three uncorrelated atoms to achieve genuine multipartite entanglement. Our results indicate that this process is unattainable if the cavities interacting with the uncorrelated atoms share classical correlations with any other cavity. However, we observe that the same outcome can be realized if all cavities are connected through a weak global dissipation channel. We compute the entanglement generation rate and find that the uncertainty principle imposes an intrinsic limit on the precision with which this rate can be measured. Furthermore, we determine that the entanglement produced is of the W-state type and calculate its entanglement entropy. We also explore the potential for this protocol to function as an entanglement generator and observe that it can tolerate certain weak losses. Additionally, we show that the protocol can enhance the multipartite entanglement of an initially entangled state. To illustrate the feasibility of generating multipartite entanglement between three uncorrelated atoms, we provide a concrete example using the Jaynes-Cummings model with Rb-87 atoms. This work contributes to the broader goal of creating and manipulating multipartite entangled states within the Rabi framework, with potential applications in secure quantum communication, quantum internet infrastructure, and high-capacity quantum data storage.

While numerous reconstruction methods exist—from conventional protocols to machine learning approaches—no single universal technique currently allows for extracting the Wigner function from the optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that nonclassical phenomena, including entanglement variations during dynamical evolution and the emergence of quantum synchronization, manifest as qualitative shifts within the optical tomograms themselves. Consequently, explicit state reconstruction is unnecessary to detect these effects. Furthermore, our findings indicate that these quantum behaviors can be clearly identified even at low gain values that would otherwise prevent the observation of optical synchronization. Therefore, the proposed state analysis via direct extraction of the Wigner function represents the first viable method for studying both quantum synchronization and entanglement dynamics, offering distinct advantages over prior approaches. These benefits are particularly evident when examining quantum states that traverse the synchronization-unsynchronization transition repeatedly over time or when only limited data points are available from the tomographic measurement process.

Recent advances in quantum information technology have enabled the manipulation of increasingly complex states, often revealing nonclassical behaviors through relatively straightforward indicators like squeezing and S-shaped quadrature distributions. However, phenomena such as squeezing can be misleading; for instance, squeezed entangled states may exhibit quantum synchronization, where both partners display conventional squeezing in one quadrature and an S-shape in the other, yet remain deeply correlated. This insight underscores the importance of using the Wigner function for reconstructing quantum states, as it provides crucial details about nonclassical features that other representations might obscure.

We utilize the formalism of optical tomography to derive the exact quantum state from the optical tomograms of a two-mode system. By examining specific examples, we show that reconstructing the Wigner function is not required to identify nonclassicality or its evolution; distinct qualitative changes in the optical tomograms themselves suffice to detect nonclassicality and track its development during dynamical evolution. This confirms that optical tomography alone is sufficient for detecting nonclassical effects and observing their nonmonotonic temporal evolution, even when the quantum correlations are weak.

In quantum optics, dynamical evolution often generates nonclassicality in only one mode of a bipartite system, which can be misleading since the total state may still be nonclassical. Using the optical tomograms of a two-mode bipartite system, we demonstrate that nonclassical behavior in a single mode can be identified without reconstructing the full quantum state's Wigner function. This study addresses the difficulty of assigning consistent roles to these systems while maintaining natural and engaging human interactions. To achieve this, systems must adhere to role specifications that define specific feature constraints and encourage meaningful conversation without overwriting the nuances of human nature. # Open-Domain Dialogue Systems Cannot Always Maintain Multiple Features in the Wild

## Abstract

Recent developments in chatbots have enabled the assignment of distinct roles, such as ensuring safety or adopting a persona, by incorporating auxiliary losses during training. However, there is a lack of understanding regarding the data efficiency needed for these systems to uphold multiple roles out-of-domain. We investigate whether open-domain systems can sustain several roles with limited extra data and whether one role can be prioritized over another. As a primary experiment, we developed a three-role benchmark using three roles—Safety, Persona, and Style (also referred to as tone)—derived from recent literature. We trained a dialog model with various combinations of these roles and probed them with carefully designed questions to measure performance across all roles, both in-domain and out-of-domain. Our findings indicate that among the roles we tested, safety and style are mutually exclusive, and assigning two roles to an model with only a small amount of extra data typically degrades performance in one of those roles significantly. Furthermore, we developed a new approach, SafetyFirst, which allows any open-domain model to prioritize the safety role with negligible additional data and memory usage. Evaluations on our benchmark and a larger scale evaluation (1,000 instances) confirm that SafetyFirst outperforms other methods across all three roles, including the ones not used in its training. To assemble these scales out-of-domain benchmarks, we discuss several data curation techniques, including LLM-assisted methods.

A prevalent strategy to reduce bandwidth usage involves streaming only the portion of the video within the user's current viewport, a process that necessitates accurate viewpoint prediction. Current prediction techniques predominantly focus on head movement patterns, modeling them as random variables to determine the probable future view. Firstly, a short-term body and content-aware prediction model generates probable future viewports based on historical body and video contents. Secondly, a content-aware probability map-based model predicts probable future viewports utilizing probability maps derived from past viewports. Thirdly, a unified probabilistic head movement model predicts probable future head movements within a short time interval using a Markov chain. Finally, a fusion module integrates the probable future viewports from the collaborative body and content-aware model with those from the Markov model to determine the ultimate future viewport. Experimental results indicate that the proposed scheme significantly enhances viewpoint prediction accuracy across various video contents and user behaviors compared to existing methods.
