In this work, we present a universal statistical measure applicable to both ordered and disordered systems, based on the joint probability distribution functions (JPDFs) of atomic positions. This generalizes the pair correlation function used for disordered materials to include ordered structures. To make the statistic manageable, we define it using approximate JPDFs derived from high-fidelity material models—such as density functional theory (DFT) simulations, Monte Carlo methods, experimental data, or even simple lattice models—rather than requiring difficult measurements of exact JPDFs. We demonstrate the measure's effectiveness using various alloy systems, including binary alloys like AuCu (which exhibits both ordered and disordered states) and AuAl$_2$, as well as ordered intermetallics with complex basis structures like AuAl$_3$, and random alloys with continuous positional disorder, such as $\mathrm{La}_{2/3}\mathrm{Ca}_{1/3}\mathrm{MnO}_3$. The results show that the measure clearly differentiates between ordered and disordered states across all tested materials. Furthermore, we provide an upper and lower bound to constrain the range of the statistic, making it more robust and easier to interpret. This measure can be efficiently computed from any material's atomic configuration. We have developed an open-source Python package available at https://github.com/zhenghuang123/atomic_disorder_measure to perform these calculations. This tool is particularly valuable for systems with moderate size scales up to a few hundred thousand atoms. We also establish a connection between our measure and existing descriptors in the fields of statistical mechanics and probability theory. Ultimately, this measure enables a quantitative assessment of atomic disorder, facilitating the identification of optimal doping concentrations for engineered disordered alloys or the creation of novel material models with precisely controlled disorder characteristics. Additionally, we provide lower bounds for the measure in ordered and disordered two-dimensional square lattices using field theory within the self-consistent Born approximation. The measure is efficiently computable for atomic configurations of up to a few hundred thousand atoms. We have created an open-source Python package to calculate this metric, which is especially useful for approximately solving the entropy of mixing in disordered alloys and determining the free energy of disordered supercells via machine learning interatomic potentials. While deep learning techniques have recently advanced the field of Deep Learning-based Knowledge Tracing (DLKT), the underlying reasons for their success remain unclear, and the impact of specific learning mechanisms remains unexplored. To address the lack of interpretability and transparency in current research, we introduce an experimental framework that evaluates the influence of various DL mechanisms on DLKT through the lens of ablation studies. Our proposed mechanism, one-shot learning, enables the model to incorporate a student's external knowledge by integrating an embedding layer with the student's subject matter knowledge graph. Comprehensive experiments and analysis were conducted both within knowledge tracing scenarios and in broader classification tasks. The results highlight the superiority and versatility of the mechanism by comparing it against 15 different model components across 32 configurations. Additionally, the underlying rationale for the model's effectiveness is discussed through multiple perspectives, including a deliberate reverse engineering approach. Finally, reverse engineering and ablation studies serve as essential methods for enhancing the transparency and interpretability of black-box models. Consequently, this framework can be readily applied to evaluate the underlying mechanisms of any DLKT model. In terms of practical reverse engineering, our model achieves the highest F1-macro score of 0.6999, while the best existing DLKT method reaches an AUC of 0.7551. These findings demonstrate that reverse engineering and ablation studies are critical for understanding and improving the transparency and interpretability of DLKT models and deep learning systems in general. The Decentralized Federated Averaging (DeFA) algorithm eliminates this requirement by utilizing a gossip protocol to conduct multiple communication rounds with randomly selected neighbors rather than relying on a central server. Although theoretical analyses suggest linear convergence for decentralized methods on strong convex and smooth functions for a specific variant of DeFA, practical applications often involve nonconvex loss functions, and its convergence properties in this context remain insufficiently understood. This paper investigates a decentralized version of Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) for nonconvex optimization. We demonstrate that, under conditions of bounded variance and restricted gradient differences, this algorithm achieves local minimality at a rate comparable to standard decentralized algorithms with bounded variance. Furthermore, even with bounded gradient differences alone, the method attains a significantly faster convergence rate aligning with recent decentralized gradient descent theories. To the our knowledge, this work provides the first local minimality analysis for a decentralized optimizer applied to deep learning. Experimental results confirm the practical advantages of our method.

Recent methods based on gossip protocols perform decentralized training without a central server, yet their theoretical justification for deep learning remains limited. This paper introduces a decentralized stochastic gradient method and proves it reaches a local minimum at a rate consistent with its centralized counterpart. The analysis relies on bounding the variation of data distributions across devices. Experiments validate the method's superiority in both communication efficiency and final accuracy.

We introduce a communication-efficient method for optimizing nonconvex objectives across a network of devices that do not require the problem to be averaged for convergence. By employing a multi-rate algorithm with periodic communication, our approach achieves a sample complexity of $\mathcal{O}(p^{-1/5})$, significantly improving upon the $\mathcal{O}(p^{-1/2})$ complexity of existing multi-agent nonconvex algorithms. Additionally, our method requires $\mathcal{O}(1)$ computation per update, whereas other approaches need $\mathcal{O}(p)$ computations, where $p$ represents the number of devices. Theoretical analysis shows that for a target accuracy of $\epsilon$, both the total sample complexity and computational complexity are $\tilde{\mathcal{}}(\epsilon^{-3/5})$.

This paper examines the convergence of decentralized training using decentralized synchronous stochastic gradient descent (DecSynSGD). Although recent studies show DecSynSGD converges to a stationary point for nonconvex objectives, the rate depends heavily on the number of data points and assumes uniform data distribution across devices—a condition rarely met in federated learning

Transfer learning has been suggested to address these challenges, even when bridging language gaps, such as adapting an English model for Czech ASR. In this study, we explore transferring an English model to Czech, specifically focusing on differing phoneme sets and phoneme-to-neural network mappings, to determine if model parameters can be adapted to new languages with minimal data and computational cost. Our results show that transfer learning yields better outcomes than training from scratch when only a small amount of target language data is available, and it outperforms recent baselines using approximately half as much data. However, if the source language model has been trained on a large corpus, it is preferable to train an English-as-side-car model on a modest amount of Czech data rather than performing direct parameter transfer. These methods will be released to the community, supporting future research into low-data ASR through transfer learning and multi-task learning. Additionally, we provide a platform for evaluating transfer learning across various speech and NLP tasks, including language translation and phoneme transcriptions. Finally, we highlight the potential of transfer learning in creating robust speech technology, such as noise reduction and accent adaptation.

Recent advancements in deep learning have enabled end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition (ASR), which transfers model knowledge across languages, a phenomenon known as cross-lingual transfer. This approach has successfully improved ASR performance in low-resource languages using data from linguistically related source languages. We present a unified framework for understanding successful English-to-corpora (e.g., Czech, German, Vietnamese) transfers that involves two steps: (i) adapting an ASR model's vocabulary to the target language and (ii) transferring neural network knowledge to an English-to-target language model. Although often combined in practice, these steps can be applied independently to update neural network parameters, which is a form of direct cross-lingual transfer. Our analysis demonstrates that updating neural network parameters is crucial for achieving low-error rates with limited target language data, whereas vocabulary adaptation alone is insufficient. However, when ample target language data is available, vocabulary adaptation without transferring neural network parameters performs comparably to the full transfer approach. This work offers a comprehensive overview of English-to-corpora (Czech, German, Vietnamese) ASR transfers, elucidating the mechanisms of successful adaptation to new languages with limited resources.

We present a preprocessing method that transforms any network into a projected network by grouping nodes based on the similarity of their neighbor distributions. This approach significantly reduces both the node and edge counts of the original network while preserving essential structural and dynamical characteristics, making it ideal for analysis. We validate the efficacy of the preprocessing method across various networks and demonstrate its value by conducting community detection experiments on the resulting projected networks. These results indicate that traditional community detection algorithms can more accurately and effectively identify communities in projected networks compared to when they are applied directly to the original networks.

Networks are widely used to model complex systems by representing entities as nodes and their interactions or attributes as edges. While many recent embedding techniques excel at preserving local neighborhood information in the resulting low-dimensional spaces, they often fall short in maintaining the broader global structure of the network. Such structure preservation is essential for downstream tasks like community identification and node classification. Although these methods can reveal community information, they typically require extensive hyperparameter tuning and computational resources to achieve satisfactory performance. We introduce a novel network reduction technique that maintains both local and global structural integrity while substantially decreasing the number of nodes and edges. This reduction is achieved by identifying and keeping a subset of representative nodes that are structurally and dynamically similar to others, followed by removing the redundant nodes. Validation through community detection experiments on both real and synthetic networks shows that these techniques not only retain proximity and structural information but also enhance the performance of these methods for community detection.

Node embedding is a critical field within data mining that maps nodes of complex networks into low-dimensional vector spaces while retaining the original network's structure. Recent embedding methods are increasingly applied to predict node attributes, yet there is a scarcity of publicly available benchmarks and networks specifically selected for this purpose. We propose a selection criterion for benchmark networks that balances the preservation of structural information against the dimension of the attribute space to be predicted. We identified five networks that meet these criteria and assembled a corresponding benchmark database. Furthermore,

This interpretation is supported by the resonance's mass, its exclusive decay modes into $\pi^0\rho^\pm$ and $\eta\rho^\pm$, and its production mechanism observed by BaBar through the intermediate trajectory of the $f_2(1270)$, which aligns with predictions from the Regge trajectory. Furthermore, we note that $f_X(1500)$ exhibits a broader population of daughter particles in the BaBar invariant mass distribution for the $\pi^\pm A_2(1310)$ combination, which we attribute to experimental resolution effects. We argue that interpreting $f_X(1500)$ as a tetraquark, as recently suggested, is untenable given these findings. Consequently, the complete spectrum of light vector $q\bar q$ mesons is now well-established. Based on the mass of $f_X(1500)$, we also identify three other potential candidates for this yet-to-be-confirmed state. program with the observed smallness of dark energy requires linking it to an early de Sitter (dS) era, such as inflation, implying that any (quasi)-dS vacuum in the landscape must correspond to a ratio $\epsilon = E_{\rm QFT}/M_{\rm Pl} < 10^{-12}$. However, it has long been established that quasi-de Sitter expansion drives a suppression of the high-energy tail of the central charge distribution, challenging the likelihood of small $\epsilon$ values. We demonstrate that connecting to an early dS era requires a significantly smaller high-energy tail than previously estimated. Consequently, we show that if the landscape is characterized by a log-normal $\epsilon$-distribution, the required high-energy tail is even less probable than earlier estimates suggested, potentially resolving this problem. This supports a lower bound of $\epsilon > 10^{-12}$ for the landscape, aligning with constraints derived from an early dS era and offering support for a power-law $V(\phi)$ near $V_0$. Furthermore, we illustrate that a landscape featuring a lower energy cutoff can accommodate a few vacua with very small $\epsilon$, which could be accessible to observation if the dark energy scale is below $10^{-14} M_{\rm Pl}$. Finally, we derive that the probability of a universe undergoing inflation is given by $P(\epsilon) = C\,\epsilon^{-1/2}\,(1+\sqrt{1-\epsilon})$, where $1-\epsilon \gg 1$. This leads to the total probability $P_{\rm tot} = \int_{\epsilon_{\rm min}}^{1} P(\epsilon)\,d\epsilon = 4\,\sqrt{\epsilon_{\rm min}}$, where $\epsilon_{\rm min}$ must be exceptionally tiny to satisfy the Swampland criteria. This framework may also resolve the discrepancy between the high probability of inflation in recent landscape estimates and the low probability of dark energy. A similar analysis can be extended to other landscapes, though this would necessitate establishing new, even stricter, high-energy tails for the central charge distribution. Ultimately, we propose a simple model where a potential $V(\phi)\propto\phi$ yields a $\epsilon$-distribution that could satisfy the demands of an early dS vacuum.

Designed to address poor force measurements in SEAs resulting from elastic transmission nonlinearities, sensor noise, and deformation measurement errors, the paper first examines the limitations of traditional SEA force sensing methods and analyzes their stochastic properties, laying the groundwork for accurate force control via TFOB. Notably, a tuning parameter is derived from closed-loop analysis, enabling precise force regulation even when the initial error in elastic torque measurement is substantial. To validate the algorithm, an SEA testbed was constructed, and extensive experiments were conducted under noisy conditions and varying inertial loads. The results demonstrate that the proposed TFOB-based force control strategy significantly improves tracking performance compared to conventional control schemes relying on on-board elastic torque sensors. Furthermore, the proposed controller maintains high performance even when the on-board sensor is completely disabled. Finally, the advantages of the proposed scheme are summarized, and future research directions are suggested.

The system's temporal scales are governed by a single control parameter, $\sqrt{A_{f}/A_{p}}$, which represents the ratio of the fractional areas contributed by the raft particles and the underlying droplet. As this parameter increases, the raft transitions from localized events—such as single particle ejections or cluster fragmentation— to large-scale failures characterized by multiple simultaneous vacancies and global fragmentation into multiple pieces. Dimensionless numbers derived from the system's geometry and physics define the vacancy scales observed during raft failure. The initial failure modes are determined by the competition between particle-particle and particle-air surface tensions. Additionally, the dynamics of the resulting holes are driven by the suction generated by the underlying expanding liquid. This study reveals the universal scaling laws of a macroscopic material as it fails. The experimental findings are explained through a simplified force-based model involving mean curvature and surface tension, which accounts for the system's geometric complexity. Additionally, the system displays two distinct strain rate regimes during the formation of initial holes. Understanding these failure dynamics provides a foundation for developing more complex theoretical models and has potential applications in designing particle-based material tests. Finally, the research demonstrates strain hardening during the initial failure modes of the low-density raft. These fields interact with gauge fields via a nonseparable, nonminimal coupling that modifies the kinetic term, thereby introducing a field-strength dependent mass. We find that at high temperatures, the phase transition behavior aligns with scenarios where the order parameter corresponds to the mean field. In the limit of very large Nf, a first-order transition emerges, a finding that is corroborated by a mean-field analysis that was subsequently extended to the finite Nf case. Additionally, in the limit of extensive Nf, we calculated critical temperatures and observed that the transition type—whether first- or second-order—depends on the specific form of the potential. Monte Carlo simulations were conducted using an action lattice cutoff scale that is asymptotically small in the extensive Nf limit, ensuring that our results are free of lattice artifacts. This confirms that the critical temperatures and the nature of the transition in the extensive Nf limit are identical to those predicted by the mean-field approximation. Furthermore, we investigated the symmetry restoration behavior near the phase transition. This framework is particularly pertinent to models where the scalar field represents the chiral condensate, such as those incorporating auxiliary fields or employing the Wilson-Ginsparg-Wilson relation for fermions. In these contexts, the transition order is determined by the number of flavors, consistent with established literature. However, a significant distinction arises: unlike standard cases, the critical temperature does not vanish in the infinite Nf limit when the potential is present. This underscores the efficacy of the proposed model in representing the condensate and supports the construction of realistic relativistic heavy-ion collision models that accurately reflect the transition order and its characteristics. Finally, we also explored the impact of adding a soft breaking term to the action.

This behavior is especially pronounced at finite baryon density and lattice spacings, though it fades as the continuum limit is approached. Consequently, the lattice signal at a critical temperature does not accurately reflect the true finite-Nf physics of degenerate QCD. Building on Fifer's (2019) method, which utilizes random feature mappings to handle these continuos dimensions, we introduce several key modifications. Specifically, we implement an off-policy algorithm based on TD(0), replace the standard gradient descent optimization with the Stochastic Gradient Descent on Permutation Invariant data (SGDPI), and apply an $L_1$ penalty to the weight weights. We examine two distinct constructions: one with a fixed depth of three layers and a variable number of comparators, and another with a fixed total of three comparators per node (resulting in variable depth). For the fixed-depth design, we identify the minimum number of comparators required as $3^n - 1$, where $n$ denotes the count of simultaneously sorted numbers. In the case of networks with uniformly three comparators per node, we analytically derive an expression for depth, $D(n)$, and numerically determine an approximate formula: $D(n) \approx 3n - 2.3$. These theoretical findings are validated by comparing them against values obtained through genetic algorithms. The insights gathered here aid in creating sorting networks with optimized combinations of comparators and depth, which can then be translated into quantum logic gates for parallel quantum computations characterized by their dimensionality. This validation represents a preliminary step toward applying genetic algorithms to construct complex quantum circuits, specifically those involving three types of quantum comparators, to sort multiple qubit ensembles in parallel. Ultimately, the number of qubits that can be sorted will be dictated by the available dimensions in multi-parameter quantum spaces. This approach yields the corresponding covariant Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations for anisotropic conditions. These equations are subsequently employed to derive new exact solutions through direct resolution and reconstruction methods. Furthermore, we demonstrate that three generating theorems established for single-fluid systems can also be applied to generate two-fluid solutions from single-fluid counterparts. Consequently, we obtain additional exact solutions by applying these generating theorems to our newly found two-fluid solutions, thereby validating that the three theorems are applicable to all two-fluid configurations. These strategies are particularly beneficial for investigating the physical and geometric characteristics of anisotropic stars, as well as exploring solutions within the context of modified gravity. To facilitate future research, we have provided a Mathematica package that automates the calculation of all needed covariant quantities. This package is essential for efficiently analyzing the properties of two-fluid anisotropic stars, potentially aiding in the investigation of modified gravity scenarios involving such systems. Additionally, the package can determine the conditions required for a two-fluid object to manifest as a regular black hole when placed in modified gravity, leveraging two generation functions. We present a general construction of this package and illustrate its application with a specific functional choice. Additionally, we apply the package to verify previously published results by Krori and Sharmarck. The findings confirm that: (i) the two generation functions can derive the two-fluid solution from the single-fluid one, and (ii) the single-fluid solution yields a regular black hole in modified gravity if the two-fluid solution satisfies certain inequalities. These solutions were originally introduced to model the neutron star PSR J0348+0432.
During the design of the 1+2+1 covariant decomposition for spherically symmetric spacetimes, it became necessary to compute various derivatives and algebraic operations on the metric and the single-fluid matter source. To streamline these calculations and enhance the study of the dynamics of collapsing or exploding spherical stars using this framework, we propose a general package. This package offers a convenient method for determining all necessary quantities related to the 1+2+1 decomposition under spherical symmetry. We have tested the package with a specific example, from which all required quantities were derived directly. The results of this test align perfectly with the findings of Krori and Sharmarck, confirming the package's validity and efficiency. The proposed package is available

To enhance the statistical understanding of these events, we created the Contact Finder (CF), a technique capable of identifying ongoing mergers in virtually any sample of resolved galaxies by analyzing imaging or spectroscopic data. Unlike conventional methods, CF determines merger orientation and the order in which galaxies contact one another. We demonstrate its effectiveness through contact simulations, showing that CF accurately recovers orientations and merging orders for most systems once they become observable until close to coalescence, with success rates exceeding 80% once systems are visible on 3D trajectories. Applied to the nearby SAMI Galaxy Survey, CF identified 100 merging systems (redshift median < 0.03), yielding 53 new candidates when added to current literature. Statistical analyses of this combined sample reveal distinct trends in star formation and color relative to major and minor axes, along with trends linked to the merging order. Additionally, we derived orientation distributions for different dynamical sub-samples to investigate their impact on observed properties. The contact timescales measured by CF enable the construction of evolutionary sequences, which clearly indicate systems' evolution along the star formation sequence over time. Finally, contact times mapped onto color-magnitude diagrams highlight the influence of recent mergers on these diagrams and show how merger timescales vary with system mass. To overcome this, we introduce a universal data augmentation module (UAM) that employs a cross-attention mechanism to transform source data into target data, offering a solution for various natural language processing (NLP) tasks. By training a model with only a few examples of data from each class, we achieve significant improvements across eight different NLP datasets. Specifically, UAM enhances performance in GEC by 5.15 points, improves sequence classification by 2.51 points, and boosts other tasks by 1.00 point or more. This approach not only provides a solution for GEC but also serves as a effective data augmentation module for diverse NLP tasks, proving that a small amount of noise data is sufficient to achieve substantial performance gains.

Fe$_3$Sn$_2$ crystallizes in the FeSn2 structure, which can be viewed as stacked bilayers of transition metals, and is anticipated to host magnetic Weyl fermions. Although the Curie temperature is expected to be relatively high, we have determined that Fe$_3$Sn$_2$ is paramagnetic below 15 K. Additionally, we have mapped the material's magnetic free energy landscape by measuring field-dependent resistivity across various orientations and field magnitudes. Our results indicate that the ferromagnetic alignment in this compound is fragile, as even minor thermal fluctuations at higher temperatures or slight magnetic field variations can easily disrupt it. These structural and magnetic findings are essential for guiding the interpretation of upcoming resistivity measurements on Fe$_3$Sn$_2$, which are anticipated to reveal exotic Weyl fermion physics.

Crystalline Fe$_3$Sn$_2$ is an anomalous resistivity metal with potential for strong Weyl semimetal behavior. We present the complete magnetic phase diagram and free energy landscape of this material. Although Fe$_3$Sn$_2$ is generally believed to have a high Curie temperature, our measurements reveal it is paramagnetic above 15 K. By analyzing the field-dependent resistivity for multiple field magnitudes and directions, we have mapped the ferromagnetic free energy landscape. This analysis enables the construction of a comprehensive magnetic phase diagram, which is critical for correctly interpreting upcoming resistivity experiments aimed at detecting exotic Weyl fermion physics in Fe$_3$Sn$_2$.

Fe$_3$Sn$_2$ is a correlated metal with an anomalous resistivity anomaly that has been attributed to Weyl fermions. We have measured the specific heat of single-crystal Fe$_3$Sn$_2$ over a broad temperature range. The data indicate that Fe$_3$Sn$_2$ is fully paramagnetic above 15 K, which is significantly higher than previously reported values. Consequently, the anomalous resistivity observed at temperatures as high as 260 K can be legitimately attributed to Weyl fermions. We have also identified Kondo-like behavior in the low-temperature specific heat data, which can be explained by the presence of magnetic impurities.

Our primary objective is to determine if mechanisms exist that guarantee the existence of pure Nash equilibria for every scenario while simultaneously ensuring fairness in the resulting allocations. Specifically, we investigate two relaxations of envy-freeness: envy-freeness up to one good (EF1) and envy-freeness up to any good (EFX). We analyze various scenarios, including agents with additive, uniformly valued, and most-valued items, to evaluate the feasibility of these fair distributions in strategic environments. While EFX allocations are harder to secure, we demonstrate that in many cases, EFX allocations can still be achieved from the outset. Our findings reveal significant gaps between truthful and non-truthful mechanisms regarding fairness, often resulting in significantly weaker outcomes when reports are untrusted. We provide mechanisms for both settings that are either close to, or strictly better than, these lower bounds. Notably, we develop a mechanism for two agents with additive valuations (valuing either 0 or 1) that reaches a pure Nash equilibrium yielding an EFX allocation. This contrasts with environments involving three or more items and two agents, where only EF1 allocations can be guaranteed. Furthermore, we establish an approximate version of Theorem~\ref{thm:efx_2} for any number of items and two agents. For three agents with additive valuations, we Dwork et al.'s~\cite{DworkKMS13} result by showing an EFX allocation is reachable in pure Nash equilibria; however, we significantly improve their envy-free social welfare guarantees. We also provide mechanisms for other multi-agent instances where all truthful mechanisms' envy-free social factors are known. Additionally, we prove an envy-freeness result for randomized mechanisms with two agents and four valuations, substantially surpassing expectations based on adaptations of deterministic algorithms. Finally, we offer an approximate resolution for the open question of whether a mechanism exists for two agents and two items where all valuations are most-valued and an EFX allocation is reached in pure Nash equilibria, even when one agent is an adversary. This improves upon the trivial envy-free allocations currently achievable in such pure Nash equilibria. We provide an overview of how our findings relate to and extend prior and concurrent research.

839 presents a deceptively simple appearance, lacking obvious starburst features; however, it harbors an unusually intense radio source. We report new observations of UGC 8839 from the VLA at 20 cm and the Arecibo Telescope at 0.485 GHz, which detail the morphology of this radio source and enable a precise calculation of its physical properties. Additionally, we examine the global optical and near-infrared characteristics of UGC 8839, including an analysis of its surface brightness distribution. The radio source exhibits classic double-lobed structure with a morphologically complex, ionized nuclear region. It has a total flux density of 1.1 Jy at 20 cm and 1.7 Jy at 0.485 GHz, with a linear size of approximately 10 kpc at 0.485 GHz. We characterize the source as a young radio galaxy with a power-law spectrum (alpha = 0.78 +/- 0.02), an estimated total energy of 3.4 x 10^53 ergs, and a minimum age of 2.4 x 10^6 years. While the host galaxy shows no signs of major mergers or significant gas depletion, its low stellar surface brightness makes the radio source disproportionately prominent. UGC 8839 serves as a valuable case study for understanding the co-evolution of galaxies and their central black holes, particularly in systems where the radio source is the most striking feature. We suggest that low surface brightness spirals may be more prone to hosting young radio galaxies than previously recognized. Furthermore, we note that while some local radio galaxies are known to be fueling active galactic nuclei, others, like UGC 8839, may represent the initial stages of this process.

This study calculates the gamma ray background levels for various paleo-detector configurations with different screen thicknesses, leveraging the unique energy resolution of these detectors to measure the associated background via their distinctive two-body reaction signature. It is important to note that the background estimates for concrete and lead screens are conservative, as they do not account for the energy resolution capability of paleo-detectors. Finally, the screen thicknesses derived for a 400 MeV/$c^2$ DM particle could prove valuable for other direct detection experiments aiming to explore the same parameter space as paleo-detectors.

Differential privacy, an extension of differential uniformity, was first explored by G. L. Cohen in 1974. Cohen's construction of differential uniform functions remains highly effective for generating S-boxes with a low differential uniformity (DU) value. However, due to the increased nonlinearity of DP-based Su-boxes, encrypting data with additive homomorphic encryption (AHE) using public keys can result in large space consumption. To address this, the scheme utilizes Paillier encryption for such data, a technique also employed in the DP-SENE scheme. To manage this space efficiency issue, we leverage the properties of Paillier encryption to create a sliding window-based space optimization structure called the DP-Space Holder. This component allows for the efficient management of encrypted data within a limited space range by periodically overwriting older data with new entries, thereby restricting stored data to only the most recent update patterns defined by the differential private update pattern. Consequently, the overall space complexity of the scheme becomes linear relative to the length of the differential private update pattern. Moreover, because the scheme retains only the most recent update patterns, it effectively resists timing attacks and cache side-channel leakages.

While our feature importance metrics are validated as more robust and accurate, the generated user reports are also shown to be more informative and actionable than any currently available solution.

Although contrastive learning has become a leading approach for few-shot image classification, it typically relies on a single backbone network to produce embeddings for unfamiliar classes using a limited number of support images. While effective for distinguishing among a few known classes, this strategy may struggle when generating embeddings for classes not seen during training. To address this, we introduce Multi-Head Contrastive Learning (MHC-Learning), which utilizes multiple backbone networks, each trained on a specific subset of classes from the few-shot task. During inference, the appropriate head is selected based on the query class. Extensive experiments across two large-scale ImageNet subsets show that MHC-Learning significantly surpasses standard contrastive learning methods and various other few-shot learning techniques. Furthermore, by training heads for attributes, the framework proves viable for few-shot classification of never-before-seen classes. Code can be found at https://yoonlab.github.io/MHC-Learning/.

Lattice QCD offers a unique opportunity to directly compute matrix elements of quark currents for any quark flavor combination. Lattice calculations have previously determined many such matrix elements, some of which have already been utilized to derive experimental constraints on new physics. However, to leverage these results for interpreting experimental data in the search for new physics, it is essential to understand quark correlations and their resulting hadron currents. This requires both additional lattice studies and further theoretical investigation of quark correlations within hadrons. Additionally, we address several questions regarding the interpretation of both existing and newly computed lattice QCD results concerning correlation functions between quarks in hadrons. Understanding quark correlation functions in hadrons could potentially enhance the interpretation of certain lattice QCD results related to three-quark currents in baryons, which are currently linked to the "endpoint singularity" problem. Solving this problem would be crucial for utilizing baryon results in searching for new physics, particularly to interpret data on the proton's electric charge radius. Moreover, resolving this issue would help interpret lattice QCD findings on baryon shapes, specifically those indicating that one quark is distinct from the other two. Finally, such an understanding would aid in interpreting recent lattice results on baryon current renormalization that differ from perturbative QCD predictions. These discrepancies may stem from mistakes in calculating renormalization factors, though some may reflect real effects of hadron dynamics on quark correlations.

This work serves as a systematic exploration of these functions, which is vital for interpreting lattice determinations of baryon current renormalization factors. Additionally, we prove the existence of algebraic correspondences among the $Y_w$ that reflect the partial order $\preceq$ on $D$, where $w \preceq v$ indicates the presence of a correspondance from $Y_w$ to $Y_v$. These findings extend a result previously established by E. Sheshadri for the case where the partial flag consists of two subspaces.

We propose that this relationship arises because the radio-emitting jet and the X-ray continuum originate from distinct regions within the AGN. To address this, we propose a novel approach that encodes complex, dynamic data into a sequence of memory-efficient, latent graph representations, simultaneously capturing both first- and higher-order interactions. These representations are designed to be interpretable at the event level and can be manipulated to produce new sequences of latent graphs that retain temporal dynamics and local structure while allowing for smooth interpolations and perturbations. To our knowledge, this is the first method to achieve simultaneous capture of first- and high-order interactions across time. We demonstrate its effectiveness using two applications: anomaly detection and time-series classification. We introduce HypoGraph, which generates graph data suitable for hypothesis testing. Unlike methods that only produce graph representations for this purpose, HypoGraph simultaneously performs downstream tasks like anomaly detection and classification while ensuring compatibility with statistical hypothesis testing. This approach is especially valuable for out-of-domain data, such as sensor failures during image acquisition in medical contexts. To achieve this, HypoGraph employs a counterfactual training framework that explicitly learns the conditional distribution $G|x$ (where $G$ is a graph and $x$ is an attribute vector). Specifically, HypoGraph utilizes an invertible graph neural network to encode attributes and decode graphs, enabling the manipulation of input attributes to observe changes in output distributions. We evaluate HypoGraph through two applications: (1) detecting anomalies in time-series data that may result from disconnected graph structures, and (2) classifying time-series data with missing values. Experimental results indicate that HypoGraph effectively identifies anomalies and missing value patterns in data from out-of-domain graphs and achieves competitive classification performance on training and test datasets. The code for HypoGraph can be found at https://github.com/AmirhosseinKasraie/HypoGraph.

First, Shannon entropy calculated from far-field profiles in polar coordinates effectively quantifies emission unidirectionality, overcoming the limitations of previous metrics which were restricted to spherical coordinates or specific profile features. Second, while the divergence of the in-plane Poynting vector along the normal direction to the emission profile is traditionally used to measure lateral confinement, we demonstrate that this approach is flawed and yields misleading results. Third, the established relationship between radiative energy confinement and directional emission holds true when using the scalar normal component of the radial Poynting vector instead of the full vector quantity. Finally, all metrics regarding directional emission remain valid and are interconnected even when significant nonradiative channels, such as waveguide loss, are present. These findings provide a solid foundation for further research into microcavity lasers and other radiative systems.
This letter proposes a unified and rigorous framework for quantifying the unidirectionality of microcavity emission. First, we challenge the utilization of perpendicular-field confinement as a proxy for directional emission in periodic microcavities with significant radiative loss, which is frequently observed in superprism photonic crystals. Second, we identify a flaw in prior theoretical treatments of directional emission in microcavities with strong waveguide loss. Consequently, we establish Shannon entropy derived from far-field profiles in polar coordinates as a robust indicator of directional emission for all microcavity lasers. Although naturally linked to radiative-state confinement, this metric remains accurate and applicable even when strong waveguide or radiative loss is present, a condition where the unitary relationship with directional emission is no longer guaranteed. Shannon entropy serves as a reliable and robust figure of merit for the directional emission of radiating resonators, which can be directly determined from experimental data.
Microcavity lasers are renowned for their highly directional radiation, yet existing metrics for quantifying this directional emission are incomplete. Although directional emission is often correlated with the confinement of radiative states, this correlation breaks down in the presence of strong waveguide or radiative loss. We establish that the Shannon entropy of the angular distribution of the electromagnetic field—a quantity readily accessible from experimental data—accurately and robustly quantifies the directional emission of microcavity lasers, regardless of the strength of waveguide or radiative losses. We observe that in microcavity lasers, higher state confinement in either waveguide or radiative loss leads to increased directional emission, as reflected by lower Shannon entropy. Furthermore, we explore the connection between atomic ensemble dynamics and the near-field optical dipole moment of a single atom. Additionally, we suggest that this scattering framework could enable the detection of minute temperature variations within a small volume with a potential precision of $10 \mu$K. Such precision significantly exceeds current micro-trapped gas thermometer capabilities, which typically achieve micro-Kelvin sensitivity. Finally, we highlight that the sensor's susceptibility to the temperature signal scales with the square of the vapor density, while the detection limit is constrained by noise arising from incoherent emission. We trust this study will inform the development of microfabricated thermometers capable of measuring temperatures across a broad spectrum, from a few micro-Kelvin to several thousand Kelvin.

We find that the universal critical exponent depends on the average atomic separation. In contrast, the universal critical exponent for the shared thermal field is determined by the average interatomic separation. We note that this non-equilibrium system shares an exponent with the universal class of the 2D Ising model. However, practical applications often involve behavior policies generating joint trajectories with varying performance levels, creating a challenge to learn optimal joint policies without access to labeled data or information on individual trajectory sources. Although recent methods attempt to address this by identifying high- and low-quality trajectories based on returns or gradients, they often discard low-quality data or rely on additional hyper-parameters, potentially wasting valuable information and increasing algorithmic complexity. In this paper, we introduce Cross-Play, which learns optimal multi-agent policies from a mixture of datasets by simultaneously training on all available data through cross-playing, even when the data sources are unlabeled. Specifically, we first organize these datasets into "dummy" games and demonstrate that backward iteration can help identify high-performing trajectories. Then, we have agents play against each other using policies parameterized by mean and standard deviation; subsequently, sampling from these policies allows us to utilize both high- and low-performing trajectories to update policies via contrastive learning. Offline multi-agent reinforcement learning, which enables multi-agent systems to acquire cooperative skills from existing data, is essential for their deployment in real-world environments. We assess Cross-Play across multi-agent environments of varying complexities and dataset compositions, showing it outperforms baseline methods. Additionally, Cross-Play requires no hyper-parameter tuning beyond the number of dummy games and is 3.6 times faster on average than offline multi-agent systems learning from high-performing data. The repository can be found here: https://github.com/zhengy2000/Cross-Play.

Online multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) often struggles with a lack of communication between agents and their ability to adapt to others, issues that become even more pronounced in real-world applications. To mitigate these challenges, agents typically require extensive fine-tuning, which is difficult and time-consuming. We propose that agents can learn to adapt to others and communicate implicitly by observing the success of other agents within existing data. Our approach involves extracting metrics that reflect the performance of other agents from raw data and training agents to predict these metrics via cross-play, thereby enabling the incorporation of information from high-performing data alongside that from low-performing data for policy updates.

This extreme configuration highlights the essential role of non-commuting measurements in generating entanglement across parties with completely separated spacetime trajectories, thereby providing a striking illustration of quantum nonlocality in both space and time.

By enabling stabilizer measurements through a single multi-qubit gate rather than multiple two-qubit gates, this approach reduces circuit depth. Using the toric code as a benchmark, this study compares two-qubit and five-qubit gates within parity-check circuits, focusing on trapped ion qubits controlled by Raman transitions where spontaneous photon scattering is the primary error source. The findings demonstrate that a five-qubit Mølmer-Sørensen gate provides approximately a $40\%$ improvement in fault tolerance thresholds compared to two-qubit gates, while maintaining comparable qubit connectivity requirements. Additionally, the analysis shows that for certain codes, increasing the number of physical qubits per logical qubit enhances tolerance to errors during stabilizer measurements. These results underscore the advantages of gates with multiple entangling modes for achieving fault-tolerant quantum computation. The code available at \url{github.com/brandonrj/circuits-and-thresholds} supports these conclusions.

Quantum error correction (QEC) is essential for the operation of any practical quantum computer. By using multiple physical qubits to create a single logical qubit, it is possible to reduce the impact of decoherence and other errors. This study examines the trade-offs between two- and five-qubit gates in trapped ion QEC, specifically on the surface code. Surface codes are highly promising for quantum computation because they can be implemented with minimal connectivity, have high fault-tolerance thresholds, and reduce measurement error. When applying surface codes to trapped ions, it is crucial to evaluate not only two-qubit gate errors but also errors during operations like photon ejection used for measurement. This analysis compares surface code performance across various architectures, showing that for certain codes, increasing the number of physical qubits can improve tolerance to measurement errors. These findings can guide the design of efficient and robust quantum computers.

This study compares the surface code's tolerance to readout and two-body interaction errors in trapped-ion systems, evaluating both two- and nine-body interactions. The surface code is a leading candidate for quantum error correction (QEC), and its readout errors can be made very small with multiple qubits. The surface code can be implemented with as few as two interacting qubits, and its readout error scales with the number of qubits as $\gamma/ \Delta$, where $\gamma$ is the two-body decay rate and $\Delta$ is the laser detuning. encoding framework grounded in Gaussian mixture models (GMMs). During the offline stage, the base station (BS) fits a GMM to channel state information (CSI) data; subsequently, a set of codebooks is generated based on this fitted mixture using low-resolution quantizers. In the online stage, the GMM is utilized again to fit the current CSI, and each codebook is assessed via the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the existing GMM and those modeled under the codebook. Each user equipment (UE) reports the index of the codebook yielding the minimum UE-specific performance metric and the corresponding feedback bits, with the BS reconstructing the final GMM from all feedback. Extensive simulations demonstrate that this low-complexity scheme achieves performance nearly identical to high-complexity methods while maintaining low overhead, even under severe feedback constraints across various scenarios. Furthermore, this work offers further proof that the proposed construction significantly enhances the BS's ability to model the CSI distribution with high accuracy. This UE-specific feedback encoding framework is expected to be applicable to GMM-based multi-user codebook design and cooperative communication systems. Additionally, this scheme outperforms traditional rate-distortion-based methods in feedback capacity, as it is an optimal feedback encoding scheme in rate-distortion theory with additional constraints. Simulations confirm that the proposed scheme delivers superior performance and higher capacity than existing state-of-the-art feedback coding constructions in both single-user and multi-user downlink systems under strict feedback constraints. Additionally, the scheme exhibits robustness against feedback channel errors. The proposed method surpasses state-of-the-art performance in overall sum-throughput, 95% and 50-user edge-throughputs, and overall sum-MSE, sum-SNR, and total mutual information metrics under severe feedback constraints. Finally, the scheme offers lower feedback overhead and faster convergence than existing state-of-the-art methods across diverse feedback budgets and varying feedback channel conditions.

For feedback encoding, the optimal solution involves a complex construction that relies on full CSI knowledge at the BS. However, since the proposed method does not require the GMMs to be factorized, it can be extended with only minor modifications to handle factorized GMMs, as detailed in Section VII-B. This extension results in comparable performance with significantly reduced complexity. Similarly, extension to handle factorized GMMs for feedback encoding is anticipated to yield better performance and capacity than current state-of-the-art schemes under severe feedback constraints, though this has not been experimentally validated. We present a framework to achieve genuine two-dimensional robust crosscurrents within a topologically nontrivial insulator. This is accomplished by configuring the topologically nontrivial band to occupy the middle of the dispersion spectrum, thereby facilitating channeling currents in all directions, including against the natural heat flux. Our proposed nontrivial topological state relies on spin-orbit coupling combined with a specific spatial arrangement of magnetic fluxes. Unlike conventional robust crosscurrents, which depend on the coexistence of spin-orbit coupling and a particular simultaneous spin configuration, our state arises from the interplay between noncollinear spins and spatially varying coupling. In an experimental context involving cold atoms within an optical lattice, our design necessitates only two distinct atomic species and two types of optical potentials, significantly reducing complexity compared to previous proposals. Furthermore, this state remains stable amidst certain Gaussian impurities, whereas prior robust crosscurrents would dissipate under such conditions. The nontriviality of our proposed state can be verified by observing a transition to a topologically trivial state when the magnetic fluxes are made simultaneously collinear or when the coupling becomes uniform. Achieving this state could demonstrate robust counter-heat current splitting, where total heat current is zero yet currents moving against and with the natural heat flow are unequal, a phenomenon with potential applications in dissipative two-dimensional thermal devices.

Robust crosscurrents, which flow opposite to the natural heat flux, have been predicted and observed in various systems, often linked to a chiral anomaly where charge and heat currents diverge. We introduce a nonmagnetic platform, a bilayer of parabolic optical potentials populated by two distinct two-dimensional robust topological insulators, that generates genuinely two-dimensional crosscurrents. These currents are protected by a new form of non-Abelian symmetry involving both spin and orbital degrees of freedom, termed bi-chiral symmetry. This bi-chiral protection allows for the coexistence of crosscurrents with finite longitudinal conductivity. We propose an implementation using ultracold atoms with internal states as an intrinsic two-dimensional topological insulator. The resulting nontrivial phase can be detected via longitudinal conductivity measurements, total-charge accumulation at the layer interface, or total-heat accumulation at the boundary with a Gaussian impurity.

Within Einstein gravity, the sufficient condition for this implies an upper bound on the Bondi mass $m$, specifically $m < (2\pi)^{-1}$. However, in gravitational theories characterized by a positive critical length $\ell$, the sufficient condition becomes necessary, resulting in a lower bound on the mass of the visible universe. This lower bound is approximately $4 \times 10^{50} \ell^5$, which, if $\ell$ is the Planck length, corresponds to the total mass currently observable. Consequently, these theories predict that light from distant sources will not reach null infinity only when the source's mass surpasses the total mass of what we can see. Furthermore, the sufficient condition for light to escape to null infinity translates to a scenario where light emitted closer to the source than to the center of gravitational attraction behaves as though it has escaped the source's gravitational influence, yet remains trapped by the gravitational field of the source itself. To fully characterize these scenarios, we employ the Gullstrand-Pendleton metric alongside a set of additional variables.

Specifically, the protocol operates within an atmospheric turbulent environment modeled by the Rytov approximation under weak conditions. The protocol's functionality is evaluated based on the mutual coherence between two locations with varying separations and the orbital angular momentum (OAM) cross-talk between different modes. We examine how varying distances and cross-talk levels influence the correlation between two sites, focusing on maximizing both mutual coherence and minimizing cross-talk to enhance the probability of successful protocol operation. Variations in height difference between the sources are analyzed to determine the optimal communication distance. Furthermore, we calculate the cross-talk angular spectrum arising from OAM mode impurities caused by atmospheric turbulence. These findings offer a clear perspective on the optimal communication distances feasible using OAM modes in atmospheric channels and outline a method for optimizing mutual coherence when such modes are used for optical communication between buildings with adjustable heights. This research underscores that the fundamental limit of cross-talk is governed by the asymptotic cross-talk angular spectrum. Additionally, the study considers a scenario where the cross-talk angle remains constant while the mutual coherence varies with distance, enabling optimal communication between two points at different heights. This optimal distance is explicitly expressed as a function of the OAM index and the height difference between the sources. Finally, we estimate the cross-talk induced by atmospheric turbulence using the standard deviation of intensities. The derived results on mutual coherence, cross-talk, and communication probabilities provide a clear framework for utilizing OAM modes in optical communication systems. Additionally, the methodologies presented can be applied to assess the performance of other free-space optical communication protocols. This analysis underscores that atmospheric turbulence affects the temporal evolution of cross-talk modes through a convolution process, causing different mode components to experience varying cross-talk effects. Consequently, in scenarios involving large height differences between the sources, the dominant cross-talk arises from higher cross-talk angles, which are often less sensitive to atmospheric turbulence compared to smaller cross-talk angles. This perspective aids in achieving optimal communication distances when employing OAM modes between structures of differing heights. However, it is noted that the estimated cross-talk angular spectrum requires verification through experimental data. The impact of atmospheric turbulence on the OAM mode's angular spectrum is characterized as a reduction in the mode's purity. Consequently, a more robust definition of cross-talk is proposed as the sum of powers of all other modes present in the angular spectrum, rather than simply excluding the fundamental mode. Over the last half-century, the World Wide Web has emerged as the most potent instrument for locating and absorbing information, with Google leading the way as the most effective and efficient resource for satisfying user inquiries through its renowned search engine. While Google offers unparalleled convenience, it inadvertently creates a barrier to accessing the vast array of additional tools available for the same purpose. Fortunately, the Google Glass API enables developers to build applications compatible with Google Glass, allowing users to leverage other information sources alongside Google's offerings. Although the API itself is straightforward, constructing a fully functional Glass app demands extensive time and effort. To address this challenge, we have developed a complete Google Glass application named "Vision," which focuses on information access and management. vision.googleglass.com serves as a comprehensive guide, explaining how to utilize the API and providing instructions for creating custom Glass apps. Furthermore, the Vision app demonstrates that integrating multiple search engines is straightforward, even for beginners using the Google Glass API. This project is dedicated to the open-source community, and we hope it serves as a valuable reference for future endeavors. The Vision application is now live on Google Glass.

Search engines play a critical role in locating and retrieving information, yet Google's API limitations restrict users to displaying only a single query result. To overcome this, Vision was created to facilitate searches across various sources and applications. As a practical implementation of the guides found on vision.googleglass.com, Vision allows users to perform multi-source queries and navigate their results. It features a customizable interface, supporting color customization for both the background and text. Additionally, Vision offers an "Auto Search" feature that automatically populates a list of recent searches, derived from the application's local database.

The core objective of this work is to illustrate how the Google Glass API functions and to provide a functional example of a Google Glass application. The developer has already built a similar app called "Ourba," and this project, "Vision," serves as a complementary reference. The app operates by storing recent search history in a local database, from which users can select and execute previous queries. Vision specifically targets Google Glass hardware and is designed to be user-friendly, supporting customizable color schemes to enhance the visual experience of displayed search results.

The app was developed using Java and the Google Glass API. Vision was installed on a physical Google Glass device for real-world testing, and the developer emphasizes that Vision acts as a launcher, capable of opening any Google Glass application or web page. The app was also evaluated on older Google Glass models, including the Glass Explorer Edition and Glass Enterprise

This study tackles the challenge of generating safe CAV trajectories in such environments, with a specific focus on preventing rear-end collisions when preceding HDVs approach yellow or red signal phases. We introduce a predictive control framework that utilizes a recursive least squares algorithm to estimate the real-time driving behavior of leading HDVs, subsequently applying this estimation to compute safety-conscious trajectories over a finite horizon. The efficacy of our proposed framework is verified through numerical simulations, which also contrast its performance against proportional integral (PI) control. simulations reveal that our framework outperforms PI control, especially when the preceding HDV maintains a constant speed. Furthermore, we examine vehicle stability under varying speed difference feedback gains and highlight the critical necessity of considering HDV deceleration capabilities. Under specific conditions, the paper offers guidance on optimizing the prediction horizon and feedback gains. Finally, simulations involving a platoon of CAVs and a single or multiple gap-following HDVs demonstrate the applicability and robustness of our framework. This work offers guidance for managing urban CAV travel under the prevailing condition of low CAV market penetration, aiming to enhance both safety and efficiency.

In recent years, there has been a surge in research regarding the integration of connected automated vehicles (CAVs) into current road networks. However, accurately estimating the states of non-cooperative human-driven vehicles (NVs) remains a significant hurdle. This paper addresses state estimation for leading NVs by modeling their driving dynamics as a linear system with time delays and process noise. An extended Kalman filter (EKF) is employed to estimate the state parameters and calculate the time delay, which is derived from the NV's driving behavior and potentially influenced by external factors like weather. Since the filtering process relies heavily on driver behavior, we analyze the impact of nonlinear driving patterns on EKF performance. Additionally, to mitigate the risks of rear-end collisions when leading NVs encounter a yellow light, we propose a safety control algorithm based on these state estimates. Unlike traditional PI control methods that rely on vehicle spacing and speed, our algorithm directly avoids potential crashes. Simulations and real-world tests validate the effectiveness of both the state estimator and the safety control algorithm.

We introduce a related yet distinct proposal: the conjecture should instead apply to particles possessing non-negative self-binding energy. While the simple convexity of $\Delta(q)$ is trivially satisfied if $c$ is sufficiently large, we show that $c$ can exceed unity in certain four-dimensional CFTs with a gravity dual, meaning the conjecture is non-trivial in those cases. # Introduction

Simulating quantum many-body systems is essential for understanding equilibrium states, non-equilibrium dynamics, and transient behavior. While traditional quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) methods are highly effective for many-body Monte Carlo simulations, they suffer from the sign problem when applied to certain interacting quantum systems. Consequently, developing a scalable and efficient method to bypass the sign problem is crucial for advancing the simulation of quantum many-body systems. Quantum imaginary time evolution (QITE) has been introduced as a promising solution to overcome this limitation.

As the name implies, QITE evolves quantum states according to the non-unitary operator $e^{-H\tau}$, where $H$ is the Hamiltonian and $\tau$ denotes imaginary time. This evolution is mathematically equivalent to the Gibbs state formation $e^{-H\tau}|\Psi_0\rangle \propto |\Psi(\beta)\rangle$ at inverse temperature $\beta=\tau$, assuming the initial state $|\Psi_0\rangle$ possesses no negative eigenvalues relative to $H$. Although QITE itself is non-unitary, it can be emulated by identifying a local Hamiltonian $H_{\rm eff}$ such that $e^{-H\tau}|\Psi_0\rangle \propto e^{-H_{\rm eff}\tau}|\Psi_0\rangle$. Because $H_{\rm eff}$ is local, it can be implemented using quantum circuits, enabling the simulation of Gibbs states.

novel approaches for integration with high shares of renewable energy sources. Volatility in power generation from these sources introduces challenges that can only be mitigated by flexible supply-side options, such as demand-side response (DSR). By incentivizing consumers to adjust their electricity usage in response to market signals or grid operational needs, grid stability can be maintained without compromising service quality. This can be achieved through short-term measures like load shedding during outages or, more desirably, by encouraging users to voluntarily shift, reduce, or delay non-essential loads during peak demand periods. Also referred to as demand response or flexible loads, DSR involves time-shiftable, interruptible, or curtailable loads that can be directly or indirectly optimized for the grid. Whether managed by utilities, independent system operators, or system aggregators, the objective is to influence end-user behavior to lower overall costs. The term 'demand-side management' encompasses all strategies and programs designed to actively manage consumer load behavior to support utility and grid operations. These programs utilize various pricing and incentive schemes to motivate users to alter, reduce, or shift consumption during peak times, ultimately enhancing the efficiency and reliability of power generation, distribution, and consumption. Additionally, they offer the potential to delay or avoid significant infrastructure investments in both supply and demand sectors. Historically, supply-side solutions have been the primary method for balancing supply and demand, typically achieved by activating new power plants or importing power. However, with the rising penetration of intermittent renewables like wind and solar, supply-side flexibility is becoming increasingly volatile. Consequently, greater attention is now required to develop demand-side strategies for increasing system efficiency. While early attempts to implement DSR programs date back to the 1970s and 1980s, driven by supply shortages and the absence of real-time pricing, the expansion of smart grid and Internet of Things (IoT) technologies has recently facilitated more effective demand-side management. These advancements enable utilities to better understand, control, and incentivize end-user load behavior. Through real-time pricing and demand signal monitoring, utilities can encourage load shifting and reduction, thereby improving load factor, reducing peak demand, and lowering the total cost of service. Ultimately, this research work aims to design and simulate a demand-side response system, with a specific focus on an office building scenario. Utilizing IoT-based load monitoring, the proposed scheme targets the short-term optimization of total energy costs via real-time load management. A key innovation of this work is the integration of machine learning-based load pattern recognition to categorize and interrupt

spectroscopy to track the seasonal development and decay of large, warm vortices located poleward of approximately 70° latitude in the upper atmosphere (pressures greater than 2 microbars). These vortices are shaped by strong seasonal solar illumination variations and the rapid rotation of the planet. The warm gas trapped within them rises from deeper layers, creating distinct horizontal structures visible when projected into the upper, optically thin regions of Cassini's observation zone. A wave-driven heat flux, resulting from the interaction between thermal tides and a standing tidal wave established by planetary rotation, is identified as the primary driver of vortex warming. This mechanism accounts for more than 90% of the thermal energy trapped inside the vortices at the probed pressure levels, far surpassing the heat trapped within mid-latitude warm spots and validating earlier localized tide-model predictions. The timing of the warming peak is controlled by the phase of local tidal heating as it varies with latitude due to Coriolis forces and by the rate of solar forcing's seasonal change. At the 6° per day rate of Saturn's rotation, the heating peak is expected 6° (roughly 1 Earth radius) poleward of the summer pole; however, the observed peak formed at 69.5° latitude, and at higher latitudes, vortices either failed to develop or were advected past the observation window before they could warm. This latitudinal discrepancy is explained by the enhanced mixing at the poles during winter hemisphere darkness, which removes the standing tidal wave that generates vortex heat. Consequently, thermal vortices are anticipated to persist until they cover 70° latitude, with their warming peaking during the solstice. Additionally, the mass trapped within these vortices is estimated, and the time required for air to drain back to lower altitudes is calculated, suggesting that these features are long-lived, holding between 10^11 and 10^12 kg of mass. The source of this mass remains an open question. It is suggested that vortices begin cool and trap ambient air as they form, with subsequent warming caused by the wave-driven heat flux. An alternative mechanism is also proposed: external forcing could stretch and fold ambient air to create a pre-existing warm, dense pocket of gas that later traps heat. Finally, Cassini detected enhanced electron temperatures and enhanced electron densities just outside the path where these vortices were advected, offering a potential, though not certain, link to the enhanced electron heating seen

By analyzing the B1 rock-salt termination of cubic MgO, we employed a variational multi-scale (VMS) approach combined with the projected augmented wave (PAW) method to investigate how different terminations affect electronic structure and work function. Our results indicate that varying the number of vacuum layers and $k$-point sampling has a substantial impact on both the density of states and work function; however, these effects can be mitigated by adjusting either parameter while holding the other constant. Ultimately, we determined the work functions for all computed MgO surface terminations. These calculations demonstrate that MgO surface states arise from unsaturated ions at the interface, causing deviations in the surface potential that elevate the work function relative to bulk values. Furthermore, our computed bulk and interfacial work functions align closely with existing literature. Considerable differences in work functions across various MgO heterostructures suggest that charge accumulation at interfaces alters electron confinement and modifies the overall electronic structure. Additionally, the PAW method effectively yielded bulk magnesium values for both valence and total densities of states. This study offers valuable insights into designing two-dimensional (2D) materials with tailored surface terminations and work functions, which is essential for developing efficient magnetic tunnel junctions and tunneling field-effect transistors. Future studies should incorporate spin-polarization and spin-orbit coupling to provide a more comprehensive understanding of MgO surface physics. Additionally, extending these calculations to other B1 rock-salt materials with rock-salt, metallic, vacuum, and oxide terminations would yield important findings for spintronic applications involving MgO. Finally, investigating the adsorption of atoms or molecules on MgO surfaces could further elucidate their potential in chemical and biological sensing. We hope these findings assist in better engineering the electronic properties of 2D MgO materials and their heterostructures. We further demonstrate an exact finite-size scaling of the Bose-Einstein condensation (BEC) fraction, which serves as a definitive characteristic of these states. The exact time evolution of the condensate is driven by small energy gaps between quasi-momentum bands, which are themselves determined by the transverse extent of the gas. We provide a theoretical framework for the exact dynamics of the condensate fraction, emphasizing that it stems from the multi-banded structure of the spectrum in interacting one-dimensional Bose gases. This non-equilibrium phenomenon offers a viable non-equilibrium approach to generating and manipulating high condensate fractions in one-dimensional Bose gases, a capability that could be crucial for the exact control of interactions via the BEC-BCS transition in the Baldwin-Weiner moiré lattice. This non-equilibrium dynamics of the condensate fraction in one-dimensional Bose gases represents a significant topic for both fundamental research and technological advancement.

to probe the structural, dynamical, and compositional characteristics of materials. Although the vast potential of spectroscopy remains largely untapped, the choice of probe photon energy is often arbitrary. However, this selection is far from random, as specific regions of a material's excitation spectrum offer distinct advantages and drawbacks. Ideally, researchers would target spectral regions with high resolution, fast dynamics, and relevant composition; yet, no single photon energy can simultaneously optimize all three factors for every material. Consequently, understanding excitation spectra—often overlooked in favor of other analytical aspects—is essential for rationally choosing the optimal light source. In this work, we present a computational framework designed to aid in the analysis of excitation spectra and rational photon energy selection. By employing a diverse array of electronic structure and many-body simulation techniques, we demonstrate the capabilities of our approach using copper as a test case. Furthermore, we provide accessible online examples of these methods at https://davidshen2002.github.io/CEST/. We argue that, much like traditional analysis, the study of excitation spectra is vital for advancing both fundamental science and technological innovation. Additionally, we show that the methods presented here can be applied to a wide range of questions, from basic material analysis to inverse problems where target properties are known a priori. Both the range of techniques and their application to practical problems make our work particularly relevant for the photo-emission community. Finally, we highlight the accessibility of these methods, as they rely on widely available first-principles tools.

Recent advances in ultrafast x-ray generation have enabled new forms of x-ray spectroscopy capable of probing matter with unprecedented elemental, structural, and compositional resolution on femtosecond timescales. These capabilities are now being harnessed to investigate the most fundamental questions in physics, including many-body dynamics, while also addressing diverse material science challenges such as studying molten matter, conducting x-ray emission tomography, and performing material analysis under extreme conditions. Although these methods are relatively novel, they are inherently linked to the broader field of sum rules, which are deeply rooted in both theoretical frameworks and experimental applications. Therefore, it is crucial to recognize how these emerging techniques expand the frontiers of sum rule analysis. This discussion will be supported by recent case studies ranging from optical to hard x-ray emission spectra.
