We address Multi-Armed Bandits (MABs) with a non-stationary component, where optimal choices and pull counts must adapt over time without direct access to the optimal policy. This problem appears in scenarios like online content recommendation, where a platform must manage multiple content items (arms) to maximize user rewards (e.g., time spent, ad clicks) over a horizon $T$. Unlike standard MABs, here the expected reward function and the count distribution for at least one arm change over time. To minimize regret, it is necessary to distinguish between Type 1 arms (those with changing distributions) and Type 2 arms (those with unchanging distributions). To optimize a arbitrary allocation policy's performance, we propose a simple "2-of-3" strategy. This method separates the arms into two distinct groups, each forming a separate multi-arm bandit problem, and tests a hypothesis to identify Type 1 arms. We prove a bound on the regret of any policy given this information and show how the Type 1/Type 2 classification lowers this bound compared to not having such information. We also provide a bound on the regret of the optimal policy, which performs even better than the generic bound. Our evaluation on both synthetic and real-world datasets confirms that our algorithm can identify arm type changes and achieve up to a 4x reduction in regret.

This study investigates the mathematical foundations of GCNNs by analyzing Stacked-Convolutional Neural Networks (Stack-CNNs), a specific type of GCNN applied to one-dimensional data. By examining the forward passes, gradient computations, and matrix decompositions of Stack-CNNs, we demonstrate that these models are equivalent to performing conventional neural network operations on transformed input and weight matrices. When the convolution kernels are square, this transformation corresponds to a discrete Fourier transform (DFT); consequently, a DFT-based Stack-CNN can be viewed as an optimized, parameterized variant of a finite DFT. However, if the kernels are non-square, the transformation matrix derived from backward passes generally lacks an analytical inverse, causing the Stack-CNN to function as a latent basis transformation with uniquely learnable parameters. This finding offers fresh insights into the operation of GCNNs and suggests potential strategies for optimizing their convolutional kernels. Harmonics, defined as a collection of functions mapping integers to real numbers, are characterized by the property that the sum of any two harmonics yields another harmonic. Huygens and Varignon demonstrated in the 17th century that the sine function belongs to this set. Through complex analysis, we generalize harmonics to the complex domain and derive an extended definition of generalized harmonics. We illustrate a profound relationship between these generalized harmonics and software development, specifically focusing on functional programs.

Functional programs, created via higher-order and inductive type theory, exhibit a duality between their types and implementations, with this correspondence being made explicit through the Curry-Howard isomorphism. Similarly, type signatures and their computational meanings in Haskell are connected through the lens of type classed higher-order abstract syntax. Leveraging these perspectives, we employ the so-called harmonic method to demonstrate that functional programs are composed of harmonics, revealing the intrinsic software harmonic law.

The concept of a harmonic program, grounded in type signatures and derived from functional programs, is built upon the signature of a functional program, its type, and the assumptions of its type. A functional program qualifies as a harmonic program when its type and all associated type inferences are strictly monotonic and associative, respectively. Utilizing type classed higher-order abstract syntax, we show that this concept of harmonic programs provides a fresh interpretation of type classedness. Additionally, we derive the concepts of harmonic functions and programs from those of harmonic points and lines.

Low-dose computed tomography (CT) acquisition is increasingly common in clinical settings, yet it often results in noisy images that compromise diagnostic value. Deep learning-based denoising techniques have shown remarkable success in restoring normal-dose image quality from low-dose scans. Among these, cycleGAN has gained popularity as an unsupervised method for such translation tasks. Despite its advantages, cycleGAN has a crucial drawback: it requires two distinct data distributions, necessitating that the target distribution be well-defined. A primary objective of the High-Luminosity LHC and future hadron colliders is the discovery of heavy resonances, a process that could potentially involve EW boson decay. This paper explores the feasibility of producing resonance candidates through charged and neutral weak boson fusion, as well as Drell-Lanew processes, utilizing the EW boson collider effect in hadron colliders. Although this benefit is well-established for model-free approaches, we show that using a single learned dynamics model across multiple tasks can have a detrimental impact. This study investigates multi-task model-based reinforcement learning, where the model serves as an implicit curriculum by allowing agents to focus on one task at a time while utilizing a shared representation of the environment. We analyze the optimal model capacity required for effective multi-task learning and present findings that contradict the hypothesis that larger capacity is always beneficial. Instead, we observe that excessive capacity causes the agent to overfit to a specific task, whereas insufficient capacity prevents it from capturing all tasks equally. To address this, we propose a square root scaling of the total task count for intermediate capacity models capable of handling multiple similar tasks. Our numerical results confirm these findings and demonstrate that the recommended model capacity achieves performance comparable to the best individual task's result while simultaneously learning four distinct tasks. We further illustrate that this method effectively learns shared dynamics while maintaining separate reward functions for each task. To our knowledge, this is the first work to both identify the problem of inappropriate shared dynamics in multi-task model-based RL and provide both theoretical analysis and numerical validation of the issue along with its solutions. This work is inspired by the model capacity findings in Model-Free multi-task learning by Hessel et al.

In reinforcement learning, it is common practice to train agents on multiple tasks simultaneously by combining their loss functions. While this approach enables agents to perform well on any of the learned tasks, it risks causing the agent to "forget" how to execute tasks it has not seen recently. We investigate whether the agent can retain knowledge of unseen tasks if trained on a sequence of tasks rather than a batch. Specifically, we focus on model-based RL using critic-only architectures, where the model predicts the next state. We provide a theoretical explanation for the difficulty of learning from sequences of tasks and how it arises from the need for the model to accurately predict both states and rewards. Additionally, we examine the effects of adding an additional output layer, increasing capacity, and employing actor-critic methods. Since our work relies on a simplified setting of linear functions and diagonal covariance, we also conduct extensive experiments with non-linear networks to validate our findings.

These proofs share significant similarities and employ nearly identical techniques. To clarify these connections, we present a unified framework that offers a pedagogically accessible overview of the subject while maintaining mathematical rigor. This approach utilizes model theory, specifically the notion of arithmetical definability and the representation of recursive functions, to illuminate the relationships between these theorems. This paper aims to provide researchers and educators with a comprehensive and unified viewpoint on these developments in mathematical logic from the 1930s and beyond, facilitating a deeper understanding of the subject.

Sequential sampling design is utilized when the total population is unknown prior to the study, allowing units to be selected individually or with a matching algorithm for successive batches. This paper presents a new approach for obtaining a sequential probability sample that ensures the inclusion probability is proportional to each unit's size on a specific variable, while also achieving spatial balance among all units within a defined study area. This technique is particularly valuable for developing auxiliary-variable-assisted sampling methods, which can significantly reduce variance and enhance the efficiency of estimates for population parameters. Furthermore, the method is applicable to spatially balancing any entity, whether it be a point, line, polygon, or even the presence/absence of a species. In this work, spatial balance is measured using a method originally developed for ecology to assess species co-occurrence.

Since numerous image hypotheses often align with both the measurements and prior knowledge, the objective shifts from identifying a single optimal solution to exploring the range of probable hypotheses by sampling the posterior distribution. This paper introduces a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN capable of generating multiple such posterior samples. In contemporary imaging, sensors capture data across vast dimensions, necessitating algorithms that can integrate these measurements into actionable insights. Meanwhile, in generative modeling, there is a growing emphasis on techniques that can conditionally sample from data distributions. This work examines sampling from conditional distributions in both deterministic and stochastic settings, showing that they can be formulated as an optimal transport problem solvable through optimal score matching. We assess the approach on conditional inversion tasks such as MRI reconstruction, colorization, and super-resolution. A key advantage of this method is its ability to handle high-dimensional conditional distributions—even when only a subset of variables is observed—without requiring extensive data.

Imaging systems frequently suffer from missing or corrupted measurements due to hardware or software failures. Traditional conditional inference seeks a single solution, but in imaging, multiple hypotheses often satisfy the observed data and prior knowledge equally well. Consequently, it is preferable to explore this solution space rather than converge on one point. This article presents a conditional Markov Neural Operator that can conditionally simulate such posterior distributions. The model combines a conditional flow conditional on an initial network with a conditional flow conditioned on a conditional distribution, termed the Conditional Neural Operator (CNO). We test the CNO on imaging applications including MRI reconstruction, colorization, and super-resolution. The model achieves performance and diversity similar to other state-of-the-art techniques while offering greater flexibility.

This study introduces a cooperative, adaptive THz FSO communication framework designed to enhance link reliability and maintain connectivity under adverse atmospheric conditions. In this model, a source user (SU) directs its adaptive THz FSO beam toward a neighboring user (NU), which then relays data to the destination user (DU). Statistical analyses of atmospheric attenuation and scintillation confirm the system's potential for sustained high-throughput. Simulation results compare direct and cooperative communication schemes across varying atmospheric states, assessing average end-to-end data rates, link reliability, and the impact of SU-NU channel misalignment on the end-to-end connection. Furthermore, an optimized adaptive cooperation model is proposed and validated through simulations. These findings confirm that the cooperative, adaptive communication system significantly improves reliability and end-to-end data rates, particularly when the NU is within line-of-sight of the DU and atmospheric turbulence is present. Additionally, the system proves more robust against THz beam misalignment errors than NU position estimation inaccuracies, effectively mitigating the impacts of atmospheric turbulence and mist. Finally, the model is extended to address full duplex communication scenarios.
Additionally, this paper introduces a cooperative, adaptive free-space optical (FSO) communication system utilizing a nonlinear amplify-and-forward (NAF) technique to achieve maximum entropy in the mutual information of both direct and cooperative end-to-end links, thereby optimizing average end-to-end data throughput. The study derives the end-to-end channel statistics for the proposed configuration and determines the optimal threshold SNRs analytically and numerically across various atmospheric conditions. The research confirms that the adaptive threshold NAF (ATNAF) technique yields higher reliability and throughput than the direct scheme in misty atmospheres, while the cooperative scheme with a threshold relay (THR) achieves greater reliability and throughput in turbulent conditions. Moreover, the adaptive threshold NAF (ATNAF) method enhances both reliability and end-to-end data rates more effectively than the direct scheme when mist is present, and compared to the THR scheme when turbulence occurs. It is also verified that the ATNAF technique maintains higher end-to-end data rates and reliability than both the direct and THR schemes under combined mist and turbulent conditions. Finally, the system is extended to support full duplex communication.

Because an FRB's observed properties depend on both its intrinsic characteristics and the intervening interstellar medium (ISM), analyzing high-time-resolution data can reveal information about the ISM. Precision nowcasting, which covers short-term predictions up to two hours, is essential for mitigating extreme weather events. Although data assimilation remains the gold standard for numerical weather models, these systems often fail to capture rapid weather changes and struggle with lead times exceeding 90 minutes. Probabilistic prediction remains a key objective, and model ensembles are a common strategy to address both issues. However, generating reliable ensembles requires significant data, and optimizing small models for specific tasks remains an open challenge. This paper examines the transferability of a point-forecasting convolutional neural network (CNN) optimized for 15-minute lead times to other prediction horizons. Although the primary goal was not precipitation nowcasting, the resulting CNN demonstrated improved precision for forecasts up to 60 minutes ahead. Further analysis reveals that increasing network depth and reducing the input context both enhance performance across different lead times. This study aims to inspire strategies for optimizing deep learning models for small, probabilistic forecasting systems tailored to specific tasks and lead times.

### 1 Introduction

Automatic Speech Translation (AST) seeks to convert spoken utterances in one language into text in another. In multi-language and real-world scenarios, it is impractical to train models only on in-domain data due to limited availability and the need to handle diverse domains. Consequently, developing zero-shot AST, which addresses unseen language pairs and domains, is crucial. This paper focuses on solving zero-shot problems within an end-to-end AST framework.

Recent advancements in sequence-to-sequence models and attention mechanisms have enabled sophisticated AST models that process both audio and text through a unified architecture. However, these models typically require extensive training data for a specific language pair and domain, a constraint that is particularly challenging in multi-language environments where data is often scarce. Although models trained on rich in-domain data achieve strong results, they often fail to generalize to zero-shot language pairs and domains.

This study achieves linear complexity, $O(N)$, for potential evaluation using source densities on the boundary, $L$, and the Gaussian measure, $\mu$, by applying the boundary integral formulation of Newtonian potentials and executing boundary quadrature via the boundary-filling algorithm introduced in our prior research. Additionally, we directly compute the cumulative distribution function (CDF) and potentially valuable quantiles of $\mu$ over the entire domain. We validate the proposed direct quantile computation against the widely used rejection method for comparing outcomes across different densities. Through a value study, we optimize the source boundary quadrature's resolution, ensuring the algorithm's total complexity is governed solely by the boundary quadrature step. We demonstrate that for any domain with a simply or doubly connected boundary, a minimum of two source boundaries are necessary to evaluate potentials with the desired accuracy. Finally, we apply the method to calculate gravitational potentials and quantiles for various galaxy models, comparing the results with established literature findings. The code is available on GitHub under the license: https://github.com/AmirHosseinDehghan/NewtonianPotentials/blob/main/LICENSE.
